abstract: Although the visual and auditory systems share the same basic tasks of informing an organism about its environment, most con(cid:173) nectionist work on hearing to date has been devoted to the very different problem of speech recognition . VVe believe that the most fundamental task of the auditory system is the analysis of acoustic signals into components corresponding to individual sound sources, which Bregman has called auditory scene analysis . Computational and connectionist work on auditory scene analysis is reviewed, and the outline of a general model that includes these approaches is described.

paragraphs: This paper examines hearing as the task of organizing acoustic input into representations of individual sound sources. The authors argue that this process, called auditory scene analysis, is fundamental to how an organism learns about its environment through sound. Their focus is the organization of the acoustic scene, extending the discussion beyond recognizing speech.

The work reviews computational and connectionist approaches to auditory scene analysis. In this framing, the central question is how components of a received acoustic signal can be assigned to the sources that produced them. That question links hearing to the broader perceptual task of identifying meaningful entities in an environment from incoming sensory information.

Building on the reviewed approaches, the authors describe the outline of a general model that includes them. The contribution is therefore a synthesis and proposed modeling framework. Its value is to place separate computational approaches within a shared account of source organization and to identify auditory scene analysis as a central target for neural-network models of hearing.
summary.tldr: The paper reviews neural and computational approaches to separating sound sources and outlines a general auditory scene analysis model.

title: Connectionist Models for Auditory Scene Analysis

abstract: Optimal Brain Damage (OBD) is a method for reducing the num(cid:173) ber of weights in a neural network. OBD estimates the increase in cost function if weights are pruned and is a valid approximation if the learning algorithm has converged into a local minimum. On the other hand it is often desirable to terminate the learning pro(cid:173) cess before a local minimum is reached (early stopping). In this paper we show that OBD estimates the increase in cost function incorrectly if the network is not in a local minimum. We also show how OBD can be extended such that it can be used in connec(cid:173) tion with early stopping. We call this new approach Early Brain Damage, EBD. EBD also allows to revive already pruned weights. We demonstrate the improvements achieved by EBD using three publicly available data sets.

On the other hand it is often desirable to terminate the learning pro(cid:173) cess before a local minimum is reached (early stopping). paragraphs: Pruning reduces a neural network's size by removing weights. Optimal Brain Damage chooses weights using an approximation to the increase in the cost function caused by removing them. That approximation assumes training has reached a local minimum, creating a conflict with early stopping, which deliberately ends learning before that point.

The paper shows that Optimal Brain Damage estimates the cost increase incorrectly when the network is away from a local minimum. It then extends the method to handle networks stopped early. The resulting approach, Early Brain Damage, makes the pruning calculation compatible with the state in which early stopping leaves the network.

Early Brain Damage also permits previously pruned weights to be revived, so a removal decision need not remain permanent. The authors demonstrate improvements on three publicly available datasets. The central contribution is to resolve a specific mismatch between a pruning approximation and a training procedure. By adapting the cost estimate to early stopping, the method supports using those two ways of controlling a network together.
summary.tldr: Early Brain Damage corrects pruning estimates for networks stopped before a local minimum and allows removed weights to be restored.

title: Early Brain Damage

abstract: Given unlimited computational resources, it is best to use a crite(cid:173) rion of minimal expected generalisation error to select a model and determine its parameters. However, it may be worthwhile to sac(cid:173) rifice some generalisation performance for higher learning speed. A method for quantifying sub-optimality is set out here, so that this choice can be made intelligently. Furthermore, the method is applicable to a broad class of models, including the ultra-fast memory-based methods such as RAMnets. This brings the added benefit of providing, for the first time, the means to analyse the generalisation properties of such models in a Bayesian framework .

paragraphs: This paper asks how to judge the predictive cost of choosing a model that learns quickly. With unlimited computation, the proposed ideal is to select a model and its parameters by minimizing expected generalization error. In practical choices, however, faster learning may justify giving up some performance on unseen data.

The authors set out a method for quantifying this departure from the ideal. That turns a loose preference for speed into a more explicit tradeoff: a model can be evaluated in terms of the generalization performance sacrificed to obtain faster learning. The method is intended to support an informed choice between those competing priorities.

Its scope includes a broad class of models, particularly very fast memory-based methods such as RAMnets. The abstract identifies an additional contribution for these methods: a way to analyze their generalization properties within a Bayesian framework. This connects fast memory-based learning to a formal account of expected predictive performance. The paper's significance lies in making the cost of computational convenience something that can be analyzed rather than merely assumed.
summary.tldr: A Bayesian analysis quantifies the generalization performance sacrificed for faster learning in RAMnets and other models.

title: The Generalisation Cost of RAMnets

abstract: In macaque inferotemporal cortex (IT), neurons have been found to re(cid:173) spond selectively to complex shapes while showing broad tuning ("in(cid:173) variance") with respect to stimulus transformations such as translation and scale changes and a limited tuning to rotation in depth. Training monkeys with novel, paperclip-like objects, Logothetis et al. 9 could in(cid:173) vestigate whether these invariance properties are due to experience with exhaustively many transformed instances of an object or if there are mech(cid:173) anisms that allow the cells to show response invariance also to previously unseen instances of that object. They found object-selective cells in an(cid:173) terior IT which exhibited limited invariance to various transformations after training with single object views. While previous models accounted for the tuning of the cells for rotations in depth and for their selectiv(cid:173) ity to a specific object relative to a population of distractor objects,14,1 the model described here attempts to explain in a biologically plausible way the additional properties of translation and size invariance. Using the same stimuli as in the experiment, we find that model IT neurons exhibit invariance properties which closely parallel those of real neurons. Simulations show that the model is capable of unsupervised learning of view-tuned neurons. We thank Peter Dayan, Marcus Dill, Shimon Edelman, Nikos Logothetis, Jonathan Mumick and Randy O'Reilly for useful discussions and comments. 216

paragraphs: The paper studies how neurons can remain selective for an object while tolerating changes in its position or size. The motivating experiments found object-selective cells in macaque inferotemporal cortex after training with single views of unfamiliar, paperclip-like objects. Those cells showed some tolerance to transformations they had not exhaustively encountered during training.

Earlier models addressed selectivity among objects and tuning to rotations in depth. This model seeks a biologically plausible explanation for the additional tolerance to translation and size changes. The distinction matters because recognizing a particular view and continuing to respond when that view moves or changes scale are related but separate properties.

Using the same stimuli as the motivating experiment, the authors find that model neurons show transformation tolerances closely resembling those of real neurons. Simulations also demonstrate unsupervised learning of neurons tuned to object views. The findings support a model account in which view selectivity coexists with limited invariance, without requiring exhaustive training on every transformed instance.
summary.tldr: A biologically motivated model reproduces limited position and size invariance in neurons selective for object views.

title: Just One View: Invariances in Inferotemporal Cell Tuning

abstract: Local linear regression performs very well in many low-dimensional forecasting problems. In high-dimensional spaces, its performance typically decays due to the well-known "curse-of-dimensionality". A possible way to approach this problem is by varying the "shape" of the weighting kernel. In this work we suggest a new, data-driven method to estimating the optimal kernel shape. Experiments us(cid:173) ing an artificially generated data set and data from the UC Irvine repository show the benefits of kernel shaping.
originalAbstract: Local linear regression performs very well in many low-dimensional forecasting problems. In high-dimensional spaces, its performance typically decays due to the well-known "curse-of-dimensionality". A possible way to approach this problem is by varying the "shape" of the weighting kernel. In this work we suggest a new, data-driven method to estimating the optimal kernel shape. Experiments us(cid:173) ing an artificially generated data set and data from the UC Irvine repository show the benefits of kernel shaping.

paragraphs: The paper studies local linear regression, which makes predictions by fitting linear relationships in a neighborhood of interest. A weighting kernel determines how observations contribute to that local fit. Although the method often works well for low-dimensional forecasting, its performance typically deteriorates as the number of dimensions increases.

The authors investigate changing the shape of the weighting kernel as a possible response to this difficulty. Kernel shape governs how the local neighborhood is weighted across the input space. They propose a data-driven method for estimating an optimal shape, allowing this aspect of the regression procedure to be chosen using the observed data.

Experiments use both an artificially generated dataset and data from the UC Irvine repository. The reported results show benefits from kernel shaping. This supports adapting neighborhood geometry as a useful component of local linear regression in the tested settings. The approach addresses an aspect of the high-dimensional problem through weighting, without establishing that kernel shaping eliminates the curse of dimensionality.
summary.tldr: A data-driven method adapts weighting-kernel shape and shows benefits for local linear regression on synthetic and repository data.

title: Optimal Kernel Shapes for Local Linear Regression

abstract: Novelty detection involves modeling the normal behaviour of a sys(cid:173) tem hence enabling detection of any divergence from normality. It has potential applications in many areas such as detection of ma(cid:173) chine damage or highlighting abnormal features in medical data. One approach is to build a hypothesis estimating the support of the normal data i.e. constructing a function which is positive in the region where the data is located and negative elsewhere. Recently kernel methods have been proposed for estimating the support of a distribution and they have performed well in practice - training involves solution of a quadratic programming problem. In this pa(cid:173) per we propose a simpler kernel method for estimating the support based on linear programming. The method is easy to implement and can learn large datasets rapidly. We demonstrate the method on medical and fault detection datasets. 1

paragraphs: Novelty detection models normal system behavior so that departures from it can be identified. One approach estimates the support of the normal-data distribution: the region where normal observations occur. A decision function then takes positive values in that region and negative values outside it, providing a way to flag unusual observations.

The paper proposes a kernel method for this task whose training problem uses linear programming. The kernel approaches discussed as predecessors instead require quadratic programming. Changing the optimization formulation is the central contribution, while the goal remains learning a function that separates the normal-data region from its surroundings.

The authors describe the method as straightforward to implement and capable of learning rapidly from large datasets. They demonstrate it on medical and fault-detection datasets, connecting the formulation to two settings where identifying abnormal observations is useful. The stated findings support the practicality of this simpler training approach; the abstract's application examples concern detecting departures from normality rather than establishing what caused each detected departure.
summary.tldr: A kernel novelty detector uses linear programming to learn normal-data regions with simple implementation and rapid training on large datasets.

title: A Linear Programming Approach to Novelty Detection

abstract: Although the study of clustering is centered around an intuitively compelling goal, it has been very di(cid:14)cult to develop a uni(cid:12)ed framework for reasoning about it at a technical level, and pro- foundly diverse approaches to clustering abound in the research community. Here we suggest a formal perspective on the di(cid:14)culty in (cid:12)nding such a uni(cid:12)cation, in the form of an impossibility theo- rem: for a set of three simple properties, we show that there is no clustering function satisfying all three. Relaxations of these prop- erties expose some of the interesting (and unavoidable) trade-o(cid:11)s at work in well-studied clustering techniques such as single-linkage, sum-of-pairs, k-means, and k-median.

Here we suggest a formal perspective on the di(cid:14)culty in (cid:12)nding such a uni(cid:12)cation, in the form of an impossibility theo- rem: for a set of three simple properties, we show that there is no clustering function satisfying all three. Relaxations of these prop- erties expose some of the interesting (and unavoidable) trade-o(cid:11)s at work in well-studied clustering techniques such as single-linkage, sum-of-pairs, k-means, and k-median.

paragraphs: Clustering has an appealing informal goal, but the paper asks why it has been difficult to place diverse clustering methods within one technical framework. Its approach is to examine properties a clustering function might be expected to satisfy. This makes the issue one of compatible mathematical requirements rather than simply competing algorithm designs.

The central result is an impossibility theorem: no clustering function can satisfy all three of the properties considered together. The conclusion is specific to that combination of requirements. It does not say that useful clustering is impossible; it establishes that these particular expectations cannot all be met by the same function.

The authors then relax the properties to reveal tradeoffs in single-linkage, sum-of-pairs, k-means, and k-median methods. This provides a way to interpret differences among familiar techniques through the requirements they accommodate or give up. The theorem's significance is that some disagreements between clustering approaches reflect unavoidable choices within the formal framework, rather than deficiencies that a single improved algorithm could eliminate.
summary.tldr: No clustering function satisfies the paper's three proposed properties simultaneously, exposing unavoidable tradeoffs among familiar methods.

title: An Impossibility Theorem for Clustering

abstract: Henry Markram Brain Mind Institute EPFL, Lausanne, Switzerland henry.markram@epﬂ.ch A key challenge for neural modeling is to explain how a continuous stream of multi-modal input from a rapidly changing environment can be processed by stereotypical recurrent circuits of integrate-and-ﬁre neurons in real-time. We propose a new computational model that is based on principles of high dimensional dynamical systems in combination with statistical learning theory. It can be implemented on generic evolved or found recurrent circuitry.
originalAbstract: Henry Markram Brain Mind Institute EPFL, Lausanne, Switzerland henry.markram@epﬂ.ch A key challenge for neural modeling is to explain how a continuous stream of multi-modal input from a rapidly changing environment can be processed by stereotypical recurrent circuits of integrate-and-ﬁre neurons in real-time. We propose a new computational model that is based on principles of high dimensional dynamical systems in combination with statistical learning theory. It can be implemented on generic evolved or found recurrent circuitry.

paragraphs: The paper addresses how neural circuits could process an ongoing stream of sensory information while the environment changes rapidly. The input is multimodal, so the problem involves multiple kinds of information arriving continuously. The computational challenge is to explain how recurrent circuits of integrate-and-fire neurons can handle this stream in real time.

The proposed model brings together principles from high-dimensional dynamical systems and statistical learning theory. The dynamical perspective concerns the evolving activity of a recurrent circuit, while the learning perspective connects that activity to computation. Together, these perspectives frame neural processing as something that happens through a circuit's changing state as inputs arrive.

A central feature of the proposal is that it can be implemented on generic recurrent circuitry, including circuitry that has evolved or is otherwise available. This makes the relationship between ordinary recurrent neural organization and real-time computation the main contribution. The abstract presents a computational model for this challenge, rather than an experimental demonstration of particular performance levels.
summary.tldr: The paper proposes a model combining dynamical systems and learning theory for real-time computation in generic recurrent neural circuits.

title: A Model for Real-Time Computation in Generic Neural Microcircuits

abstract: First-order Markov models have been successfully applied to many prob- lems, for example in modeling sequential data using Markov chains, and modeling control problems using the Markov decision processes (MDP) formalism. If a ﬁrst-order Markov model’s parameters are estimated from data, the standard maximum likelihood estimator considers only the ﬁrst-order (single-step) transitions. But for many problems, the ﬁrst- order conditional independence assumptions are not satisﬁed, and as a re- sult the higher order transition probabilities may be poorly approximated. Motivated by the problem of learning an MDP’s parameters for control, we propose an algorithm for learning a ﬁrst-order Markov model that ex- plicitly takes into account higher order interactions during training. Our algorithm uses an optimization criterion different from maximum likeli- hood, and allows us to learn models that capture longer range effects, but without giving up the beneﬁts of using ﬁrst-order Markov models. Our experimental results also show the new algorithm outperforming conven- tional maximum likelihood estimation in a number of control problems where the MDP’s parameters are estimated from data.

paragraphs: First-order Markov models describe transitions using the current state, and they are widely used for sequential modeling and control. Standard maximum-likelihood estimation fits their parameters using single-step transitions. This paper examines what happens when the data do not satisfy the model’s first-order conditional independence assumptions.

In that situation, a model fitted to single-step transitions may approximate longer-range transition probabilities poorly. The authors propose a different training objective that explicitly accounts for higher-order interactions while retaining a first-order model. The approach changes how the parameters are learned so that longer-range effects influence the resulting model.

The motivation is learning Markov decision process parameters for control, where consequences unfold across multiple transitions. Experiments show that the proposed method outperforms conventional maximum-likelihood estimation on a number of control problems with parameters learned from data. The contribution is a way to preserve the benefits of first-order models while training them to better capture effects extending beyond one step.
summary.tldr: Training first-order Markov models with higher-order interactions improves results over conventional maximum likelihood in several control problems.

title: Learning first-order Markov models for control

abstract: Finding the sparsest, or minimum ℓ0-norm, representation of a signal given an overcomplete dictionary of basis vectors is an important prob- lem in many application domains. Unfortunately, the required optimiza- tion problem is often intractable because there is a combinatorial increase in the number of local minima as the number of candidate basis vectors increases. This deﬁciency has prompted most researchers to instead min- imize surrogate measures, such as the ℓ1-norm, that lead to more tractable computational methods. The downside of this procedure is that we have now introduced a mismatch between our ultimate goal and our objective function. In this paper, we demonstrate a sparse Bayesian learning-based method of minimizing the ℓ0-norm while reducing the number of trou- blesome local minima. Moreover, we derive necessary conditions for local minima to occur via this approach and empirically demonstrate that there are typically many fewer for general problems of interest.

paragraphs: Sparse representation seeks the smallest number of dictionary elements needed to explain a signal. Directly minimizing that count is difficult because the objective has many troublesome local minima, motivating substitutes such as the ℓ₁ norm. This paper aims to stay closer to the actual sparsity objective while improving its optimization landscape.

The authors develop a sparse-Bayesian-learning-based route to ℓ₀ minimization. They derive necessary conditions for local minima under the approach, making it possible to analyze how many undesirable stationary solutions remain. The method addresses the mismatch between asking for few nonzero coefficients and optimizing a different numerical penalty.

Experiments show substantially fewer problematic local minima on general problems of interest. The contribution is not a claim that combinatorial sparse recovery becomes universally easy, but a formulation that can reduce a central obstacle while directly pursuing sparsity. It provides a reason to revisit the original objective rather than relying exclusively on tractable surrogates.
summary.tldr: A sparse Bayesian formulation pursues ℓ₀ basis selection while reducing the problematic local minima that make direct optimization difficult.

title: ℓ₀-norm Minimization for Basis Selection

abstract: This paper presents a general family of algebraic positive definite similarity functions over spaces of matrices with varying column rank. The columns can represent local regions in an image (whereby images have varying number of local parts), images of an image sequence, motion trajectories in a multibody motion, and so forth. The family of set kernels we derive is based on a group invariant tensor product lifting with parameters that can be naturally tuned to provide a cook-book of sorts covering the possible ”wish lists” from similarity measures over sets of varying cardinality. We highlight the strengths of our approach by demonstrating the set kernels for visual recognition of pedestrians using local parts representations.

The family of set kernels we derive is based on a group invariant tensor product lifting with parameters that can be naturally tuned to provide a cook-book of sorts covering the possible ”wish lists” from similarity measures over sets of varying cardinality. paragraphs: An image can be represented by a collection of local parts, but different images can contain different numbers of parts. This paper develops similarity functions for such collections through matrix representations whose columns describe constituent elements. The same formulation can accommodate other collections, including images in a sequence or trajectories associated with multibody motion.

The authors construct a family of positive definite set kernels using a group-invariant tensor-product lifting. This algebraic construction provides a structured way to compare collections with varying cardinality and column rank. Its parameters can be adjusted to obtain different desired properties of a similarity measure, making the contribution a family of comparisons rather than one fixed formula.

The paper demonstrates these kernels in pedestrian recognition using representations built from local image parts. That application shows how the mathematical construction can support recognition when objects are described through variable collections of components. The broader significance is a common similarity framework for these representations, with tunable behavior and the positive definiteness needed for kernel-based inference.
summary.tldr: The paper constructs tunable positive definite kernels for comparing variable-sized collections and demonstrates them in pedestrian recognition.

title: Algebraic Set Kernels with Application to Inference Over Local Image Representations

abstract: Gaussian processes are attractive models for probabilistic classification but unfortunately exact inference is analytically intractable. We compare Laplace’s method and Expectation Propagation (EP) focusing on marginal likelihood estimates and predictive performance. We explain theoretically and corroborate empirically that EP is superior to Laplace. We also compare to a sophisticated MCMC scheme and show that EP is surprisingly accurate.
originalAbstract: Gaussian processes are attractive models for probabilistic classification but unfortunately exact inference is analytically intractable. We compare Laplace’s method and Expectation Propagation (EP) focusing on marginal likelihood estimates and predictive performance. We explain theoretically and corroborate empirically that EP is superior to Laplace. We also compare to a sophisticated MCMC scheme and show that EP is surprisingly accurate.

paragraphs: Gaussian processes offer a probabilistic approach to classification, but their exact inference calculations cannot be carried out analytically in the setting considered here. Practical use therefore depends on approximations. This paper examines two such choices, Laplace's method and Expectation Propagation, to determine how well they support the quantities needed for classification.

The comparison focuses on marginal likelihood estimates and predictive performance. These are distinct concerns: an approximation must support predictions, while also estimating the evidence assigned to the observed data. By assessing both, the paper evaluates more than whether the methods merely produce usable class predictions in the experiments under study.

The authors provide a theoretical explanation for the superiority of Expectation Propagation over Laplace's method and corroborate that explanation empirically. They also compare Expectation Propagation with a sophisticated Markov chain Monte Carlo scheme and find it surprisingly accurate. Together, these results provide theoretical and experimental support for Expectation Propagation as an effective approximation for Gaussian process classification.
summary.tldr: Theoretical and empirical comparisons favor Expectation Propagation over Laplace's method for Gaussian process classification.

title: Assessing Approximations for Gaussian Process Classification

abstract: We propose new PAC-Bayes bounds for the risk of the weighted majority vote that depend on the mean and variance of the error of its associated Gibbs classiﬁer. We show that these bounds can be smaller than the risk of the Gibbs classiﬁer and can be arbitrarily close to zero even if the risk of the Gibbs classiﬁer is close to 1/2. Moreover, we show that these bounds can be uniformly estimated on the training data for all possible posteriors Q. Moreover, they can be improved by using a large sample of unlabelled data.
originalAbstract: We propose new PAC-Bayes bounds for the risk of the weighted majority vote that depend on the mean and variance of the error of its associated Gibbs classiﬁer. We show that these bounds can be smaller than the risk of the Gibbs classiﬁer and can be arbitrarily close to zero even if the risk of the Gibbs classiﬁer is close to 1/2. Moreover, we show that these bounds can be uniformly estimated on the training data for all possible posteriors Q. Moreover, they can be improved by using a large sample of unlabelled data.

paragraphs: A weighted majority vote combines predictions from several classifiers, while its associated Gibbs classifier selects a classifier according to the same weighting distribution. This paper develops PAC-Bayes bounds on the majority vote's prediction risk. The bounds use both the mean and the variance of the Gibbs classifier's error.

Accounting for variance makes it possible to certify stronger performance for the vote than the Gibbs risk alone might suggest. The authors show that their bounds can be smaller than the Gibbs classifier's risk. They can even approach zero while the Gibbs risk remains close to one-half, demonstrating a possible large gap between these two quantities.

The paper also shows that the bounds can be estimated from training data uniformly over every posterior weighting distribution Q. This matters because the guarantee covers the choice of weights rather than requiring one fixed choice in advance. A large unlabeled sample can further improve the bounds. These are theoretical possibilities established by the analysis, not claims that every ensemble achieves near-zero risk.
summary.tldr: PAC-Bayes bounds using error mean and variance can certify low majority-vote risk even when Gibbs risk is near one-half.

title: PAC-Bayes Bounds for the Risk of the Majority Vote and the Variance of the Gibbs Classifier

abstract: Probabilistic graphical models use local factors to represent dependence among sets of variables. For many problem domains, for instance climatology and epidemiology, in addition to local dependencies, we may also wish to model heavy-tailed statistics, where extreme deviations should not be treated as outliers. Specifying such distributions using graphical models for probability density functions (PDFs) generally lead to intractable inference and learning. Cumulative distribution networks (CDNs) provide a means to tractably specify multivariate heavy-tailed models as a product of cumulative distribution functions (CDFs). Currently, algorithms for inference and learning, which correspond to computing mixed derivatives, are exact only for tree-structured graphs. For graphs of arbitrary topology, an efficient algorithm is needed that takes advantage of the sparse structure of the model, unlike symbolic differentiation programs such as Mathematica and D* that do not. We present an algorithm for recursively decomposing the computation of derivatives for CDNs of arbitrary topology, where the decomposition is naturally described using junction trees. We compare the performance of the resulting algorithm to Mathematica and D*, and we apply our method to learning models for rainfall and H1N1 data, where we show that CDNs with cycles are able to provide a significantly better fits to the data as compared to tree-structured and unstructured CDNs and other heavy-tailed multivariate distributions such as the multivariate copula and logistic models.
originalAbstract: Probabilistic graphical models use local factors to represent dependence among sets of variables. For many problem domains, for instance climatology and epidemiology, in addition to local dependencies, we may also wish to model heavy-tailed statistics, where extreme deviations should not be treated as outliers. Specifying such distributions using graphical models for probability density functions (PDFs) generally lead to intractable inference and learning. Cumulative distribution networks (CDNs) provide a means to tractably specify multivariate heavy-tailed models as a product of cumulative distribution functions (CDFs). Currently, algorithms for inference and learning, which correspond to computing mixed derivatives, are exact only for tree-structured graphs. For graphs of arbitrary topology, an efficient algorithm is needed that takes advantage of the sparse structure of the model, unlike symbolic differentiation programs such as Mathematica and D* that do not. We present an algorithm for recursively decomposing the computation of derivatives for CDNs of arbitrary topology, where the decomposition is naturally described using junction trees. We compare the performance of the resulting algorithm to Mathematica and D*, and we apply our method to learning models for rainfall and H1N1 data, where we show that CDNs with cycles are able to provide a significantly better fits to the data as compared to tree-structured and unstructured CDNs and other heavy-tailed multivariate distributions such as the multivariate copula and logistic models.

paragraphs: Some data require models that represent local relationships while allowing extreme observations to be part of the distribution. Cumulative distribution networks address this by multiplying cumulative distribution functions to build multivariate models, including heavy-tailed ones. Their inference and learning calculations involve mixed derivatives, and existing exact methods were restricted to tree-shaped graphs.

The paper develops an algorithm for computing these derivatives on graphs of arbitrary topology, including graphs with cycles. It recursively divides the calculation into smaller pieces organized through junction trees. This decomposition exploits the model’s sparse structure, addressing a weakness of general symbolic differentiation programs that do not use that structure.

The authors compare the algorithm with Mathematica and D* and apply it to rainfall and H1N1 data. In those applications, networks containing cycles fit the data significantly better than tree-structured and unstructured networks, as well as the compared copula and logistic models. The result connects expanded exact computation to a practical benefit from representing richer dependence patterns.
summary.tldr: A junction-tree derivative algorithm enables exact computation in cyclic cumulative distribution networks, which achieve better fits in the reported applications.

title: Exact inference and learning for cumulative distribution functions on loopy graphs

abstract: We identify and investigate a strong connection between probabilistic inference and differential privacy, the latter being a recent privacy definition that permits only indirect observation of data through noisy measurement. Previous research on differential privacy has focused on designing measurement processes whose output is likely to be useful on its own. We consider the potential of applying probabilistic inference to the measurements and measurement process to derive posterior distributions over the data sets and model parameters thereof. We find that probabilistic inference can improve accuracy, integrate multiple observations, measure uncertainty, and even provide posterior distributions over quantities that were not directly measured.

paragraphs: Differentially private analysis makes data available indirectly through noisy measurements. This paper asks what can be learned by treating those measurements as observations generated by a known measurement process. Its focus shifts from making each released value useful on its own to extracting information through probabilistic inference over the releases.

The proposed perspective derives posterior distributions over datasets and their model parameters using both the observations and the process that produced them. Accounting for the measurement process matters because noise is part of the evidence-generating mechanism. A posterior can describe multiple plausible underlying explanations and the uncertainty associated with them, rather than reducing the analysis to a single measured value.

The authors find that this approach can improve accuracy, combine multiple observations, and quantify uncertainty. It can also yield posterior distributions for quantities that were never directly measured. The contribution is thus a connection between private measurement and subsequent statistical analysis, showing how inference can make the available noisy evidence more useful for a broader set of questions.
summary.tldr: Probabilistic inference over private measurements can improve accuracy, combine observations, and quantify uncertainty about measured and unmeasured quantities.

title: Probabilistic Inference and Differential Privacy

abstract: Stochastic dual coordinate ascent (SDCA) is an effective technique for solving regularized loss minimization problems in machine learning. This paper considers an extension of SDCA under the mini-batch setting that is often used in practice. Our main contribution is to introduce an accelerated mini-batch version of SDCA and prove a fast convergence rate for this method. We discuss an implementation of our method over a parallel computing system, and compare the results to both the vanilla stochastic dual coordinate ascent and to the accelerated deterministic gradient descent method of Nesterov [2007].

paragraphs: Many machine-learning methods fit models by minimizing a loss together with a regularization penalty. Stochastic dual coordinate ascent is an effective optimization technique for this setting. This paper extends it to mini-batches, where an update works with a group of coordinates, and introduces acceleration into that setting.

The principal contribution is an accelerated mini-batch algorithm with a proven fast convergence rate. Such a result characterizes how the optimization procedure approaches its solution as it proceeds. Combining acceleration with mini-batch updates is the central design issue: the paper supplies both an algorithmic extension and a theoretical account of its convergence.

The authors also discuss implementing the method on a parallel computing system. They compare its results with standard stochastic dual coordinate ascent and Nesterov's accelerated deterministic gradient descent. These comparisons place the method alongside both a closely related stochastic technique and an established accelerated alternative. The stated contribution connects convergence theory with the practical question of organizing optimization work for parallel execution.
summary.tldr: An accelerated mini-batch version of stochastic dual coordinate ascent comes with a fast convergence guarantee and a parallel implementation discussion.

title: Accelerated Mini-Batch Stochastic Dual Coordinate Ascent

abstract: Deep learning has been successfully applied to multimodal representation learning problems, with a common strategy to learning joint representations that are shared across multiple modalities on top of layers of modality-specific networks. Nonetheless, there still remains a question how to learn a good association between data modalities; in particular, a good generative model of multimodal data should be able to reason about missing data modality given the rest of data modalities. In this paper, we propose a novel multimodal representation learning framework that explicitly aims this goal. Rather than learning with maximum likelihood, we train the model to minimize the variation of information. We provide a theoretical insight why the proposed learning objective is sufficient to estimate the data-generating joint distribution of multimodal data. We apply our method to restricted Boltzmann machines and introduce learning methods based on contrastive divergence and multi-prediction training. In addition, we extend to deep networks with recurrent encoding structure to finetune the whole network. In experiments, we demonstrate the state-of-the-art visual recognition performance on MIR-Flickr database and PASCAL VOC 2007 database with and without text features.

paragraphs: Learning a shared representation across modalities does not automatically explain how well a model can infer a missing modality from the others. This paper makes that ability an explicit learning goal. It proposes a multimodal framework trained by minimizing variation of information, replacing maximum likelihood as the chosen training objective.

The authors provide theoretical insight into why this objective is sufficient to estimate the joint distribution generating the multimodal data. They apply the framework to restricted Boltzmann machines and develop learning methods using contrastive divergence and multi-prediction training. They also extend the approach to deep networks with recurrent encoding so that the entire network can be fine-tuned.

Experiments report state-of-the-art visual recognition performance on MIR-Flickr and PASCAL VOC 2007, both with and without text features. These results connect the proposed objective to recognition performance under different modality availability. The methodological contribution is a learning criterion aimed directly at relationships between modalities, supported by theory about joint-distribution estimation and implementations for both restricted Boltzmann machines and deeper networks.
summary.tldr: Training multimodal models with variation of information targets missing-modality inference and yields strong reported visual recognition results.

title: Improved Multimodal Deep Learning with Variation of Information

abstract: We consider the problem of learning causal networks with interventions, when each intervention is limited in size under Pearl's Structural Equation Model with independent errors (SEM-IE). The objective is to minimize the number of experiments to discover the causal directions of all the edges in a causal graph. Previous work has focused on the use of separating systems for complete graphs for this task. We prove that any deterministic adaptive algorithm needs to be a separating system in order to learn complete graphs in the worst case. In addition, we present a novel separating system construction, whose size is close to optimal and is arguably simpler than previous work in combinatorics. We also develop a novel information theoretic lower bound on the number of interventions that applies in full generality, including for randomized adaptive learning algorithms. For general chordal graphs, we derive worst case lower bounds on the number of interventions. Building on observations about induced trees, we give a new deterministic adaptive algorithm to learn directions on any chordal skeleton completely. In the worst case, our achievable scheme is an $\alpha$-approximation algorithm where $\alpha$ is the independence number of the graph. We also show that there exist graph classes for which the sufficient number of experiments is close to the lower bound. In the other extreme, there are graph classes for which the required number of experiments is multiplicatively $\alpha$ away from our lower bound. In simulations, our algorithm almost always performs very close to the lower bound, while the approach based on separating systems for complete graphs is significantly worse for random chordal graphs.

For complete graphs, the authors prove that deterministic adaptive algorithms must form separating systems in the worst case, and give a simpler construction of nearly optimal size. They also derive an information-theoretic lower bound that covers randomized adaptive algorithms. These bounds establish benchmarks against which experimental designs can be assessed.

Some graph classes admit experiment counts near the lower bound, while others exhibit a multiplicative gap of that size. Simulations usually place the algorithm close to the lower bound and show substantially better performance than complete-graph separating-system designs on random chordal graphs.
summary.tldr: The paper derives experiment lower bounds and adaptive methods for discovering causal directions with size-limited interventions.

title: Learning Causal Graphs with Small Interventions

abstract: We provide tight upper and lower bounds on the complexity of minimizing the average of m convex functions using gradient and prox oracles of the component functions. We show a significant gap between the complexity of deterministic vs randomized optimization. For smooth functions, we show that accelerated gradient descent (AGD) and an accelerated variant of SVRG are optimal in the deterministic and randomized settings respectively, and that a gradient oracle is sufficient for the optimal rate. For non-smooth functions, having access to prox oracles reduces the complexity and we present optimal methods based on smoothing that improve over methods using just gradient accesses.

For smooth functions, we show that accelerated gradient descent (AGD) and an accelerated variant of SVRG are optimal in the deterministic and randomized settings respectively, and that a gradient oracle is sufficient for the optimal rate. paragraphs: This paper asks how much computation is fundamentally required to minimize an average of m convex functions. It studies access to the component functions through gradient and proximal oracles. By proving matching upper and lower complexity bounds, it identifies both achievable performance and limits on improvement within the analyzed access models.

The results show a significant difference between deterministic and randomized optimization. For smooth functions, accelerated gradient descent is optimal in the deterministic setting, while an accelerated version of SVRG is optimal in the randomized setting. Gradient access alone suffices to achieve the optimal rate for these smooth problems.

For nonsmooth functions, the available operation changes the answer: access to proximal oracles reduces complexity compared with gradient access alone. The authors develop optimal methods based on smoothing that exploit this advantage. Together, the results explain how smoothness, randomization, and oracle choice shape optimization difficulty, giving a principled basis for comparing methods that have different kinds of access to the objective.
summary.tldr: Tight complexity bounds show how randomization and proximal access change the optimal cost of minimizing averages of convex functions.

title: Tight Complexity Bounds for Optimizing Composite Objectives

abstract: We introduce and analyze a new technique for model reduction for deep neural networks. While large networks are theoretically capable of learning arbitrarily complex models, overfitting and model redundancy negatively affects the prediction accuracy and model variance. Our Net-Trim algorithm prunes (sparsifies) a trained network layer-wise, removing connections at each layer by solving a convex optimization program. This program seeks a sparse set of weights at each layer that keeps the layer inputs and outputs consistent with the originally trained model. The algorithms and associated analysis are applicable to neural networks operating with the rectified linear unit (ReLU) as the nonlinear activation. We present both parallel and cascade versions of the algorithm. While the latter can achieve slightly simpler models with the same generalization performance, the former can be computed in a distributed manner. In both cases, Net-Trim significantly reduces the number of connections in the network, while also providing enough regularization to slightly reduce the generalization error. We also provide a mathematical analysis of the consistency between the initial network and the retrained model. To analyze the model sample complexity, we derive the general sufficient conditions for the recovery of a sparse transform matrix. For a single layer taking independent Gaussian random vectors of length $N$ as inputs, we show that if the network response can be described using a maximum number of $s$ non-zero weights per node, these weights can be learned from $\mathcal{O}(s\log N)$ samples.

This makes pruning an explicitly constrained approximation problem rather than simply discarding connections without checking their effect.

The paper presents parallel and cascade versions. The parallel version supports distributed computation, while the cascade version can produce slightly simpler models with the same generalization performance. Both substantially reduce connections, and the reported regularization effect slightly lowers generalization error. The authors also mathematically analyze consistency between the original and modified networks.

For one layer with independent Gaussian input vectors of length N and at most s nonzero weights per node, the weights can be learned from order s log N samples. This guarantee applies to that stated input and sparsity setting, providing a concrete theoretical basis for sparse recovery within the broader pruning approach.
summary.tldr: Net-Trim uses convex layerwise optimization to sparsify trained ReLU networks while controlling consistency with their original behavior.

title: Net-Trim: Convex Pruning of Deep Neural Networks with Performance Guarantee

abstract: Generalization performance is a central goal in machine learning, particularly when learning representations with large neural networks. A common strategy to improve generalization has been through the use of regularizers, typically as a norm constraining the parameters. Regularizing hidden layers in a neural network architecture, however, is not straightforward. There have been a few effective layer-wise suggestions, but without theoretical guarantees for improved performance. In this work, we theoretically and empirically analyze one such model, called a supervised auto-encoder: a neural network that predicts both inputs (reconstruction error) and targets jointly. We provide a novel generalization result for linear auto-encoders, proving uniform stability based on the inclusion of the reconstruction error---particularly as an improvement on simplistic regularization such as norms or even on more advanced regularizations such as the use of auxiliary tasks. Empirically, we then demonstrate that, across an array of architectures with a different number of hidden units and activation functions, the supervised auto-encoder compared to the corresponding standard neural network never harms performance and can significantly improve generalization.

paragraphs: A neural network must learn representations that remain useful beyond its training examples. Regularization helps pursue that goal, but directly constraining hidden representations is less straightforward than penalizing parameter sizes. This paper analyzes supervised autoencoders, which jointly predict the desired targets and reconstruct their inputs.

The reconstruction objective provides an additional requirement for the learned representation: it must retain information useful for recovering the input as well as predicting the target. For linear autoencoders, the authors prove a generalization result through uniform stability arising from reconstruction error. Their analysis establishes an improvement over simpler norm regularization and more advanced regularization through auxiliary tasks.

The empirical study covers architectures with different hidden-unit counts and activation functions. Across those evaluated settings, adding the supervised autoencoder objective never harms performance relative to the corresponding standard network and can significantly improve generalization. This finding is empirical for the tested architectures, while the stated theoretical guarantee is for linear autoencoders. Together, they provide complementary reasons to consider reconstruction as a regularizer.
summary.tldr: Joint input reconstruction and target prediction improve generalization in the reported experiments, with a supporting stability result for linear autoencoders.

title: Supervised autoencoders: Improving generalization performance with unsupervised regularizers

abstract: Deep Gaussian Processes (DGPs) are hierarchical generalizations of Gaussian Processes that combine well calibrated uncertainty estimates with the high flexibility of multilayer models. One of the biggest challenges with these models is that exact inference is intractable. The current state-of-the-art inference method, Variational Inference (VI), employs a Gaussian approximation to the posterior distribution. This can be a potentially poor unimodal approximation of the generally multimodal posterior. In this work, we provide evidence for the non-Gaussian nature of the posterior and we apply the Stochastic Gradient Hamiltonian Monte Carlo method to generate samples. To efficiently optimize the hyperparameters, we introduce the Moving Window MCEM algorithm. This results in significantly better predictions at a lower computational cost than its VI counterpart. Thus our method establishes a new state-of-the-art for inference in DGPs.

paragraphs: Deep Gaussian processes combine multiple layers of Gaussian-process models to provide flexible predictions with calibrated uncertainty estimates. Exact inference is intractable, so practical use depends on approximation. This paper examines the concern that a Gaussian approximation to the posterior can be inadequate when that posterior has several distinct modes.

The authors provide evidence that the posterior is non-Gaussian and use stochastic gradient Hamiltonian Monte Carlo to generate samples from it. This sampling approach changes how uncertainty over the model is represented. They also introduce Moving Window MCEM to optimize hyperparameters efficiently, addressing a separate part of the inference workflow that must remain computationally manageable.

The resulting method produces significantly better predictions at lower computational cost than its variational-inference counterpart, according to the reported findings. The authors describe it as a new state of the art for inference in deep Gaussian processes. The contribution combines evidence about posterior shape with a sampling method and a hyperparameter procedure, linking the approximation choice to both predictive quality and computational expense.
summary.tldr: Sampling-based inference with Moving Window MCEM improves predictions and lowers computational cost relative to the paper's variational-inference counterpart.

title: Inference in Deep Gaussian Processes using Stochastic Gradient Hamiltonian Monte Carlo

abstract: Many researchers have sought ways of model compression to reduce the size of a deep neural network (DNN) with minimal performance degradation in order to use DNNs in embedded systems. Among the model compression methods, a method called knowledge transfer is to train a student network with a stronger teacher network. In this paper, we propose a novel knowledge transfer method which uses convolutional operations to paraphrase teacher's knowledge and to translate it for the student. This is done by two convolutional modules, which are called a paraphraser and a translator. The paraphraser is trained in an unsupervised manner to extract the teacher factors which are defined as paraphrased information of the teacher network. The translator located at the student network extracts the student factors and helps to translate the teacher factors by mimicking them. We observed that our student network trained with the proposed factor transfer method outperforms the ones trained with conventional knowledge transfer methods.

paragraphs: This paper studies model compression through knowledge transfer, where a stronger teacher network helps train a smaller student. The motivation is to make deep networks usable in embedded systems while limiting performance degradation. Its proposed transfer method changes how the teacher's knowledge is represented for the student.

Two convolutional modules perform the transfer. A paraphraser is trained without supervision to extract teacher factors, which are transformed representations of information in the teacher network. A translator in the student extracts student factors and learns by mimicking the teacher factors. The transfer target is therefore an intermediate representation produced specifically for this exchange.

The authors report that students trained through this factor-transfer method outperform students trained with conventional knowledge-transfer methods in their experiments. This supports the idea that the form of the transferred information matters, alongside the teacher's strength. The contribution is a concrete way to prepare teacher representations and align student representations with them, so a compact network can benefit from a stronger one during training.
summary.tldr: Factor transfer trains a compact student to mimic transformed teacher representations using convolutional paraphraser and translator modules.

title: Paraphrasing Complex Network: Network Compression via Factor Transfer

abstract: Configuring deep Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs) is an exciting research avenue for low power spike event based computation. However, the spike generation function is non-differentiable and therefore not directly compatible with the standard error backpropagation algorithm. In this paper, we introduce a new general backpropagation mechanism for learning synaptic weights and axonal delays which overcomes the problem of non-differentiability of the spike function and uses a temporal credit assignment policy for backpropagating error to preceding layers. We describe and release a GPU accelerated software implementation of our method which allows training both fully connected and convolutional neural network (CNN) architectures. Using our software, we compare our method against existing SNN based learning approaches and standard ANN to SNN conversion techniques and show that our method achieves state of the art performance for an SNN on the MNIST, NMNIST, DVS Gesture, and TIDIGITS datasets.

paragraphs: Spiking neural networks offer a route toward low-power computation based on discrete spike events. Training deep versions is difficult because the function that generates a spike is not differentiable, preventing direct use of standard backpropagation. The paper introduces SLAYER as a learning mechanism that addresses this obstacle while accounting for the temporal nature of spikes.

The method learns both synaptic weights and axonal delays. Its temporal credit assignment policy sends error information back to preceding layers, connecting learning to when signals occur as well as to their strengths. This makes timing part of the training problem rather than treating the network solely as a collection of static weighted connections.

The authors release a GPU-accelerated implementation supporting fully connected and convolutional architectures. They compare the method with existing spiking-network learning approaches and techniques that convert conventional neural networks into spiking ones. Reported results reach state-of-the-art SNN performance on MNIST, NMNIST, DVS Gesture, and TIDIGITS. The findings support the proposed backpropagation mechanism as an effective training approach across the evaluated spiking-network tasks.
summary.tldr: SLAYER trains spiking networks through temporal error assignment, learning connection weights and delays while addressing non-differentiable spike generation.

title: SLAYER: Spike Layer Error Reassignment in Time

abstract: Efficient exploration remains a challenging research problem in reinforcement learning, especially when an environment contains large state spaces, deceptive local optima, or sparse rewards. To tackle this problem, we present a diversity-driven approach for exploration, which can be easily combined with both off- and on-policy reinforcement learning algorithms. We show that by simply adding a distance measure to the loss function, the proposed methodology significantly enhances an agent's exploratory behaviors, and thus preventing the policy from being trapped in local optima. We further propose an adaptive scaling method for stabilizing the learning process. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method in huge 2D gridworlds and a variety of benchmark environments, including Atari 2600 and MuJoCo. Experimental results show that our method outperforms baseline approaches in most tasks in terms of mean scores and exploration efficiency.

paragraphs: A reinforcement learning agent must explore enough to discover useful behavior before settling on a policy. That is difficult when there are many possible states, rewards are rare, or apparently promising behavior leads to an inferior local optimum. This paper introduces an exploration strategy that makes diversity an explicit part of the learning objective.

The method adds a distance measure to the loss function to encourage more exploratory behavior. It can be combined with both on-policy and off-policy algorithms, making it applicable across different training arrangements. The authors also introduce adaptive scaling to stabilize learning, addressing how the additional exploration term interacts with the rest of the optimization.

Experiments cover large two-dimensional gridworlds and benchmark environments from Atari 2600 and MuJoCo. The method improves mean scores and exploration efficiency over the compared baselines on most tasks. These findings support diversity-driven training as a practical way to help policies avoid becoming trapped in local optima, with the reported advantage spanning several kinds of environments rather than every evaluated task.
summary.tldr: Adding an adaptively scaled diversity term improves exploration and scores over baselines on most evaluated reinforcement learning tasks.

title: Diversity-Driven Exploration Strategy for Deep Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Neural network training relies on our ability to find "good" minimizers of highly non-convex loss functions. It is well known that certain network architecture designs (e.g., skip connections) produce loss functions that train easier, and well-chosen training parameters (batch size, learning rate, optimizer) produce minimizers that generalize better. However, the reasons for these differences, and their effect on the underlying loss landscape, is not well understood. In this paper, we explore the structure of neural loss functions, and the effect of loss landscapes on generalization, using a range of visualization methods. First, we introduce a simple "filter normalization" method that helps us visualize loss function curvature, and make meaningful side-by-side comparisons between loss functions. Then, using a variety of visualizations, we explore how network architecture affects the loss landscape, and how training parameters affect the shape of minimizers.

However, the reasons for these differences, and their effect on the underlying loss landscape, is not well understood. In this paper, we explore the structure of neural loss functions, and the effect of loss landscapes on generalization, using a range of visualization methods. The authors introduce filter normalization as a method for visualizing loss curvature and making meaningful side-by-side comparisons between loss functions. A comparison method matters because the goal is to study differences across networks and training choices, rather than simply produce an isolated picture of one model's loss.

It also examines the relationship between landscape structure and generalization. The contribution is an investigative framework for connecting design and training decisions to observable loss geometry, helping organize questions about why some networks train more easily and some learned solutions generalize better.

title: Visualizing the Loss Landscape of Neural Nets

abstract: We consider a decentralized learning problem, where a set of computing nodes aim at solving a non-convex optimization problem collaboratively. It is well-known that decentralized optimization schemes face two major system bottlenecks: stragglers' delay and communication overhead. In this paper, we tackle these bottlenecks by proposing a novel decentralized and gradient-based optimization algorithm named as QuanTimed-DSGD. Our algorithm stands on two main ideas: (i) we impose a deadline on the local gradient computations of each node at each iteration of the algorithm, and (ii) the nodes exchange quantized versions of their local models. The first idea robustifies to straggling nodes and the second alleviates communication efficiency. The key technical contribution of our work is to prove that with non-vanishing noises for quantization and stochastic gradients, the proposed method exactly converges to the global optimal for convex loss functions, and finds a first-order stationary point in non-convex scenarios. Our numerical evaluations of the QuanTimed-DSGD on training benchmark datasets, MNIST and CIFAR-10, demonstrate speedups of up to 3x in run-time, compared to state-of-the-art decentralized optimization methods.

Experiments training on MNIST and CIFAR-10 report runtime speedups of up to three times over state-of-the-art decentralized optimization methods, supporting the practical value of addressing both system bottlenecks together.
summary.tldr: QuanTimed-DSGD combines computation deadlines and quantized communication with convergence guarantees and observed runtime speedups of up to three times.

title: Robust and Communication-Efficient Collaborative Learning

abstract: Interpretability has become an important topic of research as more machine learning (ML) models are deployed and widely used to make important decisions. Most of the current explanation methods provide explanations through feature importance scores, which identify features that are important for each individual input. However, how to systematically summarize and interpret such per sample feature importance scores itself is challenging. In this work, we propose principles and desiderata for \emph{concept} based explanation, which goes beyond per-sample features to identify higher level human-understandable concepts that apply across the entire dataset. We develop a new algorithm, ACE, to automatically extract visual concepts. Our systematic experiments demonstrate that \alg discovers concepts that are human-meaningful, coherent and important for the neural network's predictions.

paragraphs: Many explanation methods assign importance scores to features of an individual input. This paper asks how explanations can instead identify higher-level concepts that people understand and that apply across an entire dataset.

The authors propose principles and desired properties for concept-based explanation, then develop ACE, an algorithm that automatically extracts visual concepts. The intended explanation unit is a recurring, understandable concept rather than a collection of separate feature scores for individual examples. Automatic extraction addresses the challenge of finding such concepts systematically within the data.

Systematic experiments find that ACE discovers concepts that are meaningful to people, coherent, and important for the network's predictions. These properties connect human interpretation with the behavior being explained: the concepts should make sense as groups and matter to the model. The contribution is a method for moving from individual feature attributions toward a broader account of the visual concepts associated with predictions.
summary.tldr: ACE automatically extracts visual concepts that experiments find understandable, coherent, and important to neural-network predictions.

title: Towards Automatic Concept-based Explanations

abstract: Learning a graph with a specific structure is essential for interpretability and identification of the relationships among data. But structured graph learning from observed samples is an NP-hard combinatorial problem. In this paper, we first show, for a set of important graph families it is possible to convert the combinatorial constraints of structure into eigenvalue constraints of the graph Laplacian matrix. Then we introduce a unified graph learning framework lying at the integration of the spectral properties of the Laplacian matrix with Gaussian graphical modeling, which is capable of learning structures of a large class of graph families. The proposed algorithms are provably convergent and practically amenable for big-data specific tasks. Extensive numerical experiments with both synthetic and real datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed methods. An R package containing codes for all the experimental results is submitted as a supplementary file.

paragraphs: Learning a graph from observations can help reveal relationships among variables, but a useful graph may also need a particular structure. Enforcing such structure directly leads to an NP-hard combinatorial problem. This paper develops a framework that represents structural requirements through spectral properties of the graph's Laplacian matrix.

For a set of important graph families, the authors show how to translate combinatorial restrictions into constraints on Laplacian eigenvalues. They combine those constraints with Gaussian graphical modeling to learn graphs from data. This creates a unified approach capable of handling a broad collection of graph families through a common mathematical representation.

The proposed algorithms have convergence guarantees and are presented as practical for tasks involving large datasets. Experiments on synthetic and real data demonstrate their effectiveness, with an accompanying R package supporting the experimental results. The key contribution is the translation from discrete graph structure to spectral constraints, which enables structured estimation within one framework. The stated convergence guarantees concern the algorithms; the abstract does not equate them with solving every structural problem globally.
summary.tldr: The paper learns structured graphs by translating graph-family requirements into Laplacian eigenvalue constraints within Gaussian graphical modeling.

title: Structured Graph Learning Via Laplacian Spectral Constraints

abstract: Importance sampling (IS) is a common reweighting strategy for off-policy prediction in reinforcement learning. While it is consistent and unbiased, it can result in high variance updates to the weights for the value function. In this work, we explore a resampling strategy as an alternative to reweighting. We propose Importance Resampling (IR) for off-policy prediction, which resamples experience from a replay buffer and applies standard on-policy updates. The approach avoids using importance sampling ratios in the update, instead correcting the distribution before the update. We characterize the bias and consistency of IR, particularly compared to Weighted IS (WIS). We demonstrate in several microworlds that IR has improved sample efficiency and lower variance updates, as compared to IS and several variance-reduced IS strategies, including variants of WIS and V-trace which clips IS ratios. We also provide a demonstration showing IR improves over IS for learning a value function from images in a racing car simulator.

paragraphs: Off-policy prediction learns about one policy using experience collected under another. Importance sampling corrects this mismatch by reweighting updates, but those weights can make value-function updates highly variable. This paper explores moving the correction into the selection of experience, before the learning update is calculated.

Importance Resampling selects experience from a replay buffer and then applies standard on-policy updates. Importance ratios therefore do not appear in the update itself; the sampling distribution carries the correction. The authors analyze the method's bias and consistency, particularly in relation to Weighted Importance Sampling, making these statistical properties part of the comparison.

Across several microworlds, the method shows better sample efficiency and lower update variance than importance sampling and several approaches intended to reduce its variance. The comparisons include variants of Weighted Importance Sampling and V-trace. A further demonstration learns a value function from images in a racing simulator and improves over importance sampling. Together, these results support resampling as a useful alternative location for off-policy correction.
summary.tldr: Importance Resampling corrects off-policy data through replay selection, producing lower-variance updates and improved sample efficiency in the reported tests.

title: Importance Resampling for Off-policy Prediction

abstract: Inner product-based convolution has been the founding stone of convolutional neural networks (CNNs), enabling end-to-end learning of visual representation. By generalizing inner product with a bilinear matrix, we propose the neural similarity which serves as a learnable parametric similarity measure for CNNs. Neural similarity naturally generalizes the convolution and enhances flexibility. Further, we consider the neural similarity learning (NSL) in order to learn the neural similarity adaptively from training data. Specifically, we propose two different ways of learning the neural similarity: static NSL and dynamic NSL. Interestingly, dynamic neural similarity makes the CNN become a dynamic inference network. By regularizing the bilinear matrix, NSL can be viewed as learning the shape of kernel and the similarity measure simultaneously. We further justify the effectiveness of NSL with a theoretical viewpoint. Most importantly, NSL shows promising performance in visual recognition and few-shot learning, validating the superiority of NSL over the inner product-based convolution counterparts.

paragraphs: Convolutional neural networks traditionally use inner products to compare input features with learned kernels. This paper generalizes that comparison by introducing a bilinear matrix, creating a trainable similarity measure called neural similarity. The change adds flexibility to convolution by allowing the form of the comparison itself to be learned from training data.

The authors develop two ways to learn this measure: static neural similarity learning and dynamic neural similarity learning. The dynamic version makes the CNN a dynamic inference network. They also show that, with regularization of the bilinear matrix, the approach can be interpreted as learning the kernel's shape and the similarity measure together.

The paper offers a theoretical perspective supporting the method and reports promising results in visual recognition and few-shot learning. Those results favor neural similarity learning over the inner-product convolution counterparts in the reported evaluation. The main contribution is a more adaptable primitive for convolutional computation, with both a conceptual interpretation and empirical evidence that learning the comparison rule can improve these tasks.
summary.tldr: Neural similarity learning replaces convolution's fixed inner-product comparison with a learned bilinear measure, improving reported recognition and few-shot results.

title: Neural Similarity Learning

abstract: A soft-max function has two main efficiency measures: (1) approximation - which corresponds to how well it approximates the maximum function, (2) smoothness - which shows how sensitive it is to changes of its input. Our goal is to identify the optimal approximation-smoothness tradeoffs for different measures of approximation and smoothness. This leads to novel soft-max functions, each of which is optimal for a different application. The most commonly used soft-max function, called exponential mechanism, has optimal tradeoff between approximation measured in terms of expected additive approximation and smoothness measured with respect to Renyi Divergence. We introduce a soft-max function, called piece-wise linear soft-max, with optimal tradeoff between approximation, measured in terms of worst-case additive approximation and smoothness, measured with respect to l_q-norm. The worst-case approximation guarantee of the piece-wise linear mechanism enforces sparsity in the output of our soft-max function, a property that is known to be important in Machine Learning applications Martins et al. 16, Laha et al. 18 and is not satisfied by the exponential mechanism. Moreover, the l_q-smoothness is suitable for applications in Mechanism Design and Game Theory where the piece-wise linear mechanism outperforms the exponential mechanism. Finally, we investigate another soft-max function, called power mechanism, with optimal tradeoff between expected multiplicative approximation and smoothness with respect to the Renyi Divergence, which provides improved theoretical and practical results in differentially private submodular optimization.
