paragraphs: Soft-max functions must balance favoring the largest input against responding smoothly when inputs change. This paper studies the best possible balance under different definitions of approximation and smoothness. Its central message is that the optimal construction depends on which guarantees an application needs.

The familiar exponential mechanism is optimal when approximation is measured by expected additive error and smoothness by Rényi divergence. The authors introduce a piecewise linear alternative that is optimal for worst-case additive approximation and smoothness measured with an l_q norm. Its worst-case guarantee enforces sparse outputs, a property absent from the exponential mechanism. The paper also reports advantages for this construction in mechanism design and game theory.

A third construction, the power mechanism, optimally balances expected multiplicative approximation with Rényi-divergence smoothness. It improves theoretical and practical results for differentially private submodular optimization. Together, the results provide distinct optimal choices for distinct requirements, showing why approximation quality and input sensitivity need to be specified before choosing a soft-max function.
summary.tldr: Different approximation and smoothness criteria lead to different optimal soft-max functions, including sparse piecewise linear and power mechanisms.

title: Optimal Approximation - Smoothness Tradeoffs for Soft-Max Functions

abstract: Learning heuristics for combinatorial optimization problems through graph neural networks have recently shown promising results on some classic NP-hard problems. These are single-level optimization problems with only one player. Multilevel combinatorial optimization problems are their generalization, encompassing situations with multiple players taking decisions sequentially. By framing them in a multi-agent reinforcement learning setting, we devise a value-based method to learn to solve multilevel budgeted combinatorial problems involving two players in a zero-sum game over a graph. Our framework is based on a simple curriculum: if an agent knows how to estimate the value of instances with budgets up to $B$, then solving instances with budget $B+1$ can be done in polynomial time regardless of the direction of the optimization by checking the value of every possible afterstate. Thus, in a bottom-up approach, we generate datasets of heuristically solved instances with increasingly larger budgets to train our agent. We report results close to optimality on graphs up to $100$ nodes and a $185 \times$ speedup on average compared to the quickest exact solver known for the Multilevel Critical Node problem, a max-min-max trilevel problem that has been shown to be at least $\Sigma_2^p$-hard.

paragraphs: The paper tackles graph optimization problems in which two opposing players make decisions sequentially under budgets. These problems extend single-player combinatorial optimization because a decision must account for later responses by an opponent. The authors formulate the setting as a zero-sum multi-agent reinforcement learning problem and learn a value-based solution method.

The training curriculum progresses from smaller budgets to larger ones. If an agent can estimate values for instances with budgets up to B, it can examine the possible afterstates of a decision at budget B+1. This examination takes polynomial time regardless of whether the current player maximizes or minimizes. The method uses this relationship to build training datasets from heuristically solved instances with increasing budgets.

They also report an average 185-fold speedup over the quickest known exact solver. These empirical results show how a budget-based curriculum can produce useful heuristics for a difficult three-level optimization problem.
summary.tldr: A curriculum that increases decision budgets learns near-optimal graph-game heuristics and reports substantial speedups over an exact solver.

title: Curriculum learning for multilevel budgeted combinatorial problems

abstract: In this paper, we deepen the analysis of continuous time Fictitious Play learning algorithm to the consideration of various finite state Mean Field Game settings (finite horizon, $\gamma$-discounted), allowing in particular for the introduction of an additional common noise. We first present a theoretical convergence analysis of the continuous time Fictitious Play process and prove that the induced exploitability decreases at a rate $O(\frac{1}{t})$. Such analysis emphasizes the use of exploitability as a relevant metric for evaluating the convergence towards a Nash equilibrium in the context of Mean Field Games. These theoretical contributions are supported by numerical experiments provided in either model-based or model-free settings. We provide hereby for the first time converging learning dynamics for Mean Field Games in the presence of common noise.

paragraphs: Mean field games describe strategic interactions through an aggregate population rather than tracking every opponent separately. This paper studies continuous-time fictitious play as a learning process for such games with finitely many states. Its analysis covers finite-horizon and discounted settings and allows an additional source of noise shared across participants.

The central result concerns exploitability, a measure of how much an agent could gain by deviating from the current behavior. The authors prove that this quantity decreases at a rate of O(1/t) along the analyzed process. A decreasing opportunity to benefit from deviation provides a way to assess progress toward a Nash equilibrium, linking learning dynamics to a strategically meaningful error measure.

Numerical experiments support the theoretical analysis in both model-based and model-free settings. The paper also reports converging learning dynamics for mean field games with common noise, which it identifies as a first. Together, these contributions extend the settings covered by fictitious-play analysis and establish exploitability as a useful quantity for tracking convergence.
summary.tldr: The paper proves O(1/t) exploitability decay for continuous-time fictitious play in analyzed mean field games, including settings with common noise.

title: Fictitious Play for Mean Field Games: Continuous Time Analysis and Applications

abstract: Multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) has shown recent success in increasingly complex fixed-team zero-sum environments. However, the real world is not zero-sum nor does it have fixed teams; humans face numerous social dilemmas and must learn when to cooperate and when to compete. To successfully deploy agents into the human world, it may be important that they be able to understand and help in our conflicts. Unfortunately, selfish MARL agents typically fail when faced with social dilemmas. In this work, we show evidence of emergent direct reciprocity, indirect reciprocity and reputation, and team formation when training agents with randomized uncertain social preferences (RUSP), a novel environment augmentation that expands the distribution of environments agents play in. RUSP is generic and scalable; it can be applied to any multi-agent environment without changing the original underlying game dynamics or objectives. In particular, we show that with RUSP these behaviors can emerge and lead to higher social welfare equilibria in both classic abstract social dilemmas like Iterated Prisoner's Dilemma as well in more complex intertemporal environments.

paragraphs: Success in fixed-team, zero-sum games does not fully address situations where agents must decide when to cooperate and when to compete. Social dilemmas are particularly challenging because individually selfish behavior can undermine collective outcomes. This paper investigates whether broadening agents' training experiences can encourage more flexible social behavior.

The proposed augmentation, randomized uncertain social preferences, or RUSP, expands the distribution of environments that agents encounter during training. The authors describe it as generic and scalable, applicable to multi-agent environments without altering their underlying game dynamics or original objectives. Its purpose is to create training conditions in which socially responsive strategies can emerge.

The experiments provide evidence of direct reciprocity, indirect reciprocity and reputation, and team formation. These behaviors can lead to equilibria with higher social welfare in the tested settings, which include the Iterated Prisoner's Dilemma and more complex environments with consequences unfolding over time. The contribution is evidence that the training distribution can support these behaviors, rather than a guarantee that every trained agent will cooperate.
summary.tldr: Randomized uncertain social preferences can produce reciprocity, reputation, and team formation in trained agents, supporting higher social welfare in tested dilemmas.

title: Emergent Reciprocity and Team Formation from Randomized Uncertain Social Preferences

abstract: Sampling-based methods promise scalability improvements when paired with stochastic gradient descent in training Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs). While effective in alleviating the neighborhood explosion, due to bandwidth and memory bottlenecks, these methods lead to computational overheads in preprocessing and loading new samples in heterogeneous systems, which significantly deteriorate the sampling performance. By decoupling the frequency of sampling from the sampling strategy, we propose LazyGCN, a general yet effective framework that can be integrated with any sampling strategy to substantially improve the training time. The basic idea behind LazyGCN is to perform sampling periodically and effectively recycle the sampled nodes to mitigate data preparation overhead. We theoretically analyze the proposed algorithm and show that under a mild condition on the recycling size, by reducing the variance of inner layers, we are able to obtain the same convergence rate as the underlying sampling method. We also give corroborating empirical evidence on large real-world graphs, demonstrating that the proposed schema can significantly reduce the number of sampling steps and yield superior speedup without compromising the accuracy.

We also give corroborating empirical evidence on large real-world graphs, demonstrating that the proposed schema can significantly reduce the number of sampling steps and yield superior speedup without compromising the accuracy.

paragraphs: Sampling can make graph convolutional network training more scalable by limiting the neighborhoods processed at each step. However, preparing and loading fresh samples introduces overhead, especially when memory and bandwidth become bottlenecks. This paper examines sampling frequency as a separate design choice from the strategy used to select nodes.

LazyGCN samples periodically and reuses the selected nodes between sampling operations. The framework is designed to work with any sampling strategy, allowing existing methods to reduce repeated data preparation. The central idea is that every training step need not require a newly prepared sample for training to remain effective.

The theoretical analysis obtains the same convergence rate as the underlying sampling method under a mild condition on recycling size, through reduced variance in inner layers. Experiments on large real-world graphs support the approach: it substantially reduces sampling steps and improves speed without sacrificing accuracy in the reported evaluations. The contribution connects algorithmic sampling decisions to the systems costs that can otherwise erode their expected scalability benefits.
summary.tldr: LazyGCN accelerates graph-network training by periodically sampling and reusing nodes, with a conditional guarantee of the underlying method's convergence rate.

title: GCN meets GPU: Decoupling “When to Sample” from “How to Sample”

abstract: During online decision making in Multi-Armed Bandits (MAB), one needs to conduct inference on the true mean reward of each arm based on data collected so far at each step. However, since the arms are adaptively selected--thereby yielding non-iid data--conducting inference accurately is not straightforward. In particular, sample averaging, which is used in the family of UCB and Thompson sampling (TS) algorithms, does not provide a good choice as it suffers from bias and a lack of good statistical properties (e.g. asymptotic normality). Our thesis in this paper is that more sophisticated inference schemes that take into account the adaptive nature of the sequentially collected data can unlock further performance gains, even though both UCB and TS type algorithms are optimal in the worst case. In particular, we propose a variant of TS-style algorithms--which we call doubly adaptive TS--that leverages recent advances in causal inference and adaptively reweights the terms of a doubly robust estimator on the true mean reward of each arm. Through 20 synthetic domain experiments and a semi-synthetic experiment based on data from an A/B test of a web service, we demonstrate that using an adaptive inferential scheme (while still retaining the exploration efficacy of TS) provides clear benefits in online decision making: the proposed DATS algorithm has superior empirical performance to existing baselines (UCB and TS) in terms of regret and sample complexity in identifying the best arm. In addition, we also provide a finite-time regret bound of doubly adaptive TS that matches (up to log factors) those of UCB and TS algorithms, thereby establishing that its improved practical benefits do not come at the expense of worst-case suboptimality.

paragraphs: A multi-armed bandit repeatedly chooses among actions while learning their average rewards. A finite-time regret bound also matches their bounds up to logarithmic factors. title: Online Multi-Armed Bandits with Adaptive Inference

abstract: Deep learning has advanced from fully connected architectures to structured models organized into components, e.g., the transformer composed of positional elements, modular architectures divided into slots, and graph neural nets made up of nodes. The nature of structured models is that communication among the components has a bottleneck, typically achieved by restricted connectivity and attention. In this work, we further tighten the bottleneck via discreteness of the representations transmitted between components. We hypothesize that this constraint serves as a useful form of inductive bias. Our hypothesis is motivated by past empirical work showing the benefits of discretization in non-structured architectures as well as our own theoretical results showing that discretization increases noise robustness and reduces the underlying dimensionality of the model. Building on an existing technique for discretization from the VQ-VAE, we consider multi-headed discretization with shared codebooks as the output of each architectural component. One motivating intuition is human language in which communication occurs through multiple discrete symbols. This form of communication is hypothesized to facilitate transmission of information between functional components of the brain by providing a common interlingua, just as it does for human-to-human communication. Our experiments show that discrete-valued neural communication (DVNC) substantially improves systematic generalization in a variety of architectures—transformers, modular architectures, and graph neural networks. We also show that the DVNC is robust to the choice of hyperparameters, making the method useful in practice.

The language analogy motivates the design; the empirical and theoretical results provide the paper’s evidence for its benefits.
summary.tldr: Restricting communication between neural-network components to shared discrete representations improves systematic generalization in the reported experiments.

title: Discrete-Valued Neural Communication

abstract: An increasingly common use case for machine learning models is augmenting the abilities of human decision makers. For classification tasks where neither the human nor model are perfectly accurate, a key step in obtaining high performance is combining their individual predictions in a manner that leverages their relative strengths. In this work, we develop a set of algorithms that combine the probabilistic output of a model with the class-level output of a human. We show theoretically that the accuracy of our combination model is driven not only by the individual human and model accuracies, but also by the model's confidence. Empirical results on image classification with CIFAR-10 and a subset of ImageNet demonstrate that such human-model combinations consistently have higher accuracies than the model or human alone, and that the parameters of the combination method can be estimated effectively with as few as ten labeled datapoints.

This paper studies how to combine their predictions when they provide different kinds of output: the human chooses a class, while the model supplies probabilities over classes. The aim is to make use of their respective strengths through a learned combination.

The proposed algorithms bring these two outputs together using the confusion-matrix and calibration approach identified in the title. The theoretical analysis shows that individual accuracy does not tell the whole story: the model's confidence also affects the accuracy of the combined predictor. This matters because the probability information carries something beyond the model's single preferred label.

In image-classification experiments on CIFAR-10 and a subset of ImageNet, the combinations consistently outperform either the human or the model acting alone. The authors also find that the combination parameters can be estimated effectively with as few as ten labeled examples. These are empirical findings about the evaluated combinations, alongside a theoretical explanation of why confidence matters.
summary.tldr: Combining human class choices with model probabilities improves accuracy in the reported experiments, with model confidence playing a theoretical role.

title: Combining Human Predictions with Model Probabilities via Confusion Matrices and Calibration

abstract: This paper considers incremental few-shot learning, which requires a model to continually recognize new categories with only a few examples provided. Our study shows that existing methods severely suffer from catastrophic forgetting, a well-known problem in incremental learning, which is aggravated due to data scarcity and imbalance in the few-shot setting. Our analysis further suggests that to prevent catastrophic forgetting, actions need to be taken in the primitive stage -- the training of base classes instead of later few-shot learning sessions. Therefore, we propose to search for flat local minima of the base training objective function and then fine-tune the model parameters within the flat region on new tasks. In this way, the model can efficiently learn new classes while preserving the old ones. Comprehensive experimental results demonstrate that our approach outperforms all prior state-of-the-art methods and is very close to the approximate upper bound. The source code is available at https://github.com/moukamisama/F2M.

paragraphs: Incremental few-shot learning asks a model to keep adding categories from only a handful of examples. This creates a difficult combination: new data are scarce and imbalanced, while adapting the model can erase its ability to recognize earlier categories. The paper finds severe forgetting in existing methods and examines how the initial training stage contributes to it.

The authors’ analysis suggests that protection against forgetting should begin when learning the base classes. Their approach seeks flat local minima of the base-training objective, meaning regions where parameter changes have relatively little effect on that objective. Later tasks are learned by fine-tuning within the flat region, aiming to accommodate new categories while preserving earlier knowledge.

Comprehensive experiments report better performance than all prior state-of-the-art methods in the comparison and results close to an approximate upper bound. The findings support preparing the initial model for future adaptation, with the geometry of its base-training solution providing room for subsequent few-shot updates.
summary.tldr: Finding flat minima during base training helps a model learn new few-shot categories while retaining previously learned ones.

title: Overcoming Catastrophic Forgetting in Incremental Few-Shot Learning by Finding Flat Minima

abstract: Semantic, instance, and panoptic segmentations have been addressed using different and specialized frameworks despite their underlying connections. This paper presents a unified, simple, and effective framework for these essentially similar tasks. The framework, named K-Net, segments both instances and semantic categories consistently by a group of learnable kernels, where each kernel is responsible for generating a mask for either a potential instance or a stuff class. To remedy the difficulties of distinguishing various instances, we propose a kernel update strategy that enables each kernel dynamic and conditional on its meaningful group in the input image. K-Net can be trained in an end-to-end manner with bipartite matching, and its training and inference are naturally NMS-free and box-free. Without bells and whistles, K-Net surpasses all previous published state-of-the-art single-model results of panoptic segmentation on MS COCO test-dev split and semantic segmentation on ADE20K val split with 55.2% PQ and 54.3% mIoU, respectively. Its instance segmentation performance is also on par with Cascade Mask R-CNN on MS COCO with 60%-90% faster inference speeds. Code and models will be released at https://github.com/ZwwWayne/K-Net/.

paragraphs: Image segmentation includes assigning semantic categories to pixels, separating individual objects, and combining those tasks in panoptic segmentation. These related problems often use specialized systems. K-Net provides a common framework in which learnable kernels generate masks for either potential object instances or semantic regions, allowing the tasks to share the same basic representation.

To distinguish different instances, K-Net updates each kernel dynamically using its associated group in the input image. The mask-producing components can therefore respond to image content. Training uses bipartite matching and proceeds end to end. Neither training nor inference requires bounding boxes or non-maximum suppression, simplifying the framework around its mask predictions.

The reported results reach 55.2% panoptic quality on MS COCO test-dev and 54.3% mean intersection-over-union on ADE20K validation, exceeding the previously published single-model results cited for those tasks. Instance segmentation is comparable to Cascade Mask R-CNN, with reported inference speeds 60–90% faster. Together, these findings support using one kernel-based design across several segmentation objectives.
summary.tldr: K-Net uses dynamically updated mask-generating kernels to unify semantic, instance, and panoptic segmentation with strong reported accuracy and speed.

title: K-Net: Towards Unified Image Segmentation

abstract: The stochastic multi-arm bandit problem has been extensively studied under standard assumptions on the arm's distribution (e.g bounded with known support, exponential family, etc). These assumptions are suitable for many real-world problems but sometimes they require knowledge (on tails for instance) that may not be precisely accessible to the practitioner, raising the question of the robustness of bandit algorithms to model misspecification. In this paper we study a generic \emph{Dirichlet Sampling} (DS) algorithm, based on pairwise comparisons of empirical indices computed with \textit{re-sampling} of the arms' observations and a data-dependent \textit{exploration bonus}. We show that different variants of this strategy achieve provably optimal regret guarantees when the distributions are bounded and logarithmic regret for semi-bounded distributions with a mild quantile condition. We also show that a simple tuning achieve robustness with respect to a large class of unbounded distributions, at the cost of slightly worse than logarithmic asymptotic regret. We finally provide numerical experiments showing the merits of DS in a decision-making problem on synthetic agriculture data.

paragraphs: Stochastic bandit algorithms repeatedly choose among options whose reward distributions are initially uncertain. Many guarantees assume that those distributions belong to a known family or satisfy known bounds. This paper asks how algorithms behave when such information, especially about distribution tails, is unavailable or misspecified. Its goal is to connect strong performance under standard assumptions with robustness under broader ones.

The proposed Dirichlet Sampling framework compares options pairwise using empirical indices built by resampling their observations. A data-dependent exploration bonus supplements these comparisons. Different variants of this common strategy are analyzed under different distributional assumptions, allowing the method's guarantees to be matched to the information available about rewards.

For bounded distributions, variants achieve provably optimal regret. For semi-bounded distributions, logarithmic regret holds under a mild quantile condition. A simple tuning also provides robustness across a large class of unbounded distributions, with asymptotic regret slightly worse than logarithmic. These results make the robustness trade-off explicit rather than claiming one guarantee covers every case. Numerical experiments on a synthetic agriculture decision problem illustrate the approach's merits.
summary.tldr: Dirichlet Sampling offers resampling-based bandit strategies that trade distribution-specific optimality for broader robustness with a modest regret penalty.

title: From Optimality to Robustness: Adaptive Re-Sampling Strategies in Stochastic Bandits

abstract: Proteins are the main machinery of life and protein functions are largely determined by their 3D structures. The measurement of the pairwise proximity between amino acids of a protein, known as inter-residue contact map, well characterizes the structural information of a protein. Protein contact prediction (PCP) is an essential building block of many protein structure related applications. The prevalent approach to contact prediction is based on estimating the inter-residue contacts using hand-crafted coevolutionary features derived from multiple sequence alignments (MSAs). To mitigate the information loss caused by hand-crafted features, some recently proposed methods try to learn residue co-evolutions directly from MSAs. These methods generally derive coevolutionary features by aggregating the learned residue representations from individual sequences with equal weights, which is inconsistent with the premise that residue co-evolutions are a reflection of collective covariation patterns of numerous homologous proteins. Moreover, non-homologous residues and gaps commonly exist in MSAs. By aggregating features from all homologs equally, the non-homologous information may cause misestimation of the residue co-evolutions. To overcome these issues, we propose an attention-based architecture, Co-evolution Transformer (CoT), for PCP. CoT jointly considers the information from all homologous sequences in the MSA to better capture global coevolutionary patterns. To mitigate the influence of the non-homologous information, CoT selectively aggregates the features from different homologs by assigning smaller weights to non-homologous sequences or residue pairs. Extensive experiments on two rigorous benchmark datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of CoT. In particular, CoT achieves a $51.6\%$ top-L long-range precision score for the Free Modeling (FM) domains on the CASP14 benchmark, which outperforms the winner group of CASP14 contact prediction challenge by $9.8\%$.

title: Co-evolution Transformer for Protein Contact Prediction

abstract: Without positional information, attention-based Transformer neural networks are permutation-invariant. Absolute or relative positional embeddings are the most popular ways to feed Transformer models with positional information. Absolute positional embeddings are simple to implement, but suffer from generalization issues when evaluating on sequences longer than seen at training time. Relative positions are more robust to input length change, but are more complex to implement and yield inferior model throughput due to extra computational and memory costs. In this paper, we propose an augmentation-based approach (CAPE) for absolute positional embeddings, which keeps the advantages of both absolute (simplicity and speed) and relative positional embeddings (better generalization). In addition, our empirical evaluation on state-of-the-art models in machine translation, image and speech recognition demonstrates that CAPE leads to better generalization performance as well as increased stability with respect to training hyper-parameters.

paragraphs: Transformers need positional information to distinguish how inputs are arranged. Absolute positional embeddings provide a straightforward way to supply it, but can generalize poorly to sequences longer than those encountered during training. Relative positional methods handle changes in input length more robustly, while adding implementation complexity and computational and memory costs.

CAPE addresses this tradeoff through an augmentation-based approach to absolute positional embeddings. Its aim is to retain the simplicity and speed of absolute embeddings while gaining the generalization advantages associated with relative positions. The intervention concerns how position is supplied to the model, making positional encoding itself a target for improving behavior beyond the training conditions.

The authors evaluate CAPE with leading models for machine translation, image recognition, and speech recognition. They report better generalization and greater stability with respect to training hyperparameters. These findings suggest that the positional representation can influence both how well a model handles new conditions and how sensitive training is to configuration choices. The evidence spans several application areas rather than a single type of sequence task.
summary.tldr: CAPE augments absolute positional embeddings to combine simple, fast computation with improved generalization and training stability.

title: CAPE: Encoding Relative Positions with Continuous Augmented Positional Embeddings

abstract: As a fundamental unsupervised learning task, hierarchical clustering has been extensively studied in the past decade. In particular, standard metric formulations as hierarchical $k$-center, $k$-means, and $k$-median received a lot of attention and the problems have been studied extensively in different models of computation. Despite all this interest, not many efficient parallel algorithms are known for these problems. In this paper we introduce a new parallel algorithm for the Euclidean hierarchical $k$-median problem that, when using machines with memory $s$ (for $s\in \Omega(\log^2 (n+\Delta+d))$), outputs a hierarchical clustering such that for every fixed value of $k$ the cost of the solution is at most an $O(\min\{d, \log n\} \log \Delta)$ factor larger in expectation than that of an optimal solution. Furthermore, we also get that for all $k$ simultanuously the cost of the solution is at most an $O(\min\{d, \log n\} \log \Delta \log (\Delta d n))$ factor bigger that the corresponding optimal solution. The algorithm requires in $O\left(\log_{s} (nd\log(n+\Delta))\right)$ rounds. Here $d$ is the dimension of the data set and $\Delta$ is the ratio between the maximum and minimum distance of two points in the input dataset. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first \emph{parallel} algorithm for the hierarchical $k$-median problem with theoretical guarantees. We further complement our theoretical results with an empirical study of our algorithm that shows its effectiveness in practice.

paragraphs: Hierarchical clustering creates nested groupings that can be examined at different numbers of clusters. This paper develops a parallel algorithm for the Euclidean hierarchical k-median problem. Its aim is to combine efficient distributed computation with guarantees on the quality of the clustering obtained at different levels of the hierarchy.

For any fixed k, the expected cost is within an O(min{d, log n} log Δ) factor of optimum. Here n counts points, d is dimension, and Δ is the ratio of largest to smallest pairwise distance. A separate guarantee covers all k simultaneously with an additional logarithmic factor. Keeping these statements separate matters because the fixed-k result is explicitly an expectation guarantee.

The algorithm assumes per-machine memory of at least order log²(n + Δ + d), and its round bound decreases as available memory grows. The authors describe it as, to their knowledge, the first parallel hierarchical k-median algorithm with theoretical guarantees. An empirical study also supports its practical effectiveness, complementing the approximation and parallel-computation analysis.
summary.tldr: A parallel Euclidean hierarchical k-median algorithm provides approximation and round-complexity guarantees, supported by an empirical study.

title: Parallel and Efficient Hierarchical k-Median Clustering

abstract: Defocus blur is one kind of blur effects often seen in images, which is challenging to remove due to its spatially variant amount. This paper presents an end-to-end deep learning approach for removing defocus blur from a single image, so as to have an all-in-focus image for consequent vision tasks. First, a pixel-wise Gaussian kernel mixture (GKM) model is proposed for representing spatially variant defocus blur kernels in an efficient linear parametric form, with higher accuracy than existing models. Then, a deep neural network called GKMNet is developed by unrolling a fixed-point iteration of the GKM-based deblurring. The GKMNet is built on a lightweight scale-recurrent architecture, with a scale-recurrent attention module for estimating the mixing coefficients in GKM for defocus deblurring. Extensive experiments show that the GKMNet not only noticeably outperforms existing defocus deblurring methods, but also has its advantages in terms of model complexity and computational efficiency.

paragraphs: Defocus blur can vary across an image, so restoring sharpness requires accounting for different blur amounts at different pixels. This paper develops an end-to-end method for producing an all-in-focus image from a single blurred input. Its starting point is a pixel-wise Gaussian kernel mixture model that represents spatially varying blur through an efficient linear parameterization.

The mixture model provides the basis for GKMNet. The network is constructed by unrolling a fixed-point iteration for the corresponding deblurring problem, translating steps of an iterative procedure into a neural architecture. A lightweight scale-recurrent design includes an attention module that estimates the mixture coefficients needed to describe the blur.

The authors report that the kernel model represents blur more accurately than existing models. Their experiments also show GKMNet noticeably outperforming existing defocus-deblurring methods while offering advantages in model complexity and computational efficiency. The approach matters because the blur representation and restoration network are developed together: a compact description of locally varying blur directly informs how the image is reconstructed.
summary.tldr: GKMNet uses pixel-wise Gaussian blur mixtures and an unrolled restoration procedure to improve single-image defocus deblurring efficiently.

title: Gaussian Kernel Mixture Network for Single Image Defocus Deblurring

abstract: Few-shot segmentation aims to train a segmentation model that can fast adapt to novel classes with few exemplars. The conventional training paradigm is to learn to make predictions on query images conditioned on the features from support images. Previous methods only utilized the semantic-level prototypes of support images as the conditional information. These methods cannot utilize all pixel-wise support information for the query predictions, which is however critical for the segmentation task. In this paper, we focus on utilizing pixel-wise relationships between support and target images to facilitate the few-shot semantic segmentation task. We design a novel Cycle-Consistent Transformer (CyCTR) module to aggregate pixel-wise support features into query ones. CyCTR performs cross-attention between features from different images, i.e. support and query images. We observe that there may exist unexpected irrelevant pixel-level support features. Directly performing cross-attention may aggregate these features from support to query and bias the query features. Thus, we propose using a novel cycle-consistent attention mechanism to filter out possible harmful support features and encourage query features to attend to the most informative pixels from support images. Experiments on all few-shot segmentation benchmarks demonstrate that our proposed CyCTR leads to remarkable improvement compared to previous state-of-the-art methods. Specifically, on Pascal-5^i and COCO-20^i datasets, we achieve 66.6% and 45.6% mIoU for 5-shot segmentation, outperforming previous state-of-the-art by 4.6% and 7.1% respectively.

paragraphs: Few-shot segmentation seeks to adapt to new object classes using only a few examples. This paper argues that summarizing support images into semantic prototypes leaves useful pixel-level information unused. Its Cycle-Consistent Transformer, or CyCTR, transfers support information through relationships between individual support and query image features.

CyCTR uses cross-attention to aggregate support features into the query representation. However, some support pixels may be irrelevant, so unrestricted attention can bias the query features. The proposed cycle-consistent attention mechanism filters potentially harmful support features and encourages attention to the most informative pixels. The method therefore combines richer access to the examples with a mechanism for selecting relevant information.

The authors report improvements over previous state-of-the-art methods on the few-shot segmentation benchmarks evaluated. For five-shot segmentation, they obtain 66.6% mIoU on Pascal-5^i and 45.6% on COCO-20^i, with reported gains of 4.6% and 7.1%, respectively. These findings support using detailed pixel relationships while controlling which support features contribute to each query prediction.
summary.tldr: CyCTR improves few-shot segmentation by transferring pixel-level support features through cycle-consistent attention that filters irrelevant information.

title: Few-Shot Segmentation via Cycle-Consistent Transformer

abstract: Extending the forecasting time is a critical demand for real applications, such as extreme weather early warning and long-term energy consumption planning. This paper studies the long-term forecasting problem of time series. Prior Transformer-based models adopt various self-attention mechanisms to discover the long-range dependencies. However, intricate temporal patterns of the long-term future prohibit the model from finding reliable dependencies. Also, Transformers have to adopt the sparse versions of point-wise self-attentions for long series efficiency, resulting in the information utilization bottleneck. Going beyond Transformers, we design Autoformer as a novel decomposition architecture with an Auto-Correlation mechanism. We break with the pre-processing convention of series decomposition and renovate it as a basic inner block of deep models. This design empowers Autoformer with progressive decomposition capacities for complex time series. Further, inspired by the stochastic process theory, we design the Auto-Correlation mechanism based on the series periodicity, which conducts the dependencies discovery and representation aggregation at the sub-series level. Auto-Correlation outperforms self-attention in both efficiency and accuracy. In long-term forecasting, Autoformer yields state-of-the-art accuracy, with a 38% relative improvement on six benchmarks, covering five practical applications: energy, traffic, economics, weather and disease. Code is available at this repository: https://github.com/thuml/Autoformer.

paragraphs: Long-term time-series forecasting requires finding useful structure despite increasingly complicated patterns far into the future. The paper identifies two difficulties with earlier Transformer approaches: reliable long-range dependencies can be hard to discover, and sparse pointwise attention used for efficiency can restrict how much information the model uses.

Autoformer addresses these difficulties through decomposition and an Auto-Correlation mechanism. Decomposition becomes an internal building block of the model, allowing the series to be progressively decomposed during processing instead of handled only in a preprocessing step. Auto-Correlation uses periodic structure to discover dependencies and aggregate representations across sub-series, shifting the unit of comparison from individual points to stretches of the series.

The authors report that Auto-Correlation improves both efficiency and accuracy over self-attention. Autoformer achieves a reported 38% relative improvement across six long-term forecasting benchmarks spanning energy, traffic, economics, weather, and disease. These findings support the value of incorporating temporal structure directly into the forecasting architecture, combining progressive decomposition with a mechanism designed around recurring patterns.
summary.tldr: Autoformer combines internal series decomposition with periodicity-based Auto-Correlation to improve long-term forecasting accuracy and efficiency.

title: Autoformer: Decomposition Transformers with Auto-Correlation for Long-Term Series Forecasting

abstract: We study the problem of estimating non-linear functionals of discrete distributions in the context of local differential privacy. The initial data $x_1,\ldots,x_n \in[K]$ are supposed i.i.d. and distributed according to an unknown discrete distribution $p = (p_1,\ldots,p_K)$. Only $\alpha$-locally differentially private (LDP) samples $z_1,...,z_n$ are publicly available, where the term 'local' means that each $z_i$ is produced using one individual attribute $x_i$. We exhibit privacy mechanisms (PM) that are interactive (i.e. they are allowed to use already published confidential data) or non-interactive. We describe the behavior of the quadratic risk for estimating the power sum functional $F_{\gamma} = \sum_{k=1}^K p_k^{\gamma}$, $\gamma >0$ as a function of $K, \, n$ and $\alpha$. In the non-interactive case, we study twol plug-in type estimators of $F_{\gamma}$, for all $\gamma >0$, that are similar to the MLE analyzed by Jiao et al. (2017) in the multinomial model. However, due to the privacy constraint the rates we attain are slower and similar to those obtained in the Gaussian model by Collier et al. (2020). In the sequentially interactive case, we introduce for all $\gamma >1$ a two-step procedure which attains the parametric rate $(n \alpha^2)^{-1/2}$ when $\gamma \geq 2$. We give lower bounds results over all $\alpha-$LDP mechanisms and over all estimators using the private samples.

paragraphs: The paper asks how accurately one can estimate nonlinear summaries of a categorical distribution when individual observations are protected by local differential privacy. The original samples are independent and identically distributed over K categories. Only privatized versions are public, with each version produced from one person's attribute under privacy level alpha.

The target summaries are power sums: add together each category probability raised to a positive power gamma. The authors study how estimation risk depends on the number of categories, sample size, and privacy level. They analyze two non-interactive plug-in estimators, where estimates of the probabilities are used to construct the desired summary, and obtain slower rates under the privacy constraint.

The paper also introduces a sequentially interactive two-step procedure for gamma greater than one. For gamma at least two, it attains the stated parametric rate of one divided by the square root of n alpha squared. Lower bounds cover all permitted local-privacy mechanisms and estimators, helping characterize the fundamental accuracy limits alongside the proposed procedures.
summary.tldr: The paper characterizes private estimation of categorical power sums and shows that an interactive procedure attains a parametric rate for powers at least two.

title: Locally differentially private estimation of functionals of discrete distributions

abstract: We introduce a new type of programming challenge called programming puzzles, as an objective and comprehensive evaluation of program synthesis, and release an open-source dataset of Python Programming Puzzles (P3). Each puzzle is defined by a short Python program $f$, and the goal is to find an input which makes $f$ return True. The puzzles are objective in that each one is specified entirely by the source code of its verifier $f$, so evaluating $f$ is all that is needed to test a candidate solution. They do not require an answer key or input/output examples, nor do they depend on natural language understanding. The dataset is comprehensive in that it spans problems of a range of difficulties and domains, ranging from trivial string manipulation problems, to classic programming puzzles (e.g., Tower of Hanoi), to interview/competitive-programming problems (e.g., dynamic programming), to longstanding open problems in algorithms and mathematics (e.g., factoring). We develop baseline enumerative program synthesis, GPT-3 and Codex solvers that are capable of solving puzzles---even without access to any reference solutions---by learning from their own past solutions. Codex performs best, solving up to 18% of 397 test problems with a single try and 80% of the problems with 1,000 tries per problem. In a small user study, we find a positive correlation between puzzle-solving performance and coding experience, and between the puzzle difficulty for humans and AI solvers. Therefore, further improvements on P3 could have a significant impact on many program synthesis areas.

paragraphs: Python Programming Puzzles defines each challenge through a short verification program. The solver must find an input that makes that program return true. Because the verifier specifies the task and checks the answer, evaluation requires neither a reference solution nor natural-language interpretation of a problem statement.

The released P3 dataset spans simple string tasks, classic puzzles, competitive-programming problems, and longstanding algorithmic or mathematical problems. The attempt budget is therefore essential to interpreting those results. A small user study also finds positive correlations between coding experience and success, and between human and AI difficulty. These findings suggest potential relevance to broader program-synthesis research.
summary.tldr: P3 evaluates program synthesis through executable Python puzzles whose solutions can be checked directly without reference answers.

title: Programming Puzzles

abstract: We propose a set of environments with dynamic tasks that involve highly deformable topologically non-trivial objects. These environments facilitate easy experimentation: offer fast runtime, support large-scale parallel data generation, are easy to connect to reinforcement learning frameworks with OpenAI Gym API. We offer several types of benchmark tasks with varying levels of complexity, provide variants with procedurally generated cloth objects and randomized material textures. Moreover, we allow users to customize the tasks: import custom objects and textures, adjust size and material properties of deformable objects.We prioritize dynamic aspects of the tasks: forgoing 2D tabletop manipulation in favor of 3D tasks, with gravity and inertia playing a non-negligible role. Such advanced challenges require insights from multiple fields: machine learning and computer vision to process high-dimensional inputs, methods from computer graphics and topology to inspire structured and interpretable representations, insights from robotics to learn advanced control policies. We aim to help researches from these fields contribute their insights and simplify establishing interdisciplinary collaborations.

paragraphs: Manipulating objects that bend and change shape presents challenges beyond controlling rigid objects. This paper introduces environments involving highly deformable objects with nontrivial topology. The tasks emphasize three-dimensional motion in which gravity and inertia have meaningful effects, making dynamic behavior a central part of the learning problem.

The environments support tasks of different complexity and include variants with procedurally generated cloth objects and randomized material textures. Users can import objects and textures or change object size and material properties. These options let researchers vary the objects and conditions involved while working within the same experimental infrastructure.

Fast execution, parallel data generation, and compatibility with the OpenAI Gym interface are intended to make experimentation accessible to reinforcement learning researchers. The authors also frame the environments as a meeting point for several fields: vision and machine learning for processing complex inputs, graphics and topology for developing representations, and robotics for learning control. The contribution is a customizable set of dynamic challenges designed to support that combined research effort.
summary.tldr: The paper provides customizable simulation environments for learning to control deformable objects in three-dimensional tasks shaped by gravity and inertia.

title: Dynamic Environments with Deformable Objects

abstract: Automatic action identification from video and kinematic data is an important machine learning problem with applications ranging from robotics to smart health. Most existing works focus on identifying coarse actions such as running, climbing, or cutting vegetables, which have relatively long durations and a complex series of motions. This is an important limitation for applications that require identification of more elemental motions at high temporal resolution. For example, in the rehabilitation of arm impairment after stroke, quantifying the training dose (number of repetitions) requires differentiating motions with sub-second durations. Our goal is to bridge this gap. To this end, we introduce a large-scale, multimodal dataset, StrokeRehab, as a new action-recognition benchmark that includes elemental short-duration actions labeled at a high temporal resolution. StrokeRehab consists of a high-quality inertial measurement unit sensor and video data of 51 stroke-impaired patients and 20 healthy subjects performing activities of daily living like feeding, brushing teeth, etc. Because it contains data from both healthy and impaired individuals, StrokeRehab can be used to study the influence of distribution shift in action-recognition tasks. When evaluated on StrokeRehab, current state-of-the-art models for action segmentation produce noisy predictions, which reduces their accuracy in identifying the corresponding sequence of actions. To address this, we propose a novel approach for high-resolution action identification, inspired by speech-recognition techniques, which is based on a sequence-to-sequence model that directly predicts the sequence of actions. This approach outperforms current state-of-the-art methods on StrokeRehab, as well as on the standard benchmark datasets 50Salads, Breakfast, and Jigsaws.

paragraphs: Many action-recognition datasets emphasize long activities, but some applications need to distinguish individual movements lasting less than a second. Stroke rehabilitation is one example: counting repetitions requires identifying these brief actions accurately. StrokeRehab introduces a benchmark designed around that finer temporal resolution rather than treating an entire daily activity as one action.

The dataset combines video and inertial sensor recordings from 51 people with stroke-related impairment and 20 healthy participants performing daily activities. Its short elemental actions have high-resolution labels. Including both groups also supports studying distribution shift, since an action-recognition model can encounter different movement patterns across the represented populations.

When tested on StrokeRehab, existing action-segmentation models produce noisy predictions that reduce action-sequence accuracy. The authors propose a speech-recognition-inspired sequence-to-sequence approach that predicts the action sequence directly. It outperforms the compared state-of-the-art methods on StrokeRehab and on 50Salads, Breakfast, and Jigsaws. The paper thus pairs a dataset exposing a specific recognition challenge with a modeling approach that improves sequence identification in the reported evaluations.
summary.tldr: StrokeRehab benchmarks brief movements using video and sensor data, and a sequence-to-sequence model improves identification of action sequences.

title: StrokeRehab: A Benchmark Dataset for Sub-second Action Identification

abstract: Contrastive representation learning seeks to acquire useful representations by estimating the shared information between multiple views of data. Here, the choice of data augmentation is sensitive to the quality of learned representations: as harder the data augmentations are applied, the views share more task-relevant information, but also task-irrelevant one that can hinder the generalization capability of representation. Motivated by this, we present a new robust contrastive learning scheme, coined RényiCL, which can effectively manage harder augmentations by utilizing Rényi divergence. Our method is built upon the variational lower bound of a Rényi divergence, but a naive usage of a variational method exhibits unstable training due to the large variance. To tackle this challenge, we propose a novel contrastive objective that conducts variational estimation of a skew Renyi divergence and provides a theoretical guarantee on how variational estimation of skew divergence leads to stable training. We show that Rényi contrastive learning objectives perform innate hard negative sampling and easy positive sampling simultaneously so that it can selectively learn useful features and ignore nuisance features. Through experiments on ImageNet, we show that Rényi contrastive learning with stronger augmentations outperforms other self-supervised methods without extra regularization or computational overhead. Also, we validate our method on various domains such as graph and tabular datasets, showing empirical gain over original contrastive methods.

paragraphs: Contrastive learning seeks useful information shared across different views of the same data. The paper focuses on the difficulty of using stronger augmentations, which can involve both task-relevant information and nuisance information that hurts generalization. It introduces RényiCL to make contrastive learning more robust when working with these harder views.

The method builds on a variational lower bound for Rényi divergence. A direct use of that approach suffers from high variance and unstable training, so the authors instead construct an objective based on skew Rényi divergence. They provide a theoretical guarantee explaining how estimating the skew divergence supports training stability.

The resulting objectives implicitly combine hard-negative sampling with easy-positive sampling, helping the model select useful features and disregard nuisance features. ImageNet experiments show that RényiCL with stronger augmentations outperforms other self-supervised methods without additional regularization or computational overhead. Experiments on graph and tabular data also show gains over the original contrastive methods, providing evidence that the proposed objective is useful beyond image representations.
summary.tldr: RényiCL uses a stable skew Rényi-divergence objective to improve contrastive learning with stronger augmentations and selectively emphasize useful features.

title: RényiCL: Contrastive Representation Learning with Skew Rényi Divergence

abstract: We consider reinforcement learning in an environment modeled by an episodic, tabular, step-dependent Markov decision process of horizon $H$ with $S$ states, and $A$ actions. The performance of an agent is measured by the regret after interacting with the environment for $T$ episodes. We propose an optimistic posterior sampling algorithm for reinforcement learning (OPSRL), a simple variant of posterior sampling that only needs a number of posterior samples logarithmic in $H$, $S$, $A$, and $T$ per state-action pair. For OPSRL we guarantee a high-probability regret bound of order at most $O(\sqrt{H^3SAT})$ ignoring $\text{poly}\log(HSAT)$ terms. The key novel technical ingredient is a new sharp anti-concentration inequality for linear forms of a Dirichlet random vector which may be of independent interest. Specifically, we extend the normal approximation-based lower bound for Beta distributions by Alfers and Dinges (1984) to Dirichlet distributions. Our bound matches the lower bound of order $\Omega(\sqrt{H^3SAT})$, thereby answering the open problems raised by Agrawal and Jia (2017) for the episodic setting.

paragraphs: Posterior sampling uses uncertainty about an environment to guide reinforcement learning decisions. This paper proposes an optimistic variant, OPSRL, for episodic tabular Markov decision processes whose dynamics can depend on the step within an episode. The setting has H steps per episode, S states, A actions, and T episodes of interaction.

OPSRL needs only logarithmically many posterior samples in H, S, A, and T for each state-action pair. The authors prove a high-probability regret bound scaling as the square root of H³SAT, apart from logarithmic factors. Regret measures the cumulative cost of learning instead of acting optimally, so the bound describes how that cost grows with interaction and problem size.

The proof relies on a sharp anti-concentration inequality for linear combinations of a Dirichlet random vector, extending an earlier normal-approximation result for Beta distributions. This technical result supports the optimistic sampling analysis and may have separate uses. The regret dependence matches the stated lower bound up to logarithmic factors, resolving the cited open questions for the episodic setting while keeping posterior sampling requirements small.
summary.tldr: OPSRL achieves high-probability regret matching the stated lower-bound scaling up to logarithmic factors while requiring only logarithmically many posterior samples.

title: Optimistic Posterior Sampling for Reinforcement Learning with Few Samples and Tight Guarantees

abstract: In this paper, we consider Byzantine-tolerant federated learning for streaming data using Gaussian process regression (GPR). In particular, a cloud and a group of agents aim to collaboratively learn a latent function where some agents are subject to Byzantine attacks. We develop a Byzantine-tolerant federated GPR algorithm, which includes three modules: agent-based local GPR, cloud-based aggregated GPR and agent-based fused GPR. We derive the upper bounds on prediction error between the mean from the cloud-based aggregated GPR and the target function provided that Byzantine agents are less than one quarter of all the agents. We also characterize the lower and upper bounds of the predictive variance. Experiments on a synthetic dataset and two real-world datasets are conducted to evaluate the proposed algorithm.

In particular, a cloud and a group of agents aim to collaboratively learn a latent function where some agents are subject to Byzantine attacks. We develop a Byzantine-tolerant federated GPR algorithm, which includes three modules: agent-based local GPR, cloud-based aggregated GPR and agent-based fused GPR. paragraphs: This paper studies a cloud and a collection of agents learning an unknown function together as data arrive over time. Some agents may be affected by Byzantine attacks, so their contributions cannot all be trusted. The goal is to make federated Gaussian process regression tolerate this source of unreliable information.

The proposed algorithm has three components. Each agent performs local Gaussian process regression, the cloud aggregates information into a cloud-level regression model, and agents perform a further fused regression step. This organization combines learning close to the incoming data with shared estimation and agent-level fusion, making robustness a concern across the collaborative procedure.

The authors derive upper bounds on the error between the cloud model's predicted mean and the target function, provided fewer than one quarter of the agents are Byzantine. They also characterize lower and upper bounds on predictive variance. These results address both prediction error and uncertainty under the stated attack-fraction condition. Experiments on one synthetic dataset and two real-world datasets evaluate the proposed algorithm.
summary.tldr: A federated Gaussian process algorithm provides prediction-error bounds when fewer than one quarter of agents are Byzantine.

title: Byzantine-tolerant federated Gaussian process regression for streaming data

abstract: Modern approaches for simulation-based inference build upon deep learning surrogates to enable approximate Bayesian inference with computer simulators. In practice, the estimated posteriors' computational faithfulness is, however, rarely guaranteed. For example, Hermans et al., 2021 have shown that current simulation-based inference algorithms can produce posteriors that are overconfident, hence risking false inferences. In this work, we introduce Balanced Neural Ratio Estimation (BNRE), a variation of the NRE algorithm designed to produce posterior approximations that tend to be more conservative, hence improving their reliability, while sharing the same Bayes optimal solution. We achieve this by enforcing a balancing condition that increases the quantified uncertainty in low simulation budget regimes while still converging to the exact posterior as the budget increases. We provide theoretical arguments showing that BNRE tends to produce posterior surrogates that are more conservative than NRE's. We evaluate BNRE on a wide variety of tasks and show that it produces conservative posterior surrogates on all tested benchmarks and simulation budgets. Finally, we emphasize that BNRE is straightforward to implement over NRE and does not introduce any computational overhead.
originalAbstract: Modern approaches for simulation-based inference build upon deep learning surrogates to enable approximate Bayesian inference with computer simulators. In practice, the estimated posteriors' computational faithfulness is, however, rarely guaranteed. For example, Hermans et al., 2021 have shown that current simulation-based inference algorithms can produce posteriors that are overconfident, hence risking false inferences. In this work, we introduce Balanced Neural Ratio Estimation (BNRE), a variation of the NRE algorithm designed to produce posterior approximations that tend to be more conservative, hence improving their reliability, while sharing the same Bayes optimal solution. We achieve this by enforcing a balancing condition that increases the quantified uncertainty in low simulation budget regimes while still converging to the exact posterior as the budget increases. We provide theoretical arguments showing that BNRE tends to produce posterior surrogates that are more conservative than NRE's. We evaluate BNRE on a wide variety of tasks and show that it produces conservative posterior surrogates on all tested benchmarks and simulation budgets. Finally, we emphasize that BNRE is straightforward to implement over NRE and does not introduce any computational overhead.

At the same time, the method retains the same Bayes-optimal solution and converges to the exact posterior as the simulation budget increases. Its design therefore addresses limited-data uncertainty without changing that limiting target.

The authors provide theoretical arguments for a tendency toward more conservative approximations than standard NRE. Across all evaluated benchmarks and simulation budgets, they observe conservative posterior surrogates. That empirical breadth supports the approach without making conservatism an unconditional guarantee. The method is also described as straightforward to add to NRE and as introducing no computational overhead.
summary.tldr: BNRE adds a balancing condition that tends to reduce posterior overconfidence while preserving NRE's Bayes-optimal target without computational overhead.

title: Towards Reliable Simulation-Based Inference with Balanced Neural Ratio Estimation

abstract: Concept bottleneck models (CBMs) enhance the interpretability of their predictions by first predicting high-level concepts given features, and subsequently predicting outcomes on the basis of these concepts. Recently, it was demonstrated that training the label predictor directly on the probabilities produced by the concept predictor as opposed to the ground-truth concepts, improves label predictions. However, this results in corruptions in the concept predictions that impact the concept accuracy as well as our ability to intervene on the concepts -- a key proposed benefit of CBMs. In this work, we investigate and address two issues with CBMs that cause this disparity in performance: having an insufficient concept set and using inexpressive concept predictor. With our modifications, CBMs become competitive in terms of predictive performance, with models that otherwise leak additional information in the concept probabilities, while having dramatically increased concept accuracy and intervention accuracy.

paragraphs: Concept bottleneck models make predictions in two steps: they first estimate understandable concepts, then use those concepts to predict an outcome. This structure is meant to make decisions easier to interpret and allows users to intervene on the intermediate concepts. However, improving outcome accuracy can come at the expense of the meaning of those concepts.

The paper examines a particular source of this tension. Training the outcome predictor on estimated concept probabilities can improve predictions compared with training on ground-truth concepts. Yet those probabilities can carry extra information beyond the intended concepts, corrupting concept predictions and weakening interventions. The authors investigate two contributing problems: a concept set that does not contain enough information and a concept predictor that is insufficiently expressive.

Their modifications address these issues and make the resulting models competitive in predictive performance with models that leak extra information through concept probabilities. At the same time, they report substantially higher concept accuracy and intervention accuracy. The finding matters because successful outcome prediction alone does not establish that a concept bottleneck remains useful as an interpretable, editable intermediate representation.
summary.tldr: Addressing insufficient concepts and weak concept predictors improves concept bottleneck accuracy and interventions while retaining competitive outcome predictions.

title: Addressing Leakage in Concept Bottleneck Models

abstract: Recent works on shared autonomy and assistive-AI technologies, such as assistive robotic teleoperation, seek to model and help human users with limited ability in a fixed task. However, these approaches often fail to account for humans' ability to adapt and eventually learn how to execute a control task themselves. Furthermore, in applications where it may be desirable for a human to intervene, these methods may have inhibited their ability to learn how to succeed with full self-control. In this paper, we focus on the problem of assistive teaching of motor control tasks such as parking a car or landing an aircraft. Despite their ubiquitous role in humans' daily activities and occupations, motor tasks are rarely taught in a uniform way due to their high complexity and variance. We propose an AI-assisted teaching algorithm that leverages skill discovery methods from reinforcement learning (RL) literature to (i) break down any motor control task into teachable skills, (ii) construct novel drill sequences, and (iii) individualize curricula to students with different capabilities. Through an extensive mix of synthetic and user studies on two motor control tasks - parking a car with a joystick and writing characters from the Balinese alphabet - we show that assisted teaching with skills improve student performance by around 40% compared to practicing full trajectories without skills, and practicing with individualized drills can result in up to 25% further improvement.

paragraphs: An assistive system can help someone complete a task without helping them learn to do it independently. This paper focuses on that distinction for motor control: activities in which people must coordinate actions over time. The objective is to teach the human skills needed for eventual self-control, accounting for their ability to improve.

The proposed teaching algorithm uses skill-discovery methods from reinforcement learning to divide motor tasks into teachable components. It then builds practice drills from these skills and individualizes the curriculum for students with different capabilities. This makes the structure of practice part of the teaching method, rather than requiring every student to rehearse complete task trajectories.

Skill-based assisted teaching improves student performance by around 40% relative to practicing full trajectories without skills. Individualized drills can provide up to 25% further improvement. These results support teaching smaller skills and adapting practice in the studied tasks.
summary.tldr: Breaking motor tasks into teachable skills and personalizing practice drills improved human learning in two studied tasks.

title: Assistive Teaching of Motor Control Tasks to Humans

abstract: Neural Architecture Search (NAS) has significantly improved productivity in the design and deployment of neural networks (NN). As NAS typically evaluates multiple models by training them partially or completely, the improved productivity comes at the cost of significant carbon footprint. To alleviate this expensive training routine, zero-shot/cost proxies analyze an NN at initialization to generate a score, which correlates highly with its true accuracy. Zero-cost proxies are currently designed by experts conducting multiple cycles of empirical testing on possible algorithms, datasets, and neural architecture design spaces. This experimentation lowers productivity and is an unsustainable approach towards zero-cost proxy design as deep learning use-cases diversify in nature. Additionally, existing zero-cost proxies fail to generalize across neural architecture design spaces. In this paper, we propose a genetic programming framework to automate the discovery of zero-cost proxies for neural architecture scoring. Our methodology efficiently discovers an interpretable and generalizable zero-cost proxy that gives state of the art score-accuracy correlation on all datasets and search spaces of NASBench-201 and Network Design Spaces (NDS). We believe that this research indicates a promising direction towards automatically discovering zero-cost proxies that can work across network architecture design spaces, datasets, and tasks.

paragraphs: Neural architecture search can require training many candidate networks before choosing one, making the search computationally expensive. Zero-cost proxies instead inspect a network at initialization and assign a score intended to track its eventual accuracy. Designing those scoring rules by hand still requires repeated experimentation, and existing rules can transfer poorly between architecture search spaces.

EZNAS automates the discovery of these rules using genetic programming. Rather than relying on experts to manually construct and test each proxy, the framework searches for a scoring procedure. The authors report discovering an interpretable proxy that generalizes across the evaluated architecture spaces, addressing both the effort of proxy design and the portability of the resulting score.

The discovered proxy achieves state-of-the-art correlation between scores and accuracy across all evaluated datasets and search spaces in NASBench-201 and Network Design Spaces. This supports automated proxy discovery as a promising way to reduce the training burden of architecture evaluation. The broader prospect of proxies working across datasets, tasks, and architecture families remains a direction suggested by these findings.
summary.tldr: EZNAS uses genetic programming to discover interpretable architecture-scoring rules with strong accuracy correlation across the evaluated search spaces.

title: EZNAS: Evolving Zero-Cost Proxies For Neural Architecture Scoring

abstract: Real-world machine-learning applications require robust models that generalize well to distribution shift settings, which is typical in real-world situations. Domain adaptation techniques aim to address this issue of distribution shift by minimizing the disparities between domains to ensure that the model trained on the source domain performs well on the target domain. Nevertheless, the existing domain adaptation methods are computationally very expensive. In this work, we aim to improve the efficiency of existing supervised domain adaptation (SDA) methods by using a subset of source data that is similar to target data for faster model training. Specifically, we propose ORIENT, a subset selection framework that uses the submodular mutual information (SMI) functions to select a source data subset similar to the target data for faster training. Additionally, we demonstrate how existing robust subset selection strategies, such as GLISTER, GRADMATCH, and CRAIG, when used with a held-out query set, fit within our proposed framework and demonstrate the connections with them. Finally, we empirically demonstrate that SDA approaches like d-SNE, CCSA, and standard Cross-entropy training, when employed together with ORIENT, achieve a) faster training and b) better performance on the target data.

paragraphs: Domain adaptation aims to help a model trained on one data distribution perform well on another. Existing methods can be computationally expensive because training uses substantial source data. ORIENT tackles the efficiency problem by selecting a source subset that resembles the target data, concentrating training on examples relevant to the destination domain.

The framework uses submodular mutual information functions to make this selection. Its role is to choose training data for supervised domain adaptation methods, allowing those methods to work with a smaller source collection. The paper also shows how GLISTER, GRADMATCH, and CRAIG fit within the framework when they use a held-out query set.

Experiments combine ORIENT with d-SNE, CCSA, and standard cross-entropy training. These combinations produce both faster training and better target-domain performance in the reported evaluations. The results suggest that source-data selection can improve adaptation efficiency while also helping predictive quality. The connections to existing selection strategies make ORIENT a common framework for understanding several approaches to choosing relevant subsets.
summary.tldr: ORIENT selects source examples similar to target data, yielding faster supervised domain adaptation and better target performance in the reported experiments.

title: ORIENT: Submodular Mutual Information Measures for Data Subset Selection under Distribution Shift

abstract: A recent line of work has established uncoupled learning dynamics such that, when employed by all players in a game, each player's regret after $T$ repetitions grows polylogarithmically in $T$, an exponential improvement over the traditional guarantees within the no-regret framework. However, so far these results have only been limited to certain classes of games with structured strategy spaces---such as normal-form and extensive-form games. The question as to whether $O(\mathrm{polylog} T)$ regret bounds can be obtained for general convex and compact strategy sets---as is the case in many fundamental models in economics and multiagent systems---while retaining efficient strategy updates is an important question. In this paper, we answer this in the positive by establishing the first uncoupled learning algorithm with $O(\log T)$ per-player regret in general convex games, that is, games with concave utility functions supported on arbitrary convex and compact strategy sets. Our learning dynamics are based on an instantiation of optimistic follow-the-regularized-leader over an appropriately lifted space using a self-concordant regularizer that is peculiarly not a barrier for the feasible region. Our learning dynamics are efficiently implementable given access to a proximal oracle for the convex strategy set, leading to $O(\log\log T)$ per-iteration complexity; we also give extensions when access to only a linear optimization oracle is assumed. Finally, we adapt our dynamics to guarantee $O(\sqrt{T})$ regret in the adversarial regime. Even in those special cases where prior results apply, our algorithm improves over the state-of-the-art regret bounds either in terms of the dependence on the number of iterations or on the dimension of the strategy sets.
