paragraphs: An action-recognition model may rely on how a person moves, the objects nearby, or the surrounding scene. Explanations that mix these sources make it difficult to understand the prediction. Describing everything in words introduces another problem: movement can be recognizable without being easy to verbalize precisely.

DANCE separates the evidence into motion dynamics, objects, and scenes. It represents motion concepts as sequences of human poses, while a large language model automatically extracts object and scene concepts. These concepts form a bottleneck through which the model must make its prediction. Consequently, the explanation structure is built into the recognition process, rather than added only after an action has been predicted.

Experiments on KTH, Penn Action, HAA500, and UCF101 report clearer explanations while maintaining competitive recognition performance. A user study also supports improved interpretability. The authors further demonstrate benefits for debugging, editing, and analyzing failures, where distinguishing movement evidence from contextual evidence helps explain why the model reached a particular decision.
summary.tldr: DANCE makes video action predictions through separate motion, object, and scene concepts to improve explanation clarity.

title: Disentangled Concepts Speak Louder Than Words: Explainable Video Action Recognition

abstract: We study stochastic gradient descent (SGD) with gradient clipping on convex functions under a generalized smoothness assumption called $(L_0,L_1)$-smoothness. Using gradient clipping, we establish a high probability convergence rate that matches the SGD rate in the $L$ smooth case up to polylogarithmic factors and additive terms. We also propose a variation of adaptive SGD with gradient clipping, which achieves the same guarantee. We perform empirical experiments to examine our theory and algorithmic choices.
originalAbstract: We study stochastic gradient descent (SGD) with gradient clipping on convex functions under a generalized smoothness assumption called $(L_0,L_1)$-smoothness. Using gradient clipping, we establish a high probability convergence rate that matches the SGD rate in the $L$ smooth case up to polylogarithmic factors and additive terms. We also propose a variation of adaptive SGD with gradient clipping, which achieves the same guarantee. We perform empirical experiments to examine our theory and algorithmic choices.

paragraphs: This paper analyzes stochastic gradient descent with gradient clipping for convex optimization. Clipping limits the size of gradient updates, and the question here is whether this modification supports strong convergence guarantees under a generalized smoothness condition. The authors work with the condition called (L0, L1)-smoothness, rather than restricting the analysis to the standard L-smooth setting.

Their main result is a high-probability convergence rate for clipped SGD. The rate matches the familiar SGD rate under standard smoothness up to polylogarithmic factors and additional additive terms. Those qualifications are part of the result: the paper establishes a close theoretical comparison between the settings, rather than an identical bound with all terms unchanged.

The authors also introduce an adaptive SGD variant that uses clipping and achieves the same guarantee. Empirical experiments examine the theory and the algorithmic choices. Together, these contributions show that clipping can support provable convergence in the stated convex, generalized-smoothness setting, with both a standard stochastic method and an adaptive alternative covered by the analysis.
summary.tldr: Clipped SGD and an adaptive variant achieve high-probability convergence guarantees for convex, generalized-smooth functions that closely match standard smooth-case rates.

title: Convergence of Clipped SGD on Convex $(L_0,L_1)$-Smooth Functions

abstract: Current semi-supervised graph anomaly detection (GAD) methods utilizes a small set of labeled normal nodes to identify abnormal nodes from a large set of unlabeled nodes in a graph. These methods posit that 1) normal nodes share a similar level of homophily and 2) the labeled normal nodes can well represent the homophily patterns in the entire normal class. However, this assumption often does not hold well since normal nodes in a graph can exhibit diverse homophily in real-world GAD datasets. In this paper, we propose RHO, namely Robust Homophily Learning, to adaptively learn such homophily patterns. RHO consists of two novel modules, adaptive frequency response filters (AdaFreq) and graph normality alignment (GNA). AdaFreq learns a set of adaptive spectral filters that capture different frequency components of the labeled normal nodes with varying homophily in the channel-wise and cross-channel views of node attributes. GNA is introduced to enforce consistency between the channel-wise and cross-channel homophily representations to robustify the normality learned by the filters in the two views. Experiments on eight real-world GAD datasets show that RHO can effectively learn varying, often under-represented, homophily in the small labeled node set and substantially outperforms state-of-the-art competing methods. Code is available at \url{https://github.com/mala-lab/RHO}.

paragraphs: Semi-supervised graph anomaly detection uses a small set of labeled normal nodes to identify unusual nodes among many unlabeled ones. Existing methods often assume that normal nodes share similar patterns of homophily, or similarity between connected nodes. They also assume the labeled examples adequately represent those patterns. The paper argues that real normal nodes can be considerably more varied.

RHO learns this variation through two components. Adaptive frequency response filters capture different graph-frequency components of the labeled normal nodes, examining attributes both within individual channels and across channels. Graph normality alignment then encourages consistency between these two views. The combination aims to learn a more robust representation of normal behavior from limited labels.

Across eight real-world graph anomaly datasets, RHO substantially outperforms state-of-the-art competing methods. The authors report that it learns varying homophily patterns, including patterns poorly represented in the small labeled set. These findings support treating normality as structurally diverse: nodes can differ in their neighborhood relationships without those differences necessarily indicating an anomaly.
summary.tldr: RHO improves graph anomaly detection by learning diverse normal-node similarity patterns and aligning complementary views of those patterns.

title: Semi-supervised Graph Anomaly Detection via Robust Homophily Learning

abstract: Drone-based multi-object tracking is essential yet highly challenging due to small targets, severe occlusions, and cluttered backgrounds. Existing RGB-based multi-object tracking algorithms heavily depend on spatial appearance cues such as color and texture, which often degrade in aerial views, compromising tracking reliability. Multispectral imagery, capturing pixel-level spectral reflectance, provides crucial spectral cues that significantly enhance object discriminability under degraded spatial conditions. However, the lack of dedicated multispectral UAV datasets has hindered progress in this domain. To bridge this gap, we introduce **MMOT**, the first challenging benchmark for drone-based multispectral multi-object tracking dataset. It features three key characteristics: (i) **Large Scale** — 125 video sequences with over 488.8K annotations across eight object categories; (ii) **Comprehensive Challenges** — covering diverse real-world challenges such as extreme small targets, high-density scenarios, severe occlusions and complex platform motion; and (iii) **Precise Oriented Annotations** — enabling accurate localization and reduced object ambiguity under aerial perspectives. To better extract spectral features and leverage oriented annotations, we further present a multispectral and orientation-aware MOT scheme adapting existing MOT methods, featuring: (i) a lightweight Spectral 3D-Stem integrating spectral features while preserving compatibility with RGB pretraining; (ii) a orientation-aware Kalman filter for precise state estimation; and (iii) an end-to-end orientation-adaptive transformer architecture. Extensive experiments across representative trackers consistently show that multispectral input markedly improves tracking performance over RGB baselines, particularly for small and densely packed objects. We believe our work will benefit the community for advancing drone-based multispectral multi-object tracking research. Our MMOT, code and benchmarks are publicly available at https://github.com/Annzstbl/MMOT.

paragraphs: MMOT addresses a data gap in tracking multiple objects from drones using multispectral imagery. Aerial targets can be tiny, crowded, or obscured, weakening the color and texture cues used by RGB trackers. Spectral reflectance supplies additional information for distinguishing objects when those spatial appearance cues become unreliable, motivating a dedicated benchmark.

The dataset contains 125 video sequences and more than 488,800 annotations spanning eight object categories. It covers small targets, dense scenes, severe occlusion, and complex drone motion. Oriented annotations describe object alignment as well as location, helping reduce ambiguity in aerial views. These features make the benchmark relevant to both spectral information use and orientation-aware tracking.

The authors also adapt tracking methods with a lightweight spectral 3D input component, an orientation-aware Kalman filter, and an orientation-adaptive transformer architecture. The spectral component retains compatibility with RGB pretraining. Across representative trackers, experiments find clear gains from multispectral inputs over RGB baselines, particularly for small and densely packed objects. The work supplies both an evaluation resource and concrete modeling components for exploiting its additional information.
summary.tldr: MMOT introduces a multispectral drone-tracking benchmark and orientation-aware methods that improve tracking, especially for small and crowded objects.

title: MMOT: The First Challenging Benchmark for Drone-based Multispectral Multi-Object Tracking

abstract: Meta-Black-Box Optimization (MetaBBO) streamlines the automation of optimization algorithm design through meta-learning. It typically employs a bi-level structure: the meta-level policy undergoes meta-training to reduce the manual effort required in developing algorithms for low-level optimization tasks. The original MetaBox (2023) provided the first open-source framework for reinforcement learning-based single-objective MetaBBO. However, its relatively narrow scope no longer keep pace with the swift advancement in this field. In this paper, we introduce MetaBox-v2 (\url{https://github.com/MetaEvo/MetaBox}) as a milestone upgrade with four novel features: 1) a unified architecture supporting RL, evolutionary, and gradient-based approaches, by which we reproduce $23$ up-to-date baselines; 2) efficient parallelization schemes, which reduce the training/testing time by $10-40$x; 3) a comprehensive benchmark suite of $18$ synthetic/realistic tasks ($1900$+ instances) spanning single-objective, multi-objective, multi-model, and multi-task optimization scenarios; 4) plentiful and extensible interfaces for custom analysis/visualization and integrating to external optimization tools/benchmarks. To show the utility of MetaBox-v2, we carry out a systematic case study that evaluates the built-in baselines in terms of the optimization performance, generalization ability and learning efficiency. Valuable insights are concluded from thorough and detailed analysis for practitioners and those new to the field.

paragraphs: Meta-black-box optimization uses learning to automate parts of optimization algorithm design. It has two levels: a higher-level policy learns how to guide lower-level optimization tasks. MetaBox-v2 expands an earlier platform focused on reinforcement learning and single-objective problems, providing a shared environment for a wider range of approaches and evaluation scenarios.

The platform supports reinforcement learning, evolutionary, and gradient-based methods, with reproductions of 23 baselines. Its parallelization schemes reportedly reduce training and testing time by factors of 10 to 40. The benchmark suite contains 18 synthetic or realistic tasks and more than 1,900 instances, spanning single-objective, multi-objective, multi-model, and multi-task settings. Extensible interfaces support analysis, visualization, and connections to external tools.

The authors demonstrate the platform through a systematic comparison of optimization performance, generalization, and learning efficiency. These are complementary questions: a method's effectiveness on a task is only one aspect of how useful its learned optimization behavior may be. The contribution is shared infrastructure for making those comparisons across a broader set of methods and problems.
summary.tldr: MetaBox-v2 broadens meta-optimization benchmarking with 23 baselines, diverse tasks, and reported 10–40-fold training and testing speedups.

title: MetaBox-v2: A Unified Benchmark Platform for Meta-Black-Box Optimization

abstract: Vision-and-Language Navigation (VLN) is a core task where embodied agents leverage their spatial mobility to navigate in 3D environments toward designated destinations based on natural language instructions. Recently, video-language large models (Video-VLMs) with strong generalization capabilities and rich commonsense knowledge have shown remarkable performance when applied to VLN tasks. However, these models still encounter the following challenges when applied to real-world 3D navigation: 1) Insufficient understanding of 3D geometry and spatial semantics; 2) Limited capacity for large-scale exploration and long-term environmental memory; 3) Poor adaptability to dynamic and changing environments.To address these limitations, we propose Dynam3D, a dynamic layered 3D representation model that leverages language-aligned, generalizable, and hierarchical 3D representations as visual input to train 3D-VLM in navigation action prediction. Given posed RGB-D images, our Dynam3D projects 2D CLIP features into 3D space and constructs multi-level 3D patch-instance-zone representations for 3D geometric and semantic understanding with a dynamic and layer-wise update strategy. Our Dynam3D is capable of online encoding and localization of 3D instances, and dynamically updates them in changing environments to provide large-scale exploration and long-term memory capabilities for navigation. By leveraging large-scale 3D-language pretraining and task-specific adaptation, our Dynam3D sets new state-of-the-art performance on VLN benchmarks including R2R-CE, REVERIE-CE and NavRAG-CE under monocular settings. Furthermore, experiments for pre-exploration, lifelong memory, and real-world robot validate the effectiveness of practical deployment.

paragraphs: Dynam3D helps navigation agents connect language instructions with a persistent understanding of three-dimensional surroundings. Video-language models bring broad knowledge, but the paper identifies weaknesses in spatial geometry, long-term environmental memory, and adaptation to changes. Its solution is a structured 3D representation used as visual input for predicting navigation actions.

Given RGB-D images with camera poses, Dynam3D projects two-dimensional CLIP features into 3D space. It organizes the result into patches, instances, and zones, providing several levels of geometric and semantic description. An online, layer-wise update strategy locates and updates instances as the environment changes, supporting exploration and memory across larger spaces.

Training combines large-scale 3D-language pretraining with navigation-specific adaptation. The authors report state-of-the-art results on R2R-CE, REVERIE-CE, and NavRAG-CE under monocular settings. Experiments involving pre-exploration, lifelong memory, and a real robot also support practical deployment. The contribution links navigation decisions to an environment representation that can accumulate knowledge while remaining responsive to changes.
summary.tldr: Dynam3D gives language-guided navigation agents an updateable, hierarchical 3D representation that supports spatial understanding and long-term memory.

title: Dynam3D: Dynamic Layered 3D Tokens Empower VLM for Vision-and-Language Navigation

abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have been used in many zero-shot learning problems, with their strong generalization ability. Recently, adopting LLMs in text-attributed graphs (TAGs) has drawn increasing attention. However, the adoption of LLMs faces two major challenges: limited information on graph structure and unreliable responses. LLMs struggle with text attributes isolated from the graph topology. Worse still, they yield unreliable predictions due to both information insufficiency and the inherent weakness of LLMs (e.g., hallucination). Towards this end, this paper proposes a novel method named Dynamic Text Bundling Supervision (DENSE) that queries LLMs with bundles of texts to obtain bundle-level labels and uses these labels to supervise graph neural networks. Specifically, we sample a set of bundles, each containing a set of nodes with corresponding texts of close proximity. We then query LLMs with the bundled texts to obtain the label of each bundle. Subsequently, the bundle labels are used to supervise the optimization of graph neural networks, and the bundles are further refined to exclude noisy items. To justify our design, we also provide theoretical analysis of the proposed method. Extensive experiments across ten datasets validate the effectiveness of the proposed method.

paragraphs: Text-attributed graphs contain both written information on nodes and relationships between those nodes. Applying a language model to isolated text can miss the graph structure, while insufficient information and hallucination can make its predictions unreliable. DENSE addresses this by changing the unit presented to the language model from an individual node to a bundle.

The method samples groups of nodes with texts in close proximity and asks a language model to label each group's bundled text. Those bundle-level labels then supervise a graph neural network, which can use graph relationships during learning. The bundles are subsequently refined to remove noisy items, allowing the grouping process to improve the supervision supplied to the graph model.

This design connects language-model labeling with a model built to process graph structure. It also makes refinement of the labeled groups part of the learning process. The authors provide theoretical analysis to justify the method and report effective performance across ten datasets, supporting bundling as a useful approach to zero-shot inference on text-attributed graphs.
summary.tldr: DENSE uses language-model labels for bundles of node texts to train graph neural networks, refining the bundles to reduce noise.

title: Dynamic Bundling with Large Language Models for Zero-Shot Inference on Text-Attributed Graphs

abstract: In this paper, we study the behavior of the Upper Confidence Bound-Variance (UCB-V) algorithm for the Multi-Armed Bandit (MAB) problems, a variant of the canonical Upper Confidence Bound (UCB) algorithm that incorporates variance estimates into its decision-making process. More precisely, we provide an asymptotic characterization of the arm-pulling rates for UCB-V, extending recent results for the canonical UCB in Kalvit and Zeevi (2021) and Khamaru and Zhang (2024). In an interesting contrast to the canonical UCB, our analysis reveals that the behavior of UCB-V can exhibit instability, meaning that the arm-pulling rates may not always be asymptotically deterministic. Besides the asymptotic characterization, we also provide non-asymptotic bounds for the arm-pulling rates in the high probability regime, offering insights into the regret analysis. As an application of this high probability result, we establish that UCB-V can achieve a more refined regret bound, previously unknown even for more complicate and advanced variance-aware online decision-making algorithms. A matching regret lower bound is also established, demonstrating the optimality of our result.
originalAbstract: In this paper, we study the behavior of the Upper Confidence Bound-Variance (UCB-V) algorithm for the Multi-Armed Bandit (MAB) problems, a variant of the canonical Upper Confidence Bound (UCB) algorithm that incorporates variance estimates into its decision-making process. More precisely, we provide an asymptotic characterization of the arm-pulling rates for UCB-V, extending recent results for the canonical UCB in Kalvit and Zeevi (2021) and Khamaru and Zhang (2024). In an interesting contrast to the canonical UCB, our analysis reveals that the behavior of UCB-V can exhibit instability, meaning that the arm-pulling rates may not always be asymptotically deterministic. Besides the asymptotic characterization, we also provide non-asymptotic bounds for the arm-pulling rates in the high probability regime, offering insights into the regret analysis. As an application of this high probability result, we establish that UCB-V can achieve a more refined regret bound, previously unknown even for more complicate and advanced variance-aware online decision-making algorithms. A matching regret lower bound is also established, demonstrating the optimality of our result.

paragraphs: UCB-V incorporates estimated reward variance into upper-confidence-bound decisions. This paper studies how often it pulls each bandit arm, extending asymptotic analyses previously developed for ordinary UCB and revealing behavior that the standard algorithm does not share.

In particular, UCB-V’s arm-pulling rates need not converge to deterministic limits. The authors also derive high-probability finite-sample bounds on those rates, providing information beyond the long-run characterization.

Those finite-sample results yield a refined regret bound, accompanied by a matching lower bound establishing optimality in the analyzed sense. The combination matters because irregular asymptotic allocation does not prevent strong regret guarantees. The paper therefore clarifies both the detailed dynamics of a familiar variance-aware algorithm and the performance limit it can attain, rather than assuming that stable sampling proportions are necessary for efficient learning.
summary.tldr: Refined analysis of UCB-V reveals unstable sampling limits and optimal variance-aware regret.

title: Precise Asymptotics and Refined Regret of Variance-Aware UCB

abstract: Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) have shown significant promise in computational science and engineering, yet they often face optimization challenges and limited accuracy. In this work, we identify directional gradient conflicts during PINN training as a critical bottleneck. We introduce a novel gradient alignment score to systematically diagnose this issue through both theoretical analysis and empirical experiments. Building on these insights, we show that (quasi) second-order optimization methods inherently mitigate gradient conflicts, thereby consistently outperforming the widely used Adam optimizer. Among them, we highlight the effectiveness of SOAP \cite{vyas2024soap} by establishing its connection to Newton’s method. Empirically, SOAP achieves state-of-the-art results on 10 challenging PDE benchmarks, including the first successful application of PINNs to turbulent flows at Reynolds numbers up to 10,000. It yields 2–10x accuracy improvements over existing methods while maintaining computational scalability, advancing the frontier of neural PDE solvers for real-world, multi-scale physical systems. All code and datasets used in this work are publicly available at: \url{https://github.com/PredictiveIntelligenceLab/jaxpi/tree/pirate}. \end{abstract}

summary.tldr: The paper links PINN training difficulties to gradient conflicts and shows how second-order optimization, especially SOAP, improves accuracy.

title: Gradient Alignment in Physics-informed Neural Networks: A Second-Order Optimization Perspective

abstract: WiFi sensing has emerged as a compelling contactless modality for human activity monitoring by capturing fine-grained variations in Channel State Information (CSI). Its ability to operate continuously and non-intrusively while preserving user privacy makes it particularly suitable for health monitoring. However, existing WiFi sensing systems struggle to generalize in real-world settings, largely due to datasets collected in controlled environments with homogeneous hardware and fragmented, session-based recordings that fail to reflect continuous daily activity.We present CSI-Bench, a large-scale, in-the-wild benchmark dataset collected using commercial WiFi edge devices across 26 diverse indoor environments with 35 real users. Spanning over 461 hours of effective data, CSI-Bench captures realistic signal variability under natural conditions. It includes task-specific datasets for fall detection, breathing monitoring, localization, and motion source recognition, as well as a co-labeled multitask dataset with joint annotations for user identity, activity, and proximity. To support the development of robust and generalizable models, CSI-Bench provides standardized evaluation splits and baseline results for both single-task and multi-task learning. CSI-Bench offers a foundation for scalable, privacy-preserving WiFi sensing systems in health and broader human-centric applications.

paragraphs: WiFi sensing uses small changes in wireless channel measurements to monitor human activity without physical contact. CSI-Bench addresses this problem by collecting data in varied indoor environments under natural conditions.

These components make the dataset a common basis for comparing methods under realistic signal variability. Its contribution is an evaluation and development resource for more generalizable sensing systems, with health monitoring and other human-centered applications motivating the choice of tasks and collection conditions.
summary.tldr: CSI-Bench provides extensive real-world WiFi recordings and standardized evaluations for several human-monitoring tasks.

title: CSI-Bench: A Large-Scale In-the-Wild Dataset for Multi-task WiFi Sensing

abstract: Novel view synthesis from monocular videos of dynamic scenes with unknown camera poses remains a fundamental challenge in computer vision and graphics. While recent advances in 3D representations such as Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) and 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) have shown promising results for static scenes, they struggle with dynamic content and typically rely on pre-computed camera poses. We present 4D3R, a pose-free dynamic neural rendering framework that decouples static and dynamic components through a two-stage approach. Our method first leverages 3D foundational models for initial pose and geometry estimation, followed by motion-aware refinement. 4D3R introduces two key technical innovations: (1) a motion-aware bundle adjustment (MA-BA) module that combines transformer-based learned priors with SAM2 for robust dynamic object segmentation, enabling more accurate camera pose refinement; and (2) an efficient Motion-Aware Gaussian Splatting (MA-GS) representation that uses control points with a deformation field MLP and linear blend skinning to model dynamic motion, significantly reducing computational cost while maintaining high-quality reconstruction. Extensive experiments on real-world dynamic datasets demonstrate that our approach achieves up to 1.8dB PSNR improvement over state-of-the-art methods, particularly in challenging scenarios with large dynamic objects, while reducing computational requirements by 5× compared to previous dynamic scene representations.

paragraphs: 4D3R reconstructs moving scenes from a single-camera video so they can be rendered from new viewpoints. Its starting challenge is that both the camera and objects may move, while the camera positions are unknown. The framework separates static and moving scene components and estimates camera geometry as part of reconstruction.

The process begins with initial geometry and camera estimates from 3D foundation models, then refines them using motion information. A motion-aware bundle adjustment module combines learned transformer priors with SAM2 segmentation to distinguish moving objects during camera refinement. For rendering, the method represents motion through control points, a neural deformation field, and blended transformations, reducing the computational burden of representing dynamic content.

They also report fivefold lower computational requirements than previous dynamic representations. These findings support treating motion estimation, camera refinement, and scene representation as connected parts of the reconstruction problem.
summary.tldr: 4D3R jointly handles unknown camera poses and scene motion to improve dynamic reconstruction while reducing computation.

title: 4D3R: Motion-Aware Neural Reconstruction and Rendering of Dynamic Scenes from Monocular Videos

abstract: Many models for sparse regression typically assume that the covariates are known completely, and without noise. Particularly in high-dimensional applications, this is often not the case. Worse yet, even estimating statistics of the noise (the noise covariance) can be a central challenge. In this paper we develop a simple variant of orthogonal matching pursuit (OMP) for precisely this setting. We show that without knowledge of the noise covariance, our algorithm recovers the support, and we provide matching lower bounds that show that our algorithm performs at the minimax optimal rate. While simple, this is the first algorithm that (provably) recovers support in a noise-distribution-oblivious manner. When knowledge of the noise-covariance is available, our algorithm matches the best-known \ell^2-recovery bounds available. We show that these too are min-max optimal. Along the way, we also obtain improved performance guarantees for OMP for the standard sparse regression problem with Gaussian noise.

paragraphs: Sparse regression seeks a model in which only some covariates have nonzero coefficients. Many approaches assume those covariates are completely observed and noise-free, which can fail in high-dimensional applications. This paper addresses noisy and missing covariates, emphasizing that even estimating the noise covariance can be difficult.

The authors develop a simple variant of orthogonal matching pursuit that recovers the support, meaning the set of variables with nonzero coefficients, without knowing the noise covariance. Matching lower bounds establish that its support-recovery rate is minimax optimal for the studied setting. This separates identifying the active variables from first having to characterize the corruption covariance.

When the noise covariance is available, the algorithm also matches the best-known bounds for coefficient recovery measured in ℓ² error. The authors establish minimax optimality for those bounds as well. Alongside these results, they improve performance guarantees for standard OMP with Gaussian noise. The paper thus distinguishes what can be recovered without covariance knowledge from the stronger coefficient-recovery guarantees available when that information is supplied.
summary.tldr: A modified orthogonal matching pursuit method achieves minimax-optimal support recovery without knowing the covariate-noise covariance.

title: Noisy and Missing Data Regression: Distribution-Oblivious Support Recovery

abstract: This paper investigates how hidden layers of deep rectifier networks are capable of transforming two or more pattern sets to be linearly separable while preserving the distances with a guaranteed degree, and proves the universal classification power of such distance preserving rectifier networks. Through the nearly isometric nonlinear transformation in the hidden layers, the margin of the linear separating plane in the output layer and the margin of the nonlinear separating boundary in the original data space can be closely related so that the maximum margin classification in the input data space can be achieved approximately via the maximum margin linear classifiers in the output layer. The generalization performance of such distance preserving deep rectifier neural networks can be well justified by the distance-preserving properties of their hidden layers and the maximum margin property of the linear classifiers in the output layer.

The generalization performance of such distance preserving deep rectifier neural networks can be well justified by the distance-preserving properties of their hidden layers and the maximum margin property of the linear classifiers in the output layer.

paragraphs: This paper studies how deep rectifier networks can transform pattern sets so that a linear boundary separates them while retaining control over distances. Its focus is the geometry of hidden representations: separating classes is useful, but the authors also want a guaranteed relationship between the transformed representation and the original data.

The analysis considers nonlinear hidden-layer transformations that approximately preserve distances. Under this construction, the margin of a linear separator at the output can be closely related to the margin of a nonlinear boundary in the input space. Consequently, maximizing the output classifier’s margin can approximately achieve maximum-margin classification in the original space.

The paper proves universal classification power for the distance-preserving rectifier networks it studies. It also uses distance preservation together with the output classifier’s maximum-margin property to justify generalization performance. The contribution is a theoretical connection between expressive hidden transformations and controlled classification geometry: the network can change which boundaries are linear while maintaining enough distance information to relate the two classification problems.
summary.tldr: The paper connects distance-preserving rectifier representations with linear separability, universal classification power, and approximate maximum-margin classification.

title: How Can Deep Rectifier Networks Achieve Linear Separability and Preserve Distances?

abstract: Submodular function minimization is a fundamental optimization problem that arises in several applications in machine learning and computer vision. The problem is known to be solvable in polynomial time, but general purpose algorithms have high running times and are unsuitable for large-scale problems. Recent work have used convex optimization techniques to obtain very practical algorithms for minimizing functions that are sums of “simple” functions. In this paper, we use random coordinate descent methods to obtain algorithms with faster \emphlinear convergence rates and cheaper iteration costs. Compared to alternating projection methods, our algorithms do not rely on full-dimensional vector operations and they converge in significantly fewer iterations.

paragraphs: Submodular function minimization appears in machine learning and computer vision, but general-purpose methods can be too slow for large problems despite polynomial-time solvability. This paper focuses on functions that decompose into sums of simpler components. That structure creates opportunities for more practical optimization than treating the whole function through a general-purpose algorithm.

The authors use random coordinate descent to develop algorithms with faster linear convergence rates and lower iteration costs. Their comparison is with alternating-projection approaches developed through convex optimization. A central computational distinction is that the new algorithms avoid full-dimensional vector operations, reducing the work involved in individual updates.

The methods also converge in substantially fewer iterations than the alternating-projection comparison. These are complementary improvements: cheaper updates address the cost of each step, while faster convergence addresses how many steps are required. The paper’s contribution is therefore a more efficient optimization route for the decomposable class. Its scope depends on the available sum-of-simple-functions structure rather than asserting the same improvement for arbitrary submodular functions.
summary.tldr: Random coordinate descent speeds up decomposable submodular minimization through cheaper updates and faster linear convergence.

title: Random Coordinate Descent Methods for Minimizing Decomposable Submodular Functions

abstract: Ordered testing procedures are multiple testing procedures that exploit a pre-specified ordering of the null hypotheses, from most to least promising. We analyze and compare the power of several recent proposals using the asymptotic framework of Li & Barber (2015). While accumulation tests including ForwardStop can be quite powerful when the ordering is very informative, they are asymptotically powerless when the ordering is weaker. By contrast, Selective SeqStep, proposed by Barber & Candes (2015), is much less sensitive to the quality of the ordering. We compare the power of these procedures in different regimes, concluding that Selective SeqStep dominates accumulation tests if either the ordering is weak or non-null hypotheses are sparse or weak. Motivated by our asymptotic analysis, we derive an improved version of Selective SeqStep which we call Adaptive SeqStep, analogous to Storey’s improvement on the Benjamini-Hochberg procedure. We compare these methods using the GEO-Query data set analyzed by (Li & Barber, 2015) and find Adaptive SeqStep has favorable performance for both good and bad prior orderings.

paragraphs: Ordered hypothesis testing uses a ranking of hypotheses supplied in advance, from most to least promising. This paper studies how the informativeness of that ordering affects the power of several testing procedures. Its analysis uses an asymptotic framework to distinguish conditions under which an ordering helps from those under which a procedure loses effectiveness.

Accumulation tests, including ForwardStop, can be powerful with a highly informative ordering but become asymptotically powerless under weaker orderings. Selective SeqStep is much less sensitive to ordering quality. In the analyzed regimes, it dominates accumulation tests when the ordering is weak or when non-null hypotheses are sparse or weak.

Motivated by these comparisons, the authors derive Adaptive SeqStep, an improved version of Selective SeqStep. On the GEO-Query dataset, it performs favorably with both good and bad prior orderings. The work shows why choosing an ordered testing procedure should account for the reliability of the ordering and the strength and prevalence of the signals being sought.
summary.tldr: An analysis of ordering-sensitive testing motivates Adaptive SeqStep, which performs favorably under both good and bad orderings.

title: Power of Ordered Hypothesis Testing

abstract: Segmental structure is a common pattern in many types of sequences such as phrases in human languages. In this paper, we present a probabilistic model for sequences via their segmentations. The probability of a segmented sequence is calculated as the product of the probabilities of all its segments, where each segment is modeled using existing tools such as recurrent neural networks. Since the segmentation of a sequence is usually unknown in advance, we sum over all valid segmentations to obtain the final probability for the sequence. An efficient dynamic programming algorithm is developed for forward and backward computations without resorting to any approximation. We demonstrate our approach on text segmentation and speech recognition tasks. In addition to quantitative results, we also show that our approach can discover meaningful segments in their respective application contexts.

paragraphs: Many sequences contain meaningful chunks, such as phrases within language, but their boundaries may be unknown. This paper builds a probabilistic sequence model around that segmental structure. For a particular segmentation, it calculates the sequence probability by multiplying the probabilities of its segments, which can be modeled using tools such as recurrent neural networks.

Rather than fixing one segmentation in advance, the model sums over all valid segmentations to obtain the sequence's probability. This incorporates uncertainty about where boundaries belong directly into the calculation. The authors develop efficient dynamic programming for both forward and backward computations, carrying out these operations without approximation.

The approach is demonstrated on text segmentation and speech recognition. Alongside quantitative results, the authors show that it can discover segments that are meaningful within those applications. The contribution is a way to combine flexible models of individual segments with exact computation over possible segmentations, making chunk structure part of the sequence model itself.
summary.tldr: A probabilistic sequence model uses exact dynamic programming to account for unknown segment boundaries and discover meaningful chunks.

title: Sequence Modeling via Segmentations

abstract: A central problem in mining massive data streams is characterizing which functions of an underlying frequency vector can be approximated efficiently. Given the prevalence of large scale linear algebra problems in machine learning, recently there has been considerable effort in extending this data stream problem to that of estimating functions of a matrix. This setting generalizes classical problems to the analogous ones for matrices. For example, instead of estimating frequent-item counts, we now wish to estimate “frequent-direction” counts. A related example is to estimate norms, which now correspond to estimating a vector norm on the singular values of the matrix. Despite recent efforts, the current understanding for such matrix problems is considerably weaker than that for vector problems. We study a number of aspects of estimating matrix norms in a stream that have not previously been considered: (1) multi-pass algorithms, (2) algorithms that see the underlying matrix one row at a time, and (3) time-efficient algorithms. Our multi-pass and row-order algorithms use less memory than what is provably required in the single-pass and entrywise-update models, and thus give separations between these models (in terms of memory). Moreover, all of our algorithms are considerably faster than previous ones. We also prove a number of lower bounds, and obtain for instance, a near-complete characterization of the memory required of row-order algorithms for estimating Schatten $p$-norms of sparse matrices. We complement our results with numerical experiments.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to estimate matrix norms when data arrive as a stream and memory is limited. These problems extend familiar streaming questions about vectors to matrices. For the norms considered here, the quantities being summarized are the matrix’s singular values, making the task a form of compactly tracking its linear-algebraic structure.

The authors investigate three aspects: allowing multiple passes through the data, receiving complete rows rather than individual entry updates, and improving running time. Numerical experiments complement the theoretical analysis of these different streaming models.
summary.tldr: New matrix-norm streaming algorithms show how multiple passes and row-wise input can reduce memory needs and improve speed.

title: Matrix Norms in Data Streams: Faster, Multi-Pass and Row-Order

abstract: We prove a multi-channel telescoping sum boosting theory for the ResNet architectures which simultaneously creates a new technique for boosting over features (in contrast with labels) and provides a new algorithm for ResNet-style architectures. Our proposed training algorithm, BoostResNet , is particularly suitable in non-differentiable architectures. Our method only requires the relatively inexpensive sequential training of $T$ “shallow ResNets”. We prove that the training error decays exponentially with the depth $T$ if the weak module classifiers that we train perform slightly better than some weak baseline. In other words, we propose a weak learning condition and prove a boosting theory for ResNet under the weak learning condition. A generalization error bound based on margin theory is proved and suggests that ResNet could be resistant to overfitting using a network with $l_1$ norm bounded weights.

paragraphs: The paper connects residual networks to boosting through a theory that combines improvements over features. Its multi-channel telescoping-sum construction leads to BoostResNet, a training algorithm that learns a sequence of shallow residual networks. The authors describe this sequential training as relatively inexpensive and particularly suitable for architectures containing nondifferentiable components.

The central guarantee depends on a weak learning condition: the module classifiers must perform slightly better than a specified weak baseline. When that condition holds, training error decreases exponentially with the number of trained blocks, or depth. The result explains how modest module-level performance can accumulate into a stronger network under the stated condition.

The authors also prove a generalization bound using margin theory. It suggests that residual networks with weights bounded in L1 norm could resist overfitting. That is a qualified implication of the bound, separate from the conditional training-error guarantee. Together, the results provide both a sequential training method and a theoretical account of when increasing depth can help.
summary.tldr: BoostResNet trains shallow residual blocks sequentially and guarantees exponentially decreasing training error under a weak learning condition.

title: Learning Deep ResNet Blocks Sequentially using Boosting Theory

abstract: We consider an $\ell_2$-regularized non-convex optimization problem for recovering signals from their noisy phaseless observations. We design and study the performance of a message passing algorithm that aims to solve this optimization problem. We consider the asymptotic setting $m,n \rightarrow \infty$, $m/n \rightarrow \delta$ and obtain sharp performance bounds, where $m$ is the number of measurements and $n$ is the signal dimension. We show that for complex signals the algorithm can perform accurate recovery with only $m=\left ( \frac{64}{\pi^2}-4\right)n\approx 2.5n$ measurements. Also, we provide sharp analysis on the sensitivity of the algorithm to noise. We highlight the following facts about our message passing algorithm: (i) Adding $\ell_2$ regularization to the non-convex loss function can be beneficial even in the noiseless setting; (ii) spectral initialization has marginal impact on the performance of the algorithm.

It formulates recovery as a nonconvex optimization problem with an ℓ₂ regularization term and develops a message passing algorithm intended to solve it. The central question is how accurately this algorithm recovers signals as measurement availability and noise change.

The analysis considers an asymptotic regime: both the number of measurements m and signal dimension n grow without bound, while their ratio approaches a fixed value. Within this setting, the authors obtain sharp performance bounds. For complex signals, they show that accurate recovery is possible with m = (64/π² − 4)n, approximately 2.5 measurements per signal dimension. They also characterize sensitivity to noise.

Two findings clarify the algorithm’s behavior. Adding ℓ₂ regularization can help even when the observations contain no noise, so its value here extends beyond handling measurement corruption. Spectral initialization has only a marginal effect on performance. Together, these results connect algorithm design choices to recovery behavior under the paper’s asymptotic analysis.
summary.tldr: An asymptotic analysis of message passing establishes sharp phaseless recovery bounds and shows that regularization can help even without noise.

title: Approximate message passing for amplitude based optimization

abstract: Bayesian neural networks (BNNs) allow us to reason about uncertainty in a principled way. Stochastic Gradient Langevin Dynamics (SGLD) enables efficient BNN learning by drawing samples from the BNN posterior using mini-batches. However, SGLD and its extensions require storage of many copies of the model parameters, a potentially prohibitive cost, especially for large neural networks. We propose a framework, Adversarial Posterior Distillation, to distill the SGLD samples using a Generative Adversarial Network (GAN). At test-time, samples are generated by the GAN. We show that this distillation framework incurs no loss in performance on recent BNN applications including anomaly detection, active learning, and defense against adversarial attacks. By construction, our framework distills not only the Bayesian predictive distribution, but the posterior itself. This allows one to compute quantities such as the approximate model variance, which is useful in downstream tasks. To our knowledge, these are the first results applying MCMC-based BNNs to the aforementioned applications.

Keeping many such samples, however, means storing many versions of the network, which can become prohibitively expensive for large models.

Adversarial Posterior Distillation addresses this storage problem by training a generative adversarial network on the parameter samples. At prediction time, the generator produces samples instead of relying on a stored collection of network copies. The object being distilled is the parameter posterior itself, extending beyond a summary of the network's predictive outputs.

That distinction matters because posterior samples support calculations such as approximate model variance, which can be useful in subsequent tasks. The authors report no performance loss from distillation in the applications they examine: anomaly detection, active learning, and defense against adversarial attacks. These findings support the approach as a practical way to retain useful Bayesian uncertainty information while changing how posterior samples are represented.
summary.tldr: Adversarial Posterior Distillation trains a GAN to generate Bayesian network parameter samples, retaining useful uncertainty information without storing every sampled network.

title: Adversarial Distillation of Bayesian Neural Network Posteriors

abstract: Many machine learning methods making use of Monte Carlo sampling in vector spaces have been shown to be improved by conditioning samples to be mutually orthogonal. Exact orthogonal coupling of samples is computationally intensive, hence approximate methods have been of great interest. In this paper, we present a unifying perspective of many approximate methods by considering Givens transformations, propose new approximate methods based on this framework, and demonstrate the ﬁrst statistical guarantees for families of approximate methods in kernel approximation. We provide extensive empirical evaluations with guidance for practitioners.

paragraphs: Monte Carlo methods use samples to approximate quantities that are difficult to compute directly. In vector-space applications, arranging samples to be mutually orthogonal has been shown to improve many machine-learning methods. Enforcing that relationship exactly can be computationally expensive, motivating approaches that approximate it more cheaply.

This paper organizes many approximate orthogonal sampling methods through a common framework based on Givens transformations. The framework provides a shared way to understand methods that might otherwise appear separate. The authors also use it to construct new approximate methods, so the unification contributes both an interpretation of existing techniques and additional algorithmic choices.

For families of approximate methods used in kernel approximation, the authors provide what they describe as the first statistical guarantees. This adds theoretical support in a setting where approximate orthogonality is used to reduce computational demands. Extensive empirical evaluations complement the theory and provide practical guidance, connecting the common framework to decisions about which approximate method to use.
summary.tldr: A Givens-transformation framework unifies approximate orthogonal Monte Carlo methods, generates new ones, and supplies statistical guarantees for kernel approximation.

title: Unifying Orthogonal Monte Carlo Methods

abstract: For recurrent neural networks trained on time series with target and exogenous variables, in addition to accurate prediction, it is also desired to provide interpretable insights into the data. In this paper, we explore the structure of LSTM recurrent neural networks to learn variable-wise hidden states, with the aim to capture different dynamics in multi-variable time series and distinguish the contribution of variables to the prediction. With these variable-wise hidden states, a mixture attention mechanism is proposed to model the generative process of the target. Then we develop associated training methods to jointly learn network parameters, variable and temporal importance w.r.t the prediction of the target variable. Extensive experiments on real datasets demonstrate enhanced prediction performance by capturing the dynamics of different variables. Meanwhile, we evaluate the interpretation results both qualitatively and quantitatively. It exhibits the prospect as an end-to-end framework for both forecasting and knowledge extraction over multi-variable data.

paragraphs: Forecasting a target from several time-varying variables raises two linked questions: what will happen next, and which variables and times contributed to that prediction? This paper modifies an LSTM to address both. Its setting includes a target variable together with exogenous variables that provide additional information for prediction.

The network learns hidden states organized by variable, with the aim of preserving distinct dynamics and separating variables' contributions. A mixture attention mechanism uses those states to model how the target is generated. Associated training methods jointly learn the network parameters and the importance of variables and time points for predicting the target.

Experiments on real datasets show enhanced predictive performance from capturing the dynamics of different variables. The authors also assess the interpretations both qualitatively and quantitatively. The resulting framework brings forecasting and interpretation into the same training process, rather than treating explanatory information as a separate output unrelated to the model's internal organization. The paper presents this as a promising route to forecasting and knowledge extraction.
summary.tldr: Variable-specific LSTM states and mixture attention jointly support forecasting and estimates of which variables and times matter.

title: Exploring interpretable LSTM neural networks over multi-variable data

abstract: Adaptive methods such as Adam and RMSProp are widely used in deep learning but are not well understood. In this paper, we seek a crisp, clean and precise characterization of their behavior in nonconvex settings. To this end, we first provide a novel view of adaptive methods as preconditioned SGD, where the preconditioner is estimated in an online manner. By studying the preconditioner on its own, we elucidate its purpose: it rescales the stochastic gradient noise to be isotropic near stationary points, which helps escape saddle points. Furthermore, we show that adaptive methods can efficiently estimate the aforementioned preconditioner. By gluing together these two components, we provide the first (to our knowledge) second-order convergence result for any adaptive method. The key insight from our analysis is that, compared to SGD, adaptive methods escape saddle points faster, and can converge faster overall to second-order stationary points.

paragraphs: Adaptive optimizers such as Adam and RMSProp are widely used, but explaining their behavior in nonconvex optimization is difficult. This paper views adaptive methods as stochastic gradient descent equipped with a preconditioner: a transformation that changes how gradient updates are scaled. The preconditioner is estimated online as optimization proceeds.

Studying that transformation separately reveals a proposed reason for its effectiveness. Near stationary points, it rescales stochastic gradient noise so that the noise is isotropic, without a preferred direction. The analysis shows how this property helps the optimizer escape saddle points. The authors also establish that adaptive methods can efficiently estimate the relevant preconditioner.

Combining these pieces yields a second-order convergence result for an adaptive method, described by the authors as the first such result to their knowledge. Their analysis indicates faster escape from saddle points than SGD and the possibility of faster overall convergence to second-order stationary points. This supplies a specific theoretical mechanism for adaptive optimization benefits rather than a universal speed guarantee for every use of Adam or RMSProp.
summary.tldr: The analysis explains how adaptive gradient scaling can reshape noise to escape saddle points faster and improve second-order convergence.

title: Escaping Saddle Points with Adaptive Gradient Methods

abstract: Archetypal analysis (AA) aims to extract patterns using self-expressive decomposition of data as convex combinations of extremal points (on the convex hull) of the data. This work presents a computationally efficient greedy AA (GAA) algorithm. GAA leverages the underlying geometry of AA, is scalable to larger datasets, and has significantly faster convergence rate. To achieve this, archetypes are learned via sparse projection of data. In the transformed space, GAA employs an iterative subset selection approach to identify archetypes based on the sparsity of convex representations. The work further presents the use of GAA algorithm for extended AA models such as robust and kernel AA. Experimental results show that GAA is considerably faster while performing comparable to existing methods for tasks such as classification, data visualization/categorization.

paragraphs: Archetypal analysis describes data using mixtures of extreme representative points, called archetypes. These points lie on the data's convex hull, and the mixture weights form convex combinations. The paper develops a greedy algorithm that uses this geometric structure to make finding archetypes more computationally efficient and scalable.

The proposed method, GAA, learns archetypes through sparse projections of the data. In the transformed space, it repeatedly selects subsets using the sparsity of convex representations. Sparsity focuses attention on representations supported by relatively few components. This connects the search for archetypes to the geometry of how data points can be expressed as mixtures.

The authors report a substantially faster convergence rate and extend the algorithm to robust and kernel versions of archetypal analysis. Experiments on classification and data visualization or categorization show considerably faster computation with performance comparable to existing approaches. The practical finding is that exploiting the representation's geometry can reduce computational expense while retaining useful downstream behavior in the tasks evaluated.
summary.tldr: A greedy geometric algorithm uses sparse projections to accelerate archetypal analysis while retaining comparable performance on evaluated tasks.

title: A Geometric Approach to Archetypal Analysis via Sparse Projections

abstract: The goal of Sparse Convex Optimization is to optimize a convex function $f$ under a sparsity constraint $s\leq s^*\gamma$, where $s^*$ is the target number of non-zero entries in a feasible solution (sparsity) and $\gamma\geq 1$ is an approximation factor. There has been a lot of work to analyze the sparsity guarantees of various algorithms (LASSO, Orthogonal Matching Pursuit (OMP), Iterative Hard Thresholding (IHT)) in terms of the Restricted Condition Number $\kappa$. The best known algorithms guarantee to find an approximate solution of value $f(x^*)+\epsilon$ with the sparsity bound of $\gamma = O\left(\kappa\min\left\{\log \frac{f(x^0)-f(x^*)}{\epsilon}, \kappa\right\}\right)$, where $x^*$ is the target solution. We present a new Adaptively Regularized Hard Thresholding (ARHT) algorithm that makes significant progress on this problem by bringing the bound down to $\gamma=O(\kappa)$, which has been shown to be tight for a general class of algorithms including LASSO, OMP, and IHT. This is achieved without significant sacrifice in the runtime efficiency compared to the fastest known algorithms. We also provide a new analysis of OMP with Replacement (OMPR) for general $f$, under the condition $s > s^* \frac{\kappa^2}{4}$, which yields Compressed Sensing bounds under the Restricted Isometry Property (RIP). When compared to other Compressed Sensing approaches, it has the advantage of providing a strong tradeoff between the RIP condition and the solution sparsity, while working for any general function $f$ that meets the RIP condition.

paragraphs: Sparse convex optimization seeks a low objective value while restricting how many coordinates of the solution are nonzero. Algorithms may need more nonzero coordinates than a target solution, and the required increase depends on the restricted condition number, kappa. This paper improves the guarantee on that sparsity overhead while retaining efficient optimization.

The proposed Adaptively Regularized Hard Thresholding algorithm reduces the sparsity approximation factor to O(kappa), improving a previous bound with an additional factor depending on accuracy or kappa. This matches a known tight bound for a broad algorithm class that includes LASSO, Orthogonal Matching Pursuit, and Iterative Hard Thresholding. The improvement comes without a significant runtime-efficiency sacrifice relative to the fastest known algorithms.

The paper also provides a new analysis of Orthogonal Matching Pursuit with Replacement for general objectives, assuming the allowed sparsity exceeds the target sparsity times kappa squared divided by four. This yields compressed-sensing guarantees under the Restricted Isometry Property and a tradeoff between that condition and solution sparsity.
summary.tldr: Adaptively Regularized Hard Thresholding improves sparse optimization guarantees to an O(kappa) sparsity overhead without significantly sacrificing runtime efficiency.

title: Sparse Convex Optimization via Adaptively Regularized Hard Thresholding

abstract: We consider the classical problem of sequential probability assignment under logarithmic loss while competing against an arbitrary, potentially nonparametric class of experts. We obtain tight bounds on the minimax regret via a new approach that exploits the self-concordance property of the logarithmic loss. We show that for any expert class with (sequential) metric entropy $\mathcal{O}(\gamma^{-p})$ at scale $\gamma$, the minimax regret is $\mathcal{O}(n^{\frac{p}{p+1}})$, and that this rate cannot be improved without additional assumptions on the expert class under consideration. As an application of our techniques, we resolve the minimax regret for nonparametric Lipschitz classes of experts.

We show that for any expert class with (sequential) metric entropy $\mathcal{O}(\gamma^{-p})$ at scale $\gamma$, the minimax regret is $\mathcal{O}(n^{\frac{p}{p+1}})$, and that this rate cannot be improved without additional assumptions on the expert class under consideration. paragraphs: This paper studies sequential probability prediction under logarithmic loss. A learner assigns probabilities over time and competes with an expert class that may be nonparametric. The central quantity is minimax regret: the smallest worst-case excess cumulative loss that a prediction strategy can guarantee relative to that comparison class.

The authors develop an analysis using self-concordance, a mathematical property of logarithmic loss. They connect regret to sequential metric entropy, which measures the complexity of the expert class at different resolutions. If that complexity grows as O(gamma to the power minus p) at scale gamma, they obtain regret O(n to the power p/(p+1)) over n rounds.

The rate cannot be improved using only that complexity assumption; stronger guarantees require additional structure in the expert class. As an application, the techniques resolve minimax regret for nonparametric Lipschitz expert classes. The contribution therefore provides both a general complexity-to-regret relationship and a matching account of its limits, using the particular geometry of logarithmic loss.
summary.tldr: Self-concordance yields tight logarithmic-loss regret bounds from expert-class complexity and resolves the rate for nonparametric Lipschitz experts.

title: Tight Bounds on Minimax Regret under Logarithmic Loss via Self-Concordance

abstract: Models trained on synthetic images often face degraded generalization to real data. As a convention, these models are often initialized with ImageNet pretrained representation. Yet the role of ImageNet knowledge is seldom discussed despite common practices that leverage this knowledge to maintain the generalization ability. An example is the careful hand-tuning of early stopping and layer-wise learning rates, which is shown to improve synthetic-to-real generalization but is also laborious and heuristic. In this work, we explicitly encourage the synthetically trained model to maintain similar representations with the ImageNet pretrained model, and propose a \emph{learning-to-optimize (L2O)} strategy to automate the selection of layer-wise learning rates. We demonstrate that the proposed framework can significantly improve the synthetic-to-real generalization performance without seeing and training on real data, while also benefiting downstream tasks such as domain adaptation. Code is available at: https://github.com/NVlabs/ASG.

paragraphs: Training on synthetic images can reduce data-collection costs, but the resulting model may perform poorly on real images. ImageNet initialization often helps, yet retaining its useful knowledge typically depends on manually tuned stopping rules and learning rates. This paper makes preservation of the pretrained representation an explicit part of synthetic-data training.

The framework encourages the evolving model to maintain representations similar to those of its ImageNet-pretrained starting point. It also uses a learning-to-optimize strategy to select layer-specific learning rates automatically. Together, these components aim to balance learning from synthetic data with retaining features that already transfer well to real visual inputs.

The reported experiments show improved synthetic-to-real generalization without training on the target real data, along with benefits for downstream domain adaptation. The role of ImageNet pretraining is essential to interpreting that result: the method preserves previously learned visual knowledge while adapting on synthetic examples. The abstract does not specify which individual representation constraints or learning-rate decisions contribute most to the gains.
summary.tldr: Preserving ImageNet representations and learning layer-specific step sizes improves transfer from synthetic images to real tasks.

title: Automated Synthetic-to-Real Generalization

abstract: In the Correlation Clustering problem, we are given a weighted graph $G$ with its edges labelled as "similar" or "dissimilar" by a binary classifier. The goal is to produce a clustering that minimizes the weight of "disagreements": the sum of the weights of "similar" edges across clusters and "dissimilar" edges within clusters. We study the correlation clustering problem under the following assumption: Every "similar" edge $e$ has weight $w_e \in [ \alpha w, w ]$ and every "dissimilar" edge $e$ has weight $w_e \geq \alpha w$ (where $\alpha \leq 1$ and $w > 0$ is a scaling parameter). We give a $(3 + 2 \log_e (1/\alpha))$ approximation algorithm for this problem. This assumption captures well the scenario when classification errors are asymmetric. Additionally, we show an asymptotically matching Linear Programming integrality gap of $\Omega(\log 1/\alpha)$.

paragraphs: Correlation clustering turns pairwise judgments into groups. A classifier labels graph edges as similar or dissimilar, and a clustering pays for disagreements: similar pairs separated into different groups and dissimilar pairs placed together. Edge weights determine how costly each disagreement is, so the objective accounts for unequal consequences of different classification errors.

The paper studies a particular asymmetry in those weights. Similar edges must have weights between alpha times a positive scale w and w, while dissimilar edges must have weights at least alpha times w. Under this assumption, the authors give an algorithm whose disagreement cost is within a factor of 3 + 2 ln(1/alpha) of the optimum.

The guarantee becomes weaker as alpha decreases and the permitted weight imbalance grows. The authors also establish a linear-programming integrality gap growing as ln(1/alpha), asymptotically matching the approximation’s dependence on that parameter. This identifies a corresponding limitation of the relaxation, rather than proving that every possible clustering algorithm must incur the same approximation factor.
summary.tldr: The paper gives a clustering approximation guarantee under asymmetric edge-weight assumptions and a matching-order linear-programming integrality gap.

title: Correlation Clustering with Asymmetric Classification Errors

abstract: Nonnegative Matrix Factorization (NMF) has become an increasingly important research topic in machine learning. Despite all the practical success, most of existing NMF models are still vulnerable to adversarial attacks. To overcome this limitation, we propose a novel Adversarial NMF (ANMF) approach in which an adversary can exercise some control over the perturbed data generation process. Different from the traditional NMF models which focus on either the regular input or certain types of noise, our model considers potential test adversaries that are beyond the pre-defined constraints, which can cope with various noises (or perturbations). We formulate the proposed model as a bilevel optimization problem and use Alternating Direction Method of Multipliers (ADMM) to solve it with convergence analysis. Theoretically, the robustness analysis of ANMF is established under mild conditions dedicating asymptotically unbiased prediction. Extensive experiments verify that ANMF is robust to a broad categories of perturbations, and achieves state-of-the-art performances on distinct real-world benchmark datasets.

paragraphs: Nonnegative matrix factorization represents data through factors whose entries are nonnegative. Although widely useful, existing approaches can be vulnerable when their input is deliberately perturbed. This paper develops Adversarial NMF, or ANMF, to make the factorization more robust to a broad range of noise and adversarial changes.

The model gives an adversary some control over how perturbed data are generated. It also considers potential test-time adversaries beyond predefined constraints, extending its scope beyond regular inputs or a particular prescribed noise type. The authors express this interaction as a bi-level optimization problem and solve it with the Alternating Direction Method of Multipliers, accompanied by convergence analysis.

Under conditions described as mild, the robustness analysis establishes asymptotically unbiased prediction. Experiments report robustness across broad categories of perturbations and state-of-the-art performance on several real-world benchmark datasets. These findings support explicitly incorporating adversarial perturbations into factorization, with the theoretical claim remaining conditional and asymptotic rather than a guarantee against every possible attack.
summary.tldr: ANMF incorporates adversarial data perturbations into a bi-level factorization model and reports broad empirical robustness.

title: Adversarial Nonnegative Matrix Factorization

abstract: The variational autoencoder (VAE) can learn the manifold of natural images on certain datasets, as evidenced by meaningful interpolating or extrapolating in the continuous latent space. However, on discrete data such as text, it is unclear if unsupervised learning can discover similar latent space that allows controllable manipulation. In this work, we find that sequence VAEs trained on text fail to properly decode when the latent codes are manipulated, because the modified codes often land in holes or vacant regions in the aggregated posterior latent space, where the decoding network fails to generalize. Both as a validation of the explanation and as a fix to the problem, we propose to constrain the posterior mean to a learned probability simplex, and performs manipulation within this simplex. Our proposed method mitigates the latent vacancy problem and achieves the first success in unsupervised learning of controllable representations for text. Empirically, our method outperforms unsupervised baselines and strong supervised approaches on text style transfer, and is capable of performing more flexible fine-grained control over text generation than existing methods.
