paragraphs: A useful latent representation should allow controlled changes to generated text when its code is manipulated. This paper investigates why sequence variational autoencoders can fail at that task. The authors find that modified codes often enter vacant regions of the aggregated posterior, where the decoder does not generalize properly.

Their solution constrains the posterior mean to a learned probability simplex and performs manipulation within that simplex. This restriction is designed to mitigate the latent vacancy problem. It also tests the proposed explanation: changing where manipulation occurs addresses the same empty regions identified as the source of decoding failures.

The authors report successful unsupervised learning of controllable text representations, describing it as the first such success. In text style transfer experiments, the method outperforms unsupervised baselines and strong supervised approaches. It also enables more flexible fine-grained control than existing methods in the reported evaluation. The contribution links a specific failure of latent-space manipulation to a geometric constraint that improves controllable generation.
summary.tldr: Constraining text VAE representations to a learned probability simplex reduces latent vacancies and improves unsupervised control of generated text.

title: On Variational Learning of Controllable Representations for Text without Supervision

abstract: Regression forests, based on ensemble approaches such as bagging or boosting, have long been recognized as the leading off-the-shelf method for regression. However, forests rely on a greedy top-down procedure such as CART to learn each tree. We extend a recent algorithm for learning classification trees, Tree Alternating Optimization (TAO), to the regression case, and use it with bagging to construct regression forests of oblique trees, having hyperplane splits at the decision nodes. In a wide range of datasets, we show that the resulting forests exceed the accuracy of state-of-the-art algorithms such as random forests, AdaBoost or gradient boosting, often considerably, while yielding forests that have usually fewer and shallower trees and hence fewer parameters and faster inference overall. This result has an immense practical impact and advocates for the power of optimization in ensemble learning.
originalAbstract: Regression forests, based on ensemble approaches such as bagging or boosting, have long been recognized as the leading off-the-shelf method for regression. However, forests rely on a greedy top-down procedure such as CART to learn each tree. We extend a recent algorithm for learning classification trees, Tree Alternating Optimization (TAO), to the regression case, and use it with bagging to construct regression forests of oblique trees, having hyperplane splits at the decision nodes. In a wide range of datasets, we show that the resulting forests exceed the accuracy of state-of-the-art algorithms such as random forests, AdaBoost or gradient boosting, often considerably, while yielding forests that have usually fewer and shallower trees and hence fewer parameters and faster inference overall. This result has an immense practical impact and advocates for the power of optimization in ensemble learning.

paragraphs: Regression forests combine multiple trees to predict numerical outcomes. Their effectiveness often depends on trees built by greedy, top-down procedures such as CART. This paper asks how much the forest can improve when the method for optimizing each tree changes, focusing on tree learning as a source of better ensemble performance.

The authors extend Tree Alternating Optimization, previously developed for classification trees, to regression. They combine it with bagging to build forests of oblique trees. These trees use hyperplane decisions at their internal nodes, giving each split a form that can involve combinations of input features. The approach therefore brings an alternative tree optimizer into the construction of regression ensembles.

Across a wide range of datasets, the resulting forests outperform random forests, AdaBoost, and gradient boosting in accuracy, often considerably. They also usually contain fewer and shallower trees, producing fewer parameters and faster overall inference. These are empirical findings with explicit qualifications: the size advantages are usual, not universal. The results show that improved tree optimization can benefit both prediction quality and deployment efficiency.
summary.tldr: Tree Alternating Optimization produces regression forests that are more accurate and usually smaller and faster in the reported evaluations.

title: Smaller, more accurate regression forests using tree alternating optimization

abstract: Bayesian optimization (BO) is a popular tool for optimizing complex and costly-to-evaluate black-box objective functions. To further reduce the number of function evaluations, any party performing BO may be interested to collaborate with others to optimize the same objective function concurrently. To do this, existing BO algorithms have considered optimizing a batch of input queries in parallel and provided theoretical bounds on their cumulative regret reflecting inefficiency. However, when the objective function values are correlated with real-world rewards (e.g., money), parties may be hesitant to collaborate if they risk incurring larger cumulative regret (i.e., smaller real-world reward) than others. This paper shows that fairness and efficiency are both necessary for the collaborative BO setting. Inspired by social welfare concepts from economics, we propose a new notion of regret capturing these properties and a collaborative BO algorithm whose convergence rate can be theoretically guaranteed by bounding the new regret, both of which share an adjustable parameter for trading off between fairness vs. efficiency. We empirically demonstrate the benefits (e.g., increased fairness) of our algorithm using synthetic and real-world datasets.

paragraphs: Bayesian optimization helps choose evaluations of an expensive black-box function. Several parties could search the same function together, sharing the work of finding good inputs. But when evaluated outcomes correspond to rewards such as money, an efficient collective search can still be unattractive if some participants receive substantially worse outcomes than others.

This paper introduces a notion of regret that incorporates both efficiency and fairness, drawing on social-welfare ideas from economics. Regret represents the cost of making less successful choices during optimization. The authors develop a collaborative algorithm alongside this measure, with an adjustable parameter in both that controls the tradeoff between collective efficiency and fairness among participants.

The analysis bounds the new regret to provide a theoretical convergence-rate guarantee. Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate benefits including increased fairness. The contribution is therefore both an evaluation criterion and an optimization procedure: it makes the distribution of search outcomes among collaborators part of the objective, rather than assessing collaboration solely through aggregate inefficiency.
summary.tldr: A collaborative Bayesian optimization method explicitly trades off overall search efficiency against fairness in participants’ accumulated rewards.

title: Collaborative Bayesian Optimization with Fair Regret

abstract: GPT-3 can perform numerous tasks when provided a natural language prompt that contains a few training examples. We show that this type of few-shot learning can be unstable: the choice of prompt format, training examples, and even the order of the examples can cause accuracy to vary from near chance to near state-of-the-art. We demonstrate that this instability arises from the bias of language models towards predicting certain answers, e.g., those that are placed near the end of the prompt or are common in the pre-training data. To mitigate this, we first estimate the model’s bias towards each answer by asking for its prediction when given a training prompt and a content-free test input such as "N/A". We then fit calibration parameters that cause the prediction for this input to be uniform across answers. On a diverse set of tasks, this contextual calibration procedure substantially improves GPT-3 and GPT-2’s accuracy (up to 30.0% absolute) across different choices of the prompt, while also making learning considerably more stable.

paragraphs: Giving a language model a few examples inside a prompt can produce strikingly uneven results. This paper shows that changing the prompt format, the examples, or even their order can move accuracy from near chance to near state-of-the-art. It connects this instability to preferences for particular answers, including answers appearing late in the prompt or frequently in pretraining data.

The proposed contextual calibration procedure measures these preferences before using the model on meaningful test inputs. It keeps the training prompt but supplies a content-free input such as N/A. The resulting answer probabilities reveal how strongly the prompt and model favor each answer without useful test content.

The authors then fit calibration parameters so that this content-free prediction becomes uniform across answers. Across diverse tasks, this adjustment substantially improves GPT-3 and GPT-2 accuracy and reduces sensitivity to prompt choices. The largest reported improvement is 30.0 percentage points. The finding shows that correcting contextual answer preferences can improve both performance and consistency in few-shot prompting.
summary.tldr: Calibrating answer probabilities with a content-free input improves few-shot language-model accuracy and reduces sensitivity to prompt choices.

title: Calibrate Before Use: Improving Few-shot Performance of Language Models

abstract: Auctions with partially-revealed information about items are broadly employed in real-world applications, but the underlying mechanisms have limited theoretical support. In this work, we study a machine learning formulation of these types of mechanisms, presenting algorithms that are no-regret from the buyer’s perspective. Specifically, a buyer who wishes to maximize his utility interacts repeatedly with a platform over a series of $T$ rounds. In each round, a new item is drawn from an unknown distribution and the platform publishes a price together with incomplete, “masked” information about the item. The buyer then decides whether to purchase the item. We formalize this problem as an online learning task where the goal is to have low regret with respect to a myopic oracle that has perfect knowledge of the distribution over items and the seller’s masking function. When the distribution over items is known to the buyer and the mask is a SimHash function mapping $\R^d$ to $\{0,1\}^{\ell}$, our algorithm has regret $\tilde \cO((Td\ell)^{\nicefrac{1}{2}})$. In a fully agnostic setting when the mask is an arbitrary function mapping to a set of size $n$ and the prices are stochastic, our algorithm has regret $\tilde \cO((Tn)^{\nicefrac{1}{2}})$.

paragraphs: The paper studies a buyer repeatedly offered items with a price and an incomplete description. Each item comes from an unknown distribution, and the buyer must decide whether to purchase it using the masked information. The learning objective is to maximize utility while gradually improving these decisions across T rounds.

Performance is measured against a myopic oracle that knows the item distribution and the seller's masking function. Regret captures the buyer's accumulated shortfall relative to that benchmark. The authors formulate the interaction as an online learning problem and give algorithms with no-regret guarantees under two different sets of conditions.

When the item distribution is known and masking uses SimHash from d-dimensional inputs to length-ell binary outputs, regret scales as the square root of Td ell, up to logarithmic factors. With an arbitrary mask taking n possible values and stochastic prices, the fully agnostic result scales as the square root of Tn. These bounds formalize how learning can reduce average regret despite partial item information.
summary.tldr: Online purchasing algorithms achieve conditional no-regret guarantees when buyers see prices and masked item information.

title: No-Regret Learning in Partially-Informed Auctions

abstract: In recent work, it has been shown that reinforcement learning (RL) is capable of solving a variety of problems at sometimes super-human performance levels. But despite continued advances in the field, applying RL to complex real-world control and optimisation problems has proven difficult. In this contribution, we demonstrate how to successfully apply RL to the optimisation of a highly complex real-world machine {–} specifically a linear particle accelerator {–} in an only partially observable setting and without requiring training on the real machine. Our method outperforms conventional optimisation algorithms in both the achieved result and time taken as well as already achieving close to human-level performance. We expect that such automation of machine optimisation will push the limits of operability, increase machine availability and lead to a paradigm shift in how such machines are operated, ultimately facilitating advances in a variety of fields, such as science and medicine among many others.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning has achieved strong results in many settings, but applying it to complex physical machinery remains difficult. This paper demonstrates its use for optimizing a linear particle accelerator. The setting is only partially observable, meaning the optimization must proceed without a complete view of the machine’s state.

A central feature of the demonstration is that learning does not require training on the real accelerator. The reported method nevertheless operates successfully on the real machine. This brings together two practical challenges: preparing a learning-based optimizer without real-machine training and using it when the available observations provide incomplete information about the system.

In the reported comparison, the method outperforms conventional optimization algorithms in both the achieved result and the time required, while approaching human-level performance. These findings establish the feasibility of the approach for the demonstrated accelerator task. The authors further anticipate that automation could improve machine availability and operability, with benefits for fields using accelerators. Those broader operational benefits are presented as expectations rather than measured outcomes of the study.
summary.tldr: A reinforcement learning method optimizes a real linear particle accelerator under partial observability without training on the real machine.

title: Learning-based Optimisation of Particle Accelerators Under Partial Observability Without Real-World Training

abstract: We consider feature representation learning problem of molecular graphs. Graph Neural Networks have been widely used in feature representation learning of molecular graphs. However, most existing methods deal with molecular graphs individually while neglecting their connections, such as motif-level relationships. We propose a novel molecular graph representation learning method by constructing a heterogeneous motif graph to address this issue. In particular, we build a heterogeneous motif graph that contains motif nodes and molecular nodes. Each motif node corresponds to a motif extracted from molecules. Then, we propose a Heterogeneous Motif Graph Neural Network (HM-GNN) to learn feature representations for each node in the heterogeneous motif graph. Our heterogeneous motif graph also enables effective multi-task learning, especially for small molecular datasets. To address the potential efficiency issue, we propose to use an edge sampler, which can significantly reduce computational resources usage. The experimental results show that our model consistently outperforms previous state-of-the-art models. Under multi-task settings, the promising performances of our methods on combined datasets shed light on a new learning paradigm for small molecular datasets. Finally, we show that our model achieves similar performances with significantly less computational resources by using our edge sampler.

paragraphs: Molecular graph learning often treats each molecule separately, even though different molecules can share recurring structural motifs. This paper uses those relationships as part of the representation-learning problem. Its aim is to let molecular representations benefit from connections across molecules, rather than drawing information only from each individual molecular graph.

The authors construct a heterogeneous graph with two kinds of nodes: molecules and motifs extracted from molecules. A Heterogeneous Motif Graph Neural Network learns representations for nodes in this shared structure. The graph also supports learning multiple tasks together, which the authors identify as especially useful for small molecular datasets. An edge sampler reduces the computational resources needed to process it.

Experiments show consistent improvements over previous state-of-the-art models. Results on combined datasets under multitask learning suggest a useful approach for smaller molecular datasets. The edge sampler preserves similar performance while using substantially fewer computational resources. Together, the findings support both the value of shared motif relationships and a practical mechanism for making this broader graph representation less expensive to use.
summary.tldr: HM-GNN learns molecular representations through shared motif relationships, improving reported performance while edge sampling reduces computation.

title: Molecular Representation Learning via Heterogeneous Motif Graph Neural Networks

abstract: Invariant Risk Minimization (IRM) is an emerging invariant feature extracting technique to help generalization with distributional shift. However, we find that there exists a basic and intractable contradiction between the model trainability and generalization ability in IRM. On one hand, recent studies on deep learning theory indicate the importance of large-sized or even overparameterized neural networks to make the model easy to train. On the other hand, unlike empirical risk minimization that can be benefited from overparameterization, our empirical and theoretical analyses show that the generalization ability of IRM is much easier to be demolished by overfitting caused by overparameterization. In this paper, we propose a simple yet effective paradigm named Sparse Invariant Risk Minimization (SparseIRM) to address this contradiction. Our key idea is to employ a global sparsity constraint as a defense to prevent spurious features from leaking in during the whole IRM process. Compared with sparisfy-after-training prototype by prior work which can discard invariant features, the global sparsity constraint limits the budget for feature selection and enforces SparseIRM to select the invariant features. We illustrate the benefit of SparseIRM through a theoretical analysis on a simple linear case. Empirically we demonstrate the power of SparseIRM through various datasets and models and surpass state-of-the-art methods with a gap up to 29%.

paragraphs: Invariant risk minimization aims to learn features that remain useful when the data distribution changes. This paper identifies a tension in using large networks for that goal: additional capacity can make training easier, yet its theoretical and empirical analyses show that overparameterization can make IRM particularly vulnerable to overfitting and damaged generalization.

SparseIRM addresses the tension by imposing a global sparsity constraint throughout the IRM process. The constraint limits the feature-selection budget and is intended to prevent spurious features from entering the learned solution. Applying sparsity during learning matters because removing features only after training can also discard useful invariant features.

The authors illustrate the benefit with a theoretical analysis of a simple linear case and evaluate the approach across multiple datasets and models. They report improvements over state-of-the-art methods reaching a gap of up to 29%. The findings support controlling feature selection throughout invariant learning, with the formal illustration scoped to the linear setting and the broader gains established experimentally. The largest reported gap describes the strongest observed improvement, rather than a uniform gain across settings.
summary.tldr: SparseIRM constrains sparsity throughout invariant risk minimization to curb spurious feature learning and improve generalization under distribution shifts.

title: Sparse Invariant Risk Minimization

abstract: Datasets often have their intrinsic symmetries, and particular deep-learning models called equivariant or invariant models have been developed to exploit these symmetries. However, if some or all of these symmetries are only approximate, which frequently happens in practice, these models may be suboptimal due to the architectural restrictions imposed on them. We tackle this issue of approximate symmetries in a setup where symmetries are mixed, i.e., they are symmetries of not single but multiple different types and the degree of approximation varies across these types. Instead of proposing a new architectural restriction as in most of the previous approaches, we present a regularizer-based method for building a model for a dataset with mixed approximate symmetries. The key component of our method is what we call equivariance regularizer for a given type of symmetries, which measures how much a model is equivariant with respect to the symmetries of the type. Our method is trained with these regularizers, one per each symmetry type, and the strength of the regularizers is automatically tuned during training, leading to the discovery of the approximation levels of some candidate symmetry types without explicit supervision. Using synthetic function approximation and motion forecasting tasks, we demonstrate that our method achieves better accuracy than prior approaches while discovering the approximate symmetry levels correctly.

paragraphs: Symmetries describe transformations under which a model’s behavior should change predictably or remain unchanged. Models can build these relationships directly into their architecture, but that can be restrictive when real data follow a symmetry only approximately. This paper considers datasets with several kinds of symmetry, each potentially holding to a different degree.

The method introduces a separate equivariance regularizer for each candidate symmetry type. Each regularizer measures how closely the model follows that symmetry. During training, the method automatically adjusts the strength of these penalties. This lets the model learn how strongly to respect different transformations while also discovering approximation levels for some candidate symmetry types without explicit supervision.

The authors evaluate the approach on synthetic function approximation and motion forecasting. They report better accuracy than prior approaches and correct discovery of approximate symmetry levels. The findings support treating symmetry as something that can be encouraged with adjustable strength. This is useful when several structural patterns coexist in the data but enforcing all of them exactly would impose an overly restrictive model.
summary.tldr: Automatically tuned equivariance penalties let models learn different strengths of approximate symmetry, improving accuracy in the reported tasks.

title: Regularizing Towards Soft Equivariance Under Mixed Symmetries

abstract: We propose iterative inversion - an algorithm for learning an inverse function without input-output pairs, but only with samples from the desired output distribution and access to the forward function. The key challenge is a distribution shift between the desired outputs and the outputs of an initial random guess, and we prove that iterative inversion can steer the learning correctly, under rather strict conditions on the function. We apply iterative inversion to learn control. Our input is a set of demonstrations of desired behavior, given as video embeddings of trajectories (without actions), and our method iteratively learns to imitate trajectories generated by the current policy, perturbed by random exploration noise. Our approach does not require rewards, and only employs supervised learning, which can be easily scaled to use state-of-the-art trajectory embedding techniques and policy representations. Indeed, with a VQ-VAE embedding, and a transformer-based policy, we demonstrate non-trivial continuous control on several tasks (videos available at https://sites.google.com/view/iter-inver). Further, we report an improved performance on imitating diverse behaviors compared to reward based methods.

paragraphs: Learning an inverse normally benefits from examples pairing inputs with outputs. Iterative inversion instead assumes access to the forward function and samples of the outputs one wants to produce. Its main challenge is that outputs from an initial random guess can differ substantially from the desired output distribution. The authors prove that their procedure can guide learning correctly under strict conditions on the function.

For control, desired behavior is supplied through video embeddings of trajectories without action labels. The method repeatedly learns to imitate trajectories produced by its current policy with added random exploration noise. The authors combine a VQ-VAE trajectory embedding with a transformer policy and demonstrate non-trivial continuous control on several tasks. The theoretical guarantee remains conditional, while the control experiments show how the iterative procedure can work with expressive trajectory and policy representations.
summary.tldr: Iterative inversion learns control from action-free behavioral demonstrations using supervised updates and exploration, with inverse-learning guarantees under strict conditions.

title: Learning Control by Iterative Inversion

abstract: In many applications of Reinforcement Learning (RL), it is critically important that the algorithm performs safely, such that instantaneous hard constraints are satisfied at each step, and unsafe states and actions are avoided. However, existing algorithms for “safe” RL are often designed under constraints that either require expected cumulative costs to be bounded or assume all states are safe. Thus, such algorithms could violate instantaneous hard constraints and traverse unsafe states (and actions) in practice. Hence, in this paper, we develop the first near-optimal safe RL algorithm for episodic Markov Decision Processes with unsafe states and actions under instantaneous hard constraints and the linear mixture model. It achieves a regret $\tilde{O}(\frac{d H^3 \sqrt{d K}}{\Delta_c})$ that nearly matches the state-of-the-art regret in the setting with only unsafe actions and that in the unconstrained setting, and is safe at each step, where $d$ is the feature-mapping dimension, $K$ is the number of episodes, $H$ is the episode length, and $\Delta_c$ is a safety-related parameter. We also provide a lower bound $\tilde{\Omega}(\max\{d H \sqrt{K}, \frac{H}{\Delta_c^2}\})$, which indicates that the dependency on $\Delta_c$ is necessary. Further, both our algorithm design and regret analysis involve several novel ideas, which may be of independent interest.

paragraphs: Safety in reinforcement learning can mean limiting accumulated costs, but that does not necessarily prevent an unsafe action or state at a particular moment. This paper addresses the stricter requirement that hard safety constraints hold at every step. Its setting includes both unsafe states and unsafe actions, so safety must cover where the learner goes as well as what it does.

The authors develop a near-optimal algorithm for episodic Markov decision processes under a linear mixture model. Within this setting, the algorithm remains safe at each step while controlling regret, the performance lost during learning. Its regret bound depends on the feature dimension, episode length, number of episodes, and a safety-related parameter.

The upper bound nearly matches existing regret results for settings with only unsafe actions and for unconstrained learning. A complementary lower bound shows that dependence on the safety parameter is unavoidable. This supports the significance of the result without claiming that every factor in the upper bound is exactly optimal.
summary.tldr: A theoretically near-optimal reinforcement learning algorithm maintains step-by-step safety with unsafe states and actions under a linear mixture model.

title: A Near-Optimal Algorithm for Safe Reinforcement Learning Under Instantaneous Hard Constraints

abstract: Although contrastive learning methods have shown prevailing performance on a variety of representation learning tasks, they encounter difficulty when the training dataset is long-tailed. Many researchers have combined contrastive learning and a logit adjustment technique to address this problem, but the combinations are done ad-hoc and a theoretical background has not yet been provided. The goal of this paper is to provide the background and further improve the performance. First, we show that the fundamental reason contrastive learning methods struggle with long-tailed tasks is that they try to maximize the mutual information between latent features and input data. As ground-truth labels are not considered in the maximization, they are not able to address imbalances between classes. Rather, we interpret the long-tailed recognition task as a mutual information maximization between latent features and ground-truth labels. This approach integrates contrastive learning and logit adjustment seamlessly to derive a loss function that shows state-of-the-art performance on long-tailed recognition benchmarks. It also demonstrates its efficacy in image segmentation tasks, verifying its versatility beyond image classification. Code is available at https://github.com/bluecdm/Long-tailed-recognition.

The authors identify a mismatch in what standard contrastive learning tries to preserve. Maximizing mutual information between latent features and input data does not explicitly account for ground-truth labels, and therefore does not address class imbalance through that objective. They instead formulate recognition around maximizing mutual information between features and labels, placing class identity directly into the information being retained.

This formulation produces a loss that integrates contrastive learning and logit adjustment within one theoretical approach. The resulting method achieves state-of-the-art performance on the reported long-tailed recognition benchmarks. It also works effectively for image segmentation, extending the empirical evidence beyond image classification. The main contribution is a principled connection between the information objective and the imbalance correction.
summary.tldr: Maximizing information between features and labels yields a unified contrastive-learning and logit-adjustment loss for long-tailed recognition.

title: Long-Tailed Recognition by Mutual Information Maximization between Latent Features and Ground-Truth Labels

abstract: Learning heuristics for vehicle routing problems (VRPs) has gained much attention due to the less reliance on hand-crafted rules. However, existing methods are typically trained and tested on the same task with a fixed size and distribution (of nodes), and hence suffer from limited generalization performance. This paper studies a challenging yet realistic setting, which considers generalization across both size and distribution in VRPs. We propose a generic meta-learning framework, which enables effective training of an initialized model with the capability of fast adaptation to new tasks during inference. We further develop a simple yet efficient approximation method to reduce the training overhead. Extensive experiments on both synthetic and benchmark instances of the traveling salesman problem (TSP) and capacitated vehicle routing problem (CVRP) demonstrate the effectiveness of our method. The code is available at: https://github.com/RoyalSkye/Omni-VRP.

This paper studies a broader generalization setting in which both can change. The challenge is to prepare a learned solver for new routing tasks beyond its original training configuration.

The authors propose a generic meta-learning framework that trains a model initialization for rapid adaptation during inference. The desired outcome is a starting model that can adjust effectively to a new task. They also introduce a simple approximation method to reduce the overhead of training within this framework.

Experiments cover the traveling salesman problem and capacitated vehicle routing problem using both synthetic instances and benchmark instances. The reported results demonstrate the method’s effectiveness in the studied setting. Its contribution is to make adaptation across problem size and distribution an explicit training objective, connecting the way a solver is initialized to how it will be used when routing tasks change.
summary.tldr: A meta-learning framework prepares neural routing solvers to adapt quickly across changes in problem size and node distribution.

title: Towards Omni-generalizable Neural Methods for Vehicle Routing Problems

abstract: We study the problem of parameter-free stochastic optimization, inquiring whether, and under what conditions, do fully parameter-free methods exist: these are methods that achieve convergence rates competitive with optimally tuned methods, without requiring significant knowledge of the true problem parameters. Existing parameter-free methods can only be considered “partially” parameter-free, as they require some non-trivial knowledge of the true problem parameters, such as a bound on the stochastic gradient norms, a bound on the distance to a minimizer, etc. In the non-convex setting, we demonstrate that a simple hyperparameter search technique results in a fully parameter-free method that outperforms more sophisticated state-of-the-art algorithms. We also provide a similar result in the convex setting with access to noisy function values under mild noise assumptions. Finally, assuming only access to stochastic gradients, we establish a lower bound that renders fully parameter-free stochastic convex optimization infeasible, and provide a method which is (partially) parameter-free up to the limit indicated by our lower bound.

paragraphs: An optimizer described as parameter-free may still need important information about the problem, such as a bound on gradient magnitudes or the distance to a solution. This paper asks when methods can genuinely avoid substantial prior knowledge while achieving convergence rates competitive with optimally tuned methods.

The answer depends on the optimization setting and the information available. In non-convex optimization, the authors show that a simple hyperparameter search produces a fully parameter-free method that outperforms more sophisticated state-of-the-art algorithms. They obtain a similar positive result for convex optimization when noisy function values are available and the noise satisfies mild assumptions.

The picture changes when a convex optimizer can access only stochastic gradients. In that setting, the paper proves a lower bound ruling out fully parameter-free optimization in the stated sense. It then gives a partially parameter-free method that reaches the limit described by that bound. The results clarify that removing tuning requirements is an information-dependent possibility: access to function values can change what is achievable, and the label parameter-free should be interpreted together with its remaining knowledge requirements.
summary.tldr: Fully parameter-free stochastic optimization is possible in some settings, but a lower bound rules it out for convex problems with gradient-only access.

title: How Free is Parameter-Free Stochastic Optimization?

abstract: How do neural networks extract patterns from pixels? Feature visualizations attempt to answer this important question by visualizing highly activating patterns through optimization. Today, visualization methods form the foundation of our knowledge about the internal workings of neural networks, as a type of mechanistic interpretability. Here we ask: How reliable are feature visualizations? We start our investigation by developing network circuits that trick feature visualizations into showing arbitrary patterns that are completely disconnected from normal network behavior on natural input. We then provide evidence for a similar phenomenon occurring in standard, unmanipulated networks: feature visualizations are processed very differently from standard input, casting doubt on their ability to "explain" how neural networks process natural images. This can be used as a sanity check for feature visualizations. We underpin our empirical findings by theory proving that the set of functions that can be reliably understood by feature visualization is extremely small and does not include general black-box neural networks. Therefore, a promising way forward could be the development of networks that enforce certain structures in order to ensure more reliable feature visualizations.

This paper investigates whether the resulting images reliably describe how a network processes natural inputs. Its central concern is the connection between an optimized visualization and the behavior that visualization is supposed to explain.

The authors first construct network circuits that make feature visualization display arbitrary patterns unrelated to normal behavior on natural images. They then provide evidence of a related phenomenon in ordinary, unmodified networks: optimized visualizations are processed very differently from standard inputs. Comparing those processing behaviors offers a sanity check for interpretations based on the generated images.

The theoretical analysis shows that the class of functions reliably understandable through feature visualization is extremely restricted and excludes general black-box neural networks. These findings challenge the assumption that a compelling visualization is sufficient evidence of a feature's natural role. The authors suggest that imposing suitable structure on networks could be a promising route toward more reliable visual explanations.
summary.tldr: Feature visualizations can be disconnected from natural-input behavior, and the paper identifies empirical and theoretical reasons to question their reliability.

title: Don’t trust your eyes: on the (un)reliability of feature visualizations

abstract: A key aspect of intelligence is the ability to demonstrate a broad spectrum of behaviors for adapting to unexpected situations. Over the past decade, advancements in deep reinforcement learning have led to groundbreaking achievements to solve complex continuous control tasks. However, most approaches return only one solution specialized for a specific problem. We introduce Quality-Diversity Actor-Critic (QDAC), an off-policy actor-critic deep reinforcement learning algorithm that leverages a value function critic and a successor features critic to learn high-performing and diverse behaviors. In this framework, the actor optimizes an objective that seamlessly unifies both critics using constrained optimization to (1) maximize return, while (2) executing diverse skills. Compared with other Quality-Diversity methods, QDAC achieves significantly higher performance and more diverse behaviors on six challenging continuous control locomotion tasks. We also demonstrate that we can harness the learned skills to adapt better than other baselines to five perturbed environments. Finally, qualitative analyses showcase a range of remarkable behaviors: adaptive-intelligent-robotics.github.io/QDAC.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning often produces one behavior specialized for a particular task. Quality-Diversity Actor-Critic, or QDAC, instead aims to learn a collection of behaviors that are both effective and varied. Such a collection can provide useful alternatives when the conditions facing an agent change.

QDAC is an off-policy actor-critic method with two critics: a value-function critic and a successor-features critic. Its actor uses a constrained optimization objective that brings the two together, pursuing high return while executing diverse skills. This makes behavioral diversity part of the learning objective alongside task performance.

Across six continuous-control locomotion tasks, QDAC achieves significantly higher performance and greater behavioral diversity than the compared quality-diversity methods. The authors also use the learned skills in five perturbed environments, where they support better adaptation than the evaluated baselines. These results connect the training objective to both a richer set of behaviors and improved responses to changed conditions in the tested environments.
summary.tldr: QDAC combines value and successor-features critics to learn diverse, high-performing skills that improve adaptation in tested perturbed environments.

title: Quality-Diversity Actor-Critic: Learning High-Performing and Diverse Behaviors via Value and Successor Features Critics

abstract: Instrumental variables (IVs) are widely used for estimating causal effects. There are two main challenges when using instrumental variables. First of all, using IV without additional assumptions such as linearity, the causal effect may still not be identifiable. Second, when selecting an IV, the validity of the selected IV is typically not testable since the causal graph is not identifiable from observational data. In this paper, we propose a method for bounding the causal effect with instrumental variables under weak confounding. In addition, we present a novel criterion to falsify the IV with side information about the confounder. We demonstrate the utility of the proposed method with simulated and real-world datasets.

paragraphs: Instrumental variables are used to estimate causal effects, but choosing an instrument does not automatically resolve uncertainty about causation. Without additional assumptions, such as linear relationships, the available evidence may not determine a unique causal effect. The paper addresses this difficulty by seeking bounds on the effect.

The proposed bounding method operates under weak confounding. Its goal is partial identification: restricting the possible causal effect to a range rather than necessarily recovering one value. This distinction matters because a useful causal conclusion can describe which effects remain possible even when exact identification is unavailable.

The paper also addresses whether a proposed instrument can be ruled out. Observational data typically cannot establish the relevant causal graph, making instrument validity difficult to test. The authors introduce a falsification criterion that uses side information about the confounder. This provides a way to reject an instrument under the criterion, rather than a general certification of validity. Simulated and real-world datasets demonstrate the utility of the proposed approach.
summary.tldr: The paper bounds causal effects under weak confounding and uses side information about confounders to help falsify proposed instrumental variables.

title: Conditional Common Entropy for Instrumental Variable Testing and Partial Identification

abstract: The efficient and theoretically sound uncertainty quantification is crucial for building trust in deep learning models. This has spurred a growing interest in conformal prediction (CP), a powerful technique that provides a model-agnostic and distribution-free method for obtaining conformal prediction sets with theoretical guarantees. However, the vulnerabilities of such CP methods with regard to dedicated data poisoning attacks have not been studied previously. To bridge this gap, for the first time, we in this paper propose a new class of black-box data poisoning attacks against CP, where the adversary aims to cause the desired manipulations of some specific examples’ prediction uncertainty results (instead of misclassifications). Additionally, we design novel optimization frameworks for our proposed attacks. Further, we conduct extensive experiments to validate the effectiveness of our attacks on various settings (e.g., the full and split CP settings). Notably, our extensive experiments show that our attacks are more effective in manipulating uncertainty results than traditional poisoning attacks that aim at inducing misclassifications, and existing defenses against conventional attacks are ineffective against our proposed attacks.

paragraphs: Conformal prediction constructs prediction sets to express uncertainty and offers theoretical guarantees through a model-agnostic, distribution-free framework. This paper studies a distinct security question: whether an adversary can poison data to manipulate the uncertainty reported for particular examples. The target is the uncertainty result itself, rather than simply causing an incorrect class prediction.

The authors introduce a class of black-box poisoning attacks designed around this objective and develop optimization frameworks for carrying them out. They evaluate the attacks in several settings, including full and split conformal prediction. This places the evaluation directly on the behavior of uncertainty estimation under deliberately corrupted data.

In the reported experiments, these dedicated attacks manipulate uncertainty more effectively than conventional poisoning attacks aimed at misclassification. Existing defenses against conventional attacks are also ineffective against the proposed attacks in the evaluations. The findings show why uncertainty systems merit their own adversarial analysis: an attack objective centered on prediction sets can expose weaknesses that classification-oriented attacks and defenses do not adequately address.
summary.tldr: Dedicated black-box poisoning attacks manipulate conformal prediction uncertainty more effectively than misclassification-focused attacks in the reported experiments.

title: Data Poisoning Attacks against Conformal Prediction

abstract: The ever-growing ecosystem of LLMs has posed a challenge in selecting the most appropriate pre-trained model to fine-tune amidst a sea of options. Given constrained resources, fine-tuning all models and making selections afterward is unrealistic. In this work, we formulate this resource-constrained selection task into predicting fine-tuning performance and illustrate its natural connection with Scaling Law. Unlike pre-training, we find that the fine-tuning scaling curve includes not just the well-known "power phase" but also the previously unobserved "pre-power phase". We also explain why existing Scaling Law fails to capture this phase transition phenomenon both theoretically and empirically. To address this, we introduce the concept of "pre-learned data size" into our Rectified Scaling Law, which overcomes theoretical limitations and fits experimental results much better. By leveraging our law, we propose a novel LLM selection algorithm that selects the near-optimal model with hundreds of times less resource consumption, while other methods may provide negatively correlated selection. The project page is available at rectified-scaling-law.github.io.

This paper frames selection as predicting eventual fine-tuning performance. It connects that prediction problem to scaling laws, which describe how performance changes with the amount of data used.

summary.tldr: A scaling law that captures a previously overlooked fine-tuning phase enables near-optimal model selection with substantially lower reported resource use.

title: Selecting Large Language Model to Fine-tune via Rectified Scaling Law

abstract: In preference-based Reinforcement Learning (RL), obtaining a large number of preference labels are both time-consuming and costly. Furthermore, the queried human preferences cannot be utilized for the new tasks. In this paper, we propose Zero-shot Cross-task Preference Alignment and Robust Reward Learning (PEARL), which learns policies from cross-task preference transfer without any human labels of the target task. Our contributions include two novel components that facilitate the transfer and learning process. The first is Cross-task Preference Alignment (CPA), which transfers the preferences between tasks via optimal transport. The key idea of CPA is to use Gromov-Wasserstein distance to align the trajectories between tasks, and the solved optimal transport matrix serves as the correspondence between trajectories. The target task preferences are computed as the weighted sum of source task preference labels with the correspondence as weights. Moreover, to ensure robust learning from these transferred labels, we introduce Robust Reward Learning (RRL), which considers both reward mean and uncertainty by modeling rewards as Gaussian distributions. Empirical results on robotic manipulation tasks from Meta-World and Robomimic demonstrate that our method is capable of transferring preference labels across tasks accurately and then learns well-behaved policies. Notably, our approach significantly exceeds existing methods when there are few human preferences. The code and videos of our method are available at: https://sites.google.com/view/pearl-preference.

PEARL aims to reuse preferences from other tasks to learn a target-task policy without human preference labels for that target. Its zero-shot claim concerns this transfer of preference supervision.

Cross-task Preference Alignment uses optimal transport to establish correspondences between trajectories from different tasks. This addresses the need to learn robustly from transferred labels. Experiments on robotic manipulation tasks in Meta-World and Robomimic report accurate preference transfer and well-behaved learned policies, with particularly strong advantages when human preferences are scarce. Together, the components connect cross-task correspondence with uncertainty-aware reward learning.
summary.tldr: PEARL transfers preferences between robotic tasks and learns uncertainty-aware rewards without collecting human preference labels for the target task.

title: PEARL: Zero-shot Cross-task Preference Alignment and Robust Reward Learning for Robotic Manipulation

abstract: A natural approach for reinforcement learning is to predict future rewards by unrolling a neural network world model, and to backpropagate through the resulting computational graph to learn a control policy. However, this method often becomes impractical for long horizons, since typical world models induce hard-to-optimize loss landscapes. Transformers are known to efficiently propagate gradients over long horizons: could they be the solution to this problem? Surprisingly, we show that commonly-used transformer world models produce circuitous gradient paths, which can be detrimental to long-range policy gradients. To tackle this challenge, we propose a class of world models called Action-conditioned World Models (AWMs), designed to provide more direct routes for gradient propagation. We integrate such AWMs into a policy gradient framework that underscores the relationship between network architectures and the policy gradient updates they inherently represent. We demonstrate that AWMs can generate optimization landscapes that are easier to navigate even when compared to those from the simulator itself. This property allows transformer AWMs to produce better policies than competitive baselines in realistic long-horizon tasks.

paragraphs: One way to train a control policy is to predict future rewards with a learned world model and backpropagate through those predictions. Over long horizons, this can create an optimization problem that is difficult to navigate. This paper asks whether transformers, known for propagating gradients over long sequences, resolve that difficulty.

The authors find that commonly used transformer world models can still create indirect gradient paths that harm long-range policy learning. They propose Action-conditioned World Models, or AWMs, designed to give gradients more direct routes. Their policy-gradient framework makes explicit how the world model's architecture determines the updates used to train the policy.

The authors demonstrate that AWMs can create easier optimization landscapes even compared with those obtained from the simulator itself. Transformer AWMs also produce better policies than competitive baselines on realistic long-horizon tasks. The findings show why choosing a transformer architecture alone is insufficient: the path connecting actions to future outcomes also affects the usefulness of the learning signal.
summary.tldr: Action-conditioned World Models improve long-horizon policy learning by giving gradients more direct paths than commonly used transformer world models.

title: Do Transformer World Models Give Better Policy Gradients?

abstract: Slicing distribution selection has been used as an effective technique to improve the performance of parameter estimators based on minimizing sliced Wasserstein distance in applications. Previous works either utilize expensive optimization to select the slicing distribution or use slicing distributions that require expensive sampling methods. In this work, we propose an optimization-free slicing distribution that provides a fast sampling for the Monte Carlo estimation of expectation. In particular, we introduce the random-path projecting direction (RPD) which is constructed by leveraging the normalized difference between two random vectors following the two input measures. From the RPD, we derive the random-path slicing distribution (RPSD) and two variants of sliced Wasserstein, i.e., the Random-Path Projection Sliced Wasserstein (RPSW) and the Importance Weighted Random-Path Projection Sliced Wasserstein (IWRPSW). We then discuss the topological, statistical, and computational properties of RPSW and IWRPSW. Finally, we showcase the favorable performance of RPSW and IWRPSW in gradient flow and the training of denoising diffusion generative models on images.

paragraphs: Sliced Wasserstein methods compare distributions through projections, making the choice of projection directions important for applications that minimize this distance. Earlier direction-selection approaches can require expensive optimization or sampling. This paper proposes a slicing distribution that avoids optimization and supports fast sampling for Monte Carlo estimation.

Its basic construction draws one random vector from each input distribution, takes their difference, and normalizes it to obtain a random-path projecting direction. From this construction, the authors define a random-path slicing distribution and two distance variants: Random-Path Projection Sliced Wasserstein and an importance-weighted version. The projection mechanism therefore depends directly on samples from the distributions being compared.

The paper examines the variants' topological, statistical, and computational properties, and demonstrates favorable performance in gradient-flow applications and training image denoising diffusion models. The contribution addresses the cost of choosing useful projections as part of distribution comparison. It provides a sample-based direction construction together with theoretical analysis and applications, without requiring a separate optimization procedure to select the slicing distribution.
summary.tldr: Random-path projections use normalized differences between distribution samples to select sliced Wasserstein directions without optimization.

title: Sliced Wasserstein with Random-Path Projecting Directions

abstract: This paper introduces Bespoke Non-Stationary (BNS) Solvers, a solver distillation approach to improve sample efficiency of Diffusion and Flow models. BNS solvers are based on a family of non-stationary solvers that provably subsumes existing numerical ODE solvers and consequently demonstrate considerable improvement in sample approximation (PSNR) over these baselines. Compared to model distillation, BNS solvers benefit from a tiny parameter space ($<$200 parameters), fast optimization (two orders of magnitude faster), maintain diversity of samples, and in contrast to previous solver distillation approaches nearly close the gap from standard distillation methods such as Progressive Distillation in the low-medium NFE regime. For example, BNS solver achieves 45 PSNR / 1.76 FID using 16 NFE in class-conditional ImageNet-64. We experimented with BNS solvers for conditional image generation, text-to-image generation, and text-2-audio generation showing significant improvement in sample approximation (PSNR) in all.

paragraphs: Diffusion and flow models generate samples through a sequence of numerical computations. This paper speeds up that process by learning a specialized solver. Its Bespoke Non-Stationary solvers adapt the numerical procedure across sampling steps, with the aim of approximating the desired samples using fewer model evaluations.

The proposed solver family provably contains existing numerical ordinary differential equation solvers as special cases. That gives it room to learn procedures beyond those established alternatives. The authors report better sample approximation and use fewer than 200 trainable solver parameters. Compared with model distillation, optimization is reported to be two orders of magnitude faster, while preserving sample diversity.

Experiments cover conditional images, text-to-image generation, and text-to-audio generation, with improved approximation measured by PSNR throughout. At low to medium numbers of function evaluations, the method nearly closes the gap to standard distillation approaches such as Progressive Distillation. The contribution is therefore a compact way to learn faster sampling procedures with substantial reported gains across several generation settings.
summary.tldr: Bespoke solvers learn a small set of sampling parameters to accelerate diffusion and flow generation while improving sample approximation.

title: Bespoke Non-Stationary Solvers for Fast Sampling of Diffusion and Flow Models

abstract: Gradient regularization (GR), which aims to penalize the gradient norm atop the loss function, has shown promising results in training modern over-parameterized deep neural networks. However, can we trust this powerful technique? This paper reveals that GR can cause performance degeneration in adaptive optimization scenarios, particularly with learning rate warmup. Our empirical and theoretical analyses suggest this is due to GR inducing instability and divergence in gradient statistics of adaptive optimizers at the initial training stage. Inspired by the warmup heuristic, we propose three GR warmup strategies, each relaxing the regularization effect to a certain extent during the warmup course to ensure the accurate and stable accumulation of gradients. With experiments on Vision Transformer family, we confirm the three GR warmup strategies can effectively circumvent these issues, thereby largely improving the model performance. Meanwhile, we note that scalable models tend to rely more on the GR warmup, where the performance can be improved by up to 3% on Cifar10 compared to baseline GR. Code is available at https://github.com/zhaoyang-0204/gnp.

title: When Will Gradient Regularization Be Harmful?

abstract: Domain randomization in reinforcement learning is an established technique for increasing the robustness of control policies learned in simulation. By randomizing properties of the environment during training, the learned policy can be robust to uncertainty along the randomized dimensions. While the environment distribution is typically specified by hand, in this paper we investigate the problem of automatically discovering this sampling distribution via entropy-regularized reward maximization of a neural sampling distribution in the form of a normalizing flow. We show that this architecture is more flexible and results in better robustness than existing approaches to learning simple parameterized sampling distributions. We demonstrate that these policies can be used to learn robust policies for contact-rich assembly tasks. Additionally, we explore how these sampling distributions, in combination with a privileged value function, can be used for out-of-distribution detection in the context of an uncertainty-aware multi-step manipulation planner.

paragraphs: Domain randomization trains a robot across varied simulated environments so that its controller can tolerate uncertainty in the properties being randomized. Usually, someone chooses the training distribution by hand. This paper instead learns that distribution, making the choice of simulated conditions part of the learning problem.

This gives the distribution more flexibility than the simple parameterized distributions used by existing approaches. The paper reports that the added flexibility produces better robustness, and demonstrates robust policies for assembly tasks involving substantial physical contact.

It explores combining the learned sampling distributions with a privileged value function to detect conditions outside the training distribution. This connects training-time environment selection with uncertainty awareness during planning. The planning component is presented as an exploration of this use, while the stated robustness gains concern the learned policies and evaluated comparisons.
summary.tldr: Learning simulation distributions with normalizing flows improves robotic policy robustness and supports exploration of uncertainty-aware skill sequencing.

title: Flow-based Domain Randomization for Learning and Sequencing Robotic Skills

abstract: As deep learning continues to be driven by ever-larger datasets, understanding which examples are most important for generalization has become a critical question. While progress in data selection continues, emerging applications require studying this problem in dynamic contexts. To bridge this gap, we pose the Incremental Data Selection (IDS) problem, where examples arrive as a continuous stream, and need to be selected without access to the full data source. In this setting, the learner must incrementally build a training dataset of predefined size while simultaneously learning the underlying task. We find that in IDS, the impact of a new sample on the model state depends fundamentally on both its geometric relationship in the feature space and its prediction error. Leveraging this insight, we propose PEAKS (Prediction Error Anchored by Kernel Similarity), an efficient data selection method tailored for IDS. Our comprehensive evaluations demonstrate that PEAKS consistently outperforms existing selection strategies. Furthermore, PEAKS yields increasingly better performance returns than random selection as training data size grows on real-world datasets. The code is available at https://github.com/BurakGurbuz97/PEAKS.

paragraphs: Choosing useful training examples becomes harder when data arrives continuously and the complete source cannot be inspected. The paper formalizes this as Incremental Data Selection. A learner must assemble a training dataset of a predefined size while simultaneously learning the task, so selection decisions occur alongside changes in the model.

The authors find that a new example’s effect on the model depends on both its prediction error and its geometric relationship to other data in feature space. PEAKS combines these two signals through prediction error anchored by kernel similarity. Its design makes the relationship between an example’s difficulty and its feature-space position central to deciding whether that example is useful.

Evaluations report that PEAKS consistently outperforms existing selection strategies. On real-world datasets, its performance advantage over random selection also becomes greater as training-data size increases. These findings support using both model error and feature geometry when selecting from a stream, particularly when a fixed dataset budget prevents retaining every arriving example.
summary.tldr: PEAKS combines prediction error with feature-space similarity to select useful training examples incrementally from a data stream.

title: PEAKS: Selecting Key Training Examples Incrementally via Prediction Error Anchored by Kernel Similarity

abstract: Binary decision diagrams (BDDs) are widely applied tools to compactly represent labeled data as directed acyclic graphs; for efficiency and interpretability reasons small BDDs are preferred. Given labeled data, minimizing BDDs is NP-complete and thus recent research focused on the influence of parameters such as the solution size $s$ on the complexity [Ordyniak et al., AAAI 2024]. Our main positive result is an algorithm that is efficient if in particular $s$, the domain size $D$, and the Hamming distance between any two data points is small, improving on previous running-time bounds. This algorithm is inspired by the witness-tree paradigm that was recently successful for computing decision trees [Komusiewicz et al., ICML 2023], whose extension to BDDs was open. We extend our algorithmic results to the case where we allow a small number of misclassified data points and complement them with lower bounds that show that the running times are tight from multiple points of view. We show that our main algorithm holds practical promise by providing a proof-of-concept implementation.

paragraphs: Binary decision diagrams represent labeled data as directed graphs without cycles. Smaller diagrams are desirable for efficiency and interpretability, but finding a minimum-size diagram is NP-complete. This paper investigates which properties of the desired diagram and the input data can make exact computation more manageable.

The main algorithm improves earlier running-time bounds when, in particular, the solution size, domain size, and Hamming distance between any two data points are small. Hamming distance measures how many positions differ between two points. The algorithm extends a witness-tree technique previously successful for decision trees to binary decision diagrams, resolving an open algorithmic extension.

The authors also extend their results to allow a small number of classification errors. Complementary lower bounds show that the running times are tight from several perspectives, clarifying the scope for further improvements. A proof-of-concept implementation provides evidence of practical promise. The result identifies structured settings where exact minimization becomes more tractable while preserving the explicit parameter conditions behind that efficiency.
summary.tldr: A witness-tree-based algorithm improves exact BDD minimization when diagram size, domain size, and pairwise data differences are small.

title: Learning Minimum-Size BDDs: Towards Efficient Exact Algorithms

abstract: In many scenarios of practical interest, labeled data from a target distribution are scarce while labeled data from a related source distribution are abundant. One particular setting of interest arises when the target label space is a subset of the source label space, leading to the framework of partial domain adaptation (PDA). Typical approaches to PDA involve minimizing a domain alignment term and a weighted empirical loss on the source data, with the aim of transferring knowledge between domains. However, a theoretical basis for this procedure is lacking, and in particular, most existing weighting schemes are heuristic. In this work, we derive generalization bounds for the PDA problem based on partial optimal transport. These bounds corroborate the use of the partial Wasserstein distance as a domain alignment term, and lead to theoretically motivated explicit expressions for the empirical source loss weights. Inspired by these bounds, we devise a practical algorithm for PDA, termed WARMPOT. Through extensive numerical experiments, we show that WARMPOT is competitive with recent approaches, and that our proposed weights improve on existing schemes.

paragraphs: Partial domain adaptation concerns transferring from a labeled source dataset when the target’s labels form a subset of the source’s labels. This makes transfer selective: source information must be used in a way that accounts for the smaller target label space. Common methods combine domain alignment with a weighted source training loss, but their weighting choices often lack theoretical justification.

The authors derive generalization bounds using partial optimal transport. These bounds support using partial Wasserstein distance to measure domain alignment and provide explicit, theoretically motivated expressions for the source loss weights. The analysis therefore addresses both parts of the usual adaptation objective within the same framework.

Building on those bounds, the paper introduces WARMPOT, a practical adaptation algorithm. Extensive numerical experiments show that it is competitive with recent methods and that the proposed weights improve on existing weighting schemes. The findings give a principled foundation to a familiar strategy while also producing a usable method. They support competitive overall performance and improved weighting, without claiming that WARMPOT universally outperforms every alternative.
summary.tldr: Partial optimal transport yields generalization bounds and principled source weights for the competitive WARMPOT adaptation algorithm.

title: Theoretical Performance Guarantees for Partial Domain Adaptation via Partial Optimal Transport

abstract: A/B testing has become the gold standard for modern technological industries for policy evaluation. Motivated by the widespread use of switchback experiments in A/B testing, this paper conducts a comprehensive comparative analysis of various switchback designs in Markovian environments. Unlike many existing works which derive the optimal design based on specific and relatively simple estimators, our analysis covers a range of state-of-the-art estimators developed in the reinforcement learning literature. It reveals that the effectiveness of different switchback designs depends crucially on (i) the size of the carryover effect and (ii) the autocorrelations among reward errors over time. Meanwhile, these findings are estimator-agnostic, i.e., they apply to all the aforementioned estimators. Based on these insights, we provide a workflow to offer guidelines for practitioners on designing switchback experiments in A/B testing.

paragraphs: Switchback experiments evaluate policies by switching between them over time. Their design must account for the fact that a policy’s effects may persist after a switch and that reward errors may be related across time. This paper compares switchback designs in Markovian environments, examining how these two features shape their effectiveness.

The analysis covers a range of state-of-the-art estimators from reinforcement learning. That scope extends beyond selecting an optimal design for one relatively simple estimator. The authors find that design effectiveness depends crucially on the magnitude of carryover effects and on reward-error autocorrelation. Both the persistence of treatment effects and the temporal pattern of errors therefore matter to the comparison.

The findings apply across all the estimators considered in the paper, which is the stated meaning of estimator-agnostic here. Using these insights, the authors provide a workflow to guide practitioners designing switchback A/B tests. The contribution connects properties of the experimental environment to design decisions while retaining relevance across several estimation methods.
summary.tldr: Switchback design effectiveness depends on carryover and reward-error autocorrelation, with findings that hold across the reinforcement-learning estimators analyzed.

title: Unraveling the Interplay between Carryover Effects and Reward Autocorrelations in Switchback Experiments

abstract: Diplomacy is a complex multiplayer game that re- quires both cooperation and competition, posing significant challenges for AI systems. Traditional methods rely on equilibrium search to generate extensive game data for training, which demands substantial computational resources. Large Lan- guage Models (LLMs) offer a promising alterna- tive, leveraging pre-trained knowledge to achieve strong performance with relatively small-scale fine-tuning. However, applying LLMs to Diplo- macy remains challenging due to the exponential growth of possible action combinations and the intricate strategic interactions among players. To address this challenge, we propose DipLLM, a fine-tuned LLM-based agent that learns equilib- rium policies for Diplomacy. DipLLM employs an autoregressive factorization framework to sim- plify the complex task of multi-unit action assign- ment into a sequence of unit-level decisions. By defining an equilibrium policy within this frame- work as the learning objective, we fine-tune the model using only 1.5% of the data required by the state-of-the-art Cicero model, surpassing its per- formance. Our results demonstrate the potential of fine-tuned LLMs for tackling complex strategic decision-making in multiplayer games.

paragraphs: Diplomacy requires players to balance cooperation and competition while coordinating actions across multiple units. For an AI agent, the number of possible combinations of unit actions grows rapidly, and the value of a decision depends on other players’ choices. Traditional approaches described in the paper generate large training datasets through computationally demanding equilibrium search.

DipLLM uses a fine-tuned language model to learn strategic policies for this setting. Its central design is an autoregressive factorization: a joint assignment of actions to many units becomes a sequence of unit-level decisions. The authors define an equilibrium policy within this framework as the learning objective, connecting the sequential prediction process to the game’s strategic interactions.

The reported model uses only 1.5% of the training data required by Cicero and surpasses its performance in the authors’ evaluation. This result supports the potential of pretrained language models for data-efficient strategic learning. The contribution combines a manageable representation of coordinated actions with a learning target grounded in multiplayer strategy.
summary.tldr: DipLLM learns Diplomacy strategies through sequential unit-level decisions, surpassing Cicero in the reported evaluation with 1.5% of its training data.

title: DipLLM: Fine-Tuning LLM for Strategic Decision-making in Diplomacy

abstract: Vector-Quantized Generative Models (VQGMs) have emerged as powerful tools for image generation. However, the key component of VQGMs—the codebook of discrete tokens—is still not well understood, e.g., which tokens are critical to generate an image of a certain concept? This paper introduces Concept-Oriented Token Explanation (CORTEX), a novel approach for interpreting VQGMs by identifying concept-specific token combinations. Our framework employs two methods: (1) a sample-level explanation method that analyzes token importance scores in individual images, and (2) a codebook-level explanation method that explores the entire codebook to find globally relevant tokens. Experimental results demonstrate CORTEX’s efficacy in providing clear explanations of token usage in the generative process, outperforming baselines across multiple pretrained VQGMs. Besides enhancing VQGMs transparency, CORTEX is useful in applications such as targeted image editing and shortcut feature detection. Our code is available at https://github.com/YangTianze009/CORTEX.

paragraphs: Vector-quantized generative models build images using discrete tokens drawn from a learned codebook. Although these models can generate compelling images, the role of individual tokens and their combinations is difficult to understand. This paper focuses on a concrete interpretation question: which combinations of tokens matter for generating a particular concept?

CORTEX, short for Concept-Oriented Token Explanation, addresses that question at two levels. Its sample-level method assigns importance to tokens within individual images, explaining their contribution in a specific example. Its codebook-level method searches across the full token collection to identify tokens with broader relevance to a concept. The two views connect explanations of particular outputs with the model's overall vocabulary.

Experiments across multiple pretrained models report clearer explanations of token usage and better results than the evaluated baselines. The paper also shows usefulness for targeted image editing and detecting shortcut features. These applications make interpretation actionable: identifying concept-related token combinations can help locate what to change in an image or what unintended cues a model may be using.
summary.tldr: CORTEX explains image-generation codebooks by identifying token combinations associated with specific concepts.

title: Concept-Centric Token Interpretation for Vector-Quantized Generative Models

abstract: Cross-modal embeddings form the foundation for multi-modal models. However, visualization methods for interpreting cross-modal embeddings have been primarily confined to traditional dimensionality reduction (DR) techniques like PCA and t-SNE. These DR methods primarily focus on feature distributions within a single modality, whilst failing to incorporate metrics (e.g., CLIPScore) across multiple modalities. This paper introduces AKRMap, a new DR technique designed to visualize cross-modal embeddings metric with enhanced accuracy by learning kernel regression of the metric landscape in the projection space. Specifically, AKRMap constructs a supervised projection network guided by a post-projection kernel regression loss, and employs adaptive generalized kernels that can be jointly optimized with the projection. This approach enables AKRMap to efficiently generate visualizations that capture complex metric distributions, while also supporting interactive features such as zoom and overlay for deeper exploration. Quantitative experiments demonstrate that AKRMap outperforms existing DR methods in generating more accurate and trustworthy visualizations. We further showcase the effectiveness of AKRMap in visualizing and comparing cross-modal embeddings for text-to-image models. Code and demo are available at https://github.com/yilinye/AKRMap.
