paragraphs: Visualizing embeddings from multiple modalities requires deciding what a useful map should preserve. The paper argues that conventional dimensionality reduction methods, including PCA and t-SNE, primarily emphasize feature distributions within individual modalities. This can leave out cross-modal measurements, such as scores describing the relationship between text and images.

AKRMap learns a projection specifically guided by these measurements. After projecting the embeddings, it uses kernel regression to estimate how the chosen metric varies across the map. A regression loss guides the projection network, while adaptive kernels are optimized together with that network. Consequently, the arrangement of points is trained to support an accurate representation of the metric landscape.

The framework also supports zooming and overlays for interactive exploration. Quantitative experiments report more accurate and trustworthy visualizations than existing dimensionality reduction methods, and examples demonstrate comparisons of text-to-image embeddings. Here, trustworthiness concerns how faithfully the visualization represents the cross-modal metric being studied, giving users a map oriented toward a particular relationship they want to inspect.
summary.tldr: AKRMap jointly learns projections and adaptive kernels to visualize cross-modal metric landscapes more accurately.

title: AKRMap: Adaptive Kernel Regression for Trustworthy Visualization of Cross-Modal Embeddings

abstract: AI for Mathematics (AI4Math) is intellectually intriguing and is crucial for AI-driven system design and verification. Extensive efforts on AI4Math have mirrored techniques in NLP, in particular, training large language models on carefully curated math datasets in text form. As a complementary yet less explored avenue, formal mathematical reasoning is grounded in formal systems such as proof assistants, which can verify the correctness of reasoning and provide automatic feedback. This position paper advocates formal mathematical reasoning as an indispensable component in future AI for math, formal verification, and verifiable generation. We summarize existing progress, discuss open challenges, and envision critical milestones to measure future success.

paragraphs: This position paper advocates a larger role for formal mathematical reasoning in AI. Much AI work on mathematics has followed the language-modeling approach: assemble mathematical text and train models on it. The authors describe formal reasoning as a complementary avenue with particular importance for designing and verifying systems.

The distinguishing feature is the use of formal systems, including proof assistants, that can check whether reasoning is correct and provide automatic feedback. This connects the production of mathematical arguments to a mechanism for verifying them. That feedback is central to the paper’s case for making formal reasoning an integral part of future AI research.

The paper surveys progress, discusses open challenges, and proposes milestones for assessing future success. Its stated position is that formal mathematical reasoning is indispensable for future AI mathematics, formal verification, and verifiable generation. The contribution is therefore a research agenda linking these areas around reasoning whose correctness can be checked within a formal system.
summary.tldr: The authors advocate formal mathematical reasoning as a core part of AI research because formal systems can verify reasoning and supply automatic feedback.

title: Position: Formal Mathematical Reasoning—A New Frontier in AI

abstract: Generative posterior sampling using diffusion models has emerged as a dominant paradigm for solving inverse problems in imaging, which usually consists of three main components: data consistency (DC) guidance, classifier-free guidance (CFG) and stochasticity. While prior arts have focused on how to develop each or all components, less attention has given to how to schedule them, leading to heuristically fixed or partially adjusted suboptimal schedules. In this work, we argue that the interactions among all three components in terms of scheduling are crucial for significantly improved performance in solving inverse problems in imaging. Our analysis shows that aggressive CFG early in sampling conflict with DC guidance, while stochasticity brings the trajectory back to higher-probability regions. Based on these findings, we propose Triadic Dynamics Aware Posterior Sampling (TriPS), which reformulates posterior sampling as a time-varying control problem and optimizes schedules following a triadic trend of decreasing DC and stochasticity scales alongside increasing CFG scale. TriPS achieves this through two strategies: template-based search over functional priors for reliable baseline schedules, and Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO)-based reinforcement learning for more flexible temporal curves. Experiments demonstrate TriPS outperforms state-of-the-art baselines in data fidelity and perceptual realism.

paragraphs: Diffusion-based imaging reconstruction balances consistency with observed data, classifier-free guidance, and sampling randomness. Their effects depend on when and how strongly each is applied. This paper argues that optimizing the three schedules together is important because treating them separately can miss interactions that shape the entire reconstruction trajectory.

The analysis finds that strong classifier-free guidance early in sampling conflicts with data-consistency guidance, while randomness can move the trajectory back toward higher-probability regions. Triadic Dynamics Aware Posterior Sampling, or TriPS, formulates scheduling as a time-varying control problem. Its schedules follow a trend of decreasing data-consistency and stochasticity scales while increasing the classifier-free guidance scale.

TriPS develops two ways to choose those schedules: searching over functional templates for reliable baseline curves, and using Group Relative Policy Optimization to learn more flexible temporal curves. Experiments report improvements over state-of-the-art baselines in both data fidelity and perceptual realism. The findings emphasize that reconstruction quality depends on coordinating guidance and randomness over time, not just selecting the individual components.
summary.tldr: TriPS jointly optimizes data-consistency guidance, classifier-free guidance, and randomness schedules to improve diffusion-based image reconstruction.

title: Triadic Dynamics Aware Diffusion Posterior Sampling for Inverse Problems: Optimizing Guidance and Stochasticity Schedules

abstract: Graph alignment, the problem of identifying corresponding nodes across multiple graphs, is fundamental to numerous applications. Most existing unsupervised methods embed node features into latent representations to enable cross-graph comparison without ground-truth correspondences. However, these methods suffer from two critical limitations: the degradation of node distinctiveness due to oversmoothing in GNN-based embeddings, and the misalignment of latent spaces across graphs caused by structural noise, feature heterogeneity, and training instability, ultimately leading to unreliable node correspondences. We propose a novel framework employing a dual-pass encoder to inject high-frequency discriminability into node features, paired with a geometry-aware functional map module that learns bijective and isometric transformations to align latent spaces while acting as a low-pass filter on correspondences, enforcing smoothness and robustness as a structural prior in map space. Extensive experiments on graph benchmarks demonstrate that our method consistently outperforms existing unsupervised alignment baselines, exhibiting superior robustness to structural inconsistencies and challenging alignment scenarios. The implementation is available at https://github.com/maysambehmanesh/GADL.

paragraphs: Graph alignment identifies nodes that correspond across different graphs. Unsupervised approaches often compare learned node representations, but two problems interfere: graph-network smoothing can make nodes difficult to distinguish, and separately learned representation spaces can become misaligned because of structural noise, different features, or unstable training.

The proposed framework addresses these problems at different stages. A dual-pass encoder injects high-frequency information that helps preserve distinctions between nodes. A geometry-aware functional map then aligns the latent spaces through learned bijective and isometric transformations, seeking one-to-one mappings that preserve geometry. This map also filters correspondences toward smoothness, providing a structural prior for robustness.

The combination preserves discriminating detail in node features while encouraging regularity in the cross-graph mapping. Extensive graph-benchmark experiments show consistent improvements over existing unsupervised alignment baselines and stronger robustness to structural inconsistencies and difficult alignment settings. The results support handling node distinctiveness and compatibility between representation spaces together, since reliable matching depends on both.
summary.tldr: A dual-pass encoder and geometry-aware latent mapping improve unsupervised graph alignment by preserving node distinctions and stabilizing cross-graph correspondences.

title: Graph Alignment via Dual-Pass Spectral Encoding and Latent Space Communication

abstract: Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) extend large language models with visual understanding, but remain vulnerable to hallucination, where outputs are fluent yet inconsistent with images. Recent studies link this issue to language bias—the tendency of LVLMs to over-rely on text while neglecting visual inputs. Yet most analyses remain empirical without uncovering its underlying cause. In this paper, we provide a systematic study of language bias and identify its root in modality misalignment during training. Our analysis shows that both Visual Instruction Tuning (VIT) and Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) often prioritize textual improvements, which may cause LVLMs to overly lean toward language modeling rather than balanced multimodal understanding. To address this, we propose two simple yet effective methods: Language Bias Regularization (LBR), which mitigates language bias through regularization during instruction tuning, and Language Bias Penalty (LBP), which penalizes language bias in the DPO training process. Extensive experiments across diverse models and benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach. LBR consistently improves performance on over ten general benchmarks, while LBP significantly reduces hallucination and improves trustworthiness. Together, these methods not only mitigate language bias but also advance the overall alignment of LVLMs, all without introducing any additional data or auxiliary models. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/lab-klc/HAVAE.

paragraphs: Vision-language models can produce fluent descriptions that conflict with an image because they rely too heavily on language patterns. This paper studies that language bias and identifies modality misalignment during training as its root. Its analysis finds that visual instruction tuning and preference optimization often favor textual improvements, potentially weakening balanced use of visual information.

The authors introduce two training modifications. Language Bias Regularization addresses the imbalance during instruction tuning, while Language Bias Penalty addresses it during Direct Preference Optimization. Both methods explicitly discourage language bias within an existing training process, and neither requires additional data or an auxiliary model.

Experiments cover multiple models and benchmarks. The regularization method consistently improves performance on more than ten general benchmarks, while the preference-training penalty substantially reduces hallucination and improves trustworthiness. The findings connect a diagnosed training imbalance to practical interventions at two stages of model alignment. They suggest that attending to how training rewards textual progress can also improve the model’s use of images.
summary.tldr: Two training penalties reduce vision-language models’ overreliance on text and improve visual alignment without extra data or auxiliary models.

title: Language Bias in LVLMs: From In-Depth Analysis to Simple and Effective Mitigation

abstract: Temporal graph neural networks (TGNNs) have gained significant traction for solving real-world temporal graph tasks. However, their interpretability remains limited, as most TGNNs fail to identify which historical interactions most influence a given prediction. Despite promising progress on interpretable TGNNs, existing methods predominantly focus on previously seen historical interactions, which we term stability patterns, while overlooking newly emerging first-time interactions, which we term transition patterns. Both types of patterns are essential for faithful temporal explanations. To address this limitation, we propose ST-TGExplainer, a self-explainable TGNN that disentangles Stability and Transition patterns in temporal graphs for a more faithful Temporal GNN Explainer. Guided by a disentangled information bottleneck objective, ST-TGExplainer learns a compact explanatory subgraph that remains predictive of the event label while explicitly suppressing label-conditioned redundancy between stability and transition patterns. Extensive experiments demonstrate that ST-TGExplainer achieves strong predictive performance and yields more faithful explanations. Code is available at https://github.com/hjchen-hdu/ST-TGExplainer.

paragraphs: Explaining a prediction on a temporal graph requires identifying which interactions matter over time. This paper separates recurring interactions, called stability patterns, from newly appearing interactions, called transition patterns. It argues that existing explanations concentrate on the former and overlook the latter, even though both are needed for faithful temporal explanations.

ST-TGExplainer builds explanation into a temporal graph neural network. It learns a compact explanatory subgraph using a disentangled information bottleneck objective. The objective keeps information useful for predicting the event label while explicitly reducing redundancy between stability and transition patterns, conditioned on that label. This encourages the two kinds of evidence to make distinct contributions to the explanation.

Extensive experiments show strong predictive performance and more faithful explanations. The findings support distinguishing persistent relationships from emerging ones when explaining temporal predictions. The compact subgraph is intended to preserve the evidence relevant to the event, while the redundancy constraint prevents the two pattern categories from simply duplicating each other’s explanatory information. Prediction and explanation are thus learned together within the model.
summary.tldr: ST-TGExplainer learns compact temporal-graph explanations that separate recurring interactions from newly emerging ones.

title: ST-TGExplainer: Disentangling Stability and Transition Patterns for Temporal GNN Interpretability

abstract: Robotic manipulation benefits from foundation models that describe goals, but today’s agents still lack a principled way to learn from their own mistakes. We ask whether natural language can serve as feedback, an error-reasoning signal that helps embodied agents diagnose what went wrong and correct course. We introduce LAGEA (Language Guided Embodied Agents), a framework that turns episodic, schema-constrained reflections from a vision language model (VLM) into temporally grounded guidance for reinforcement learning. LAGEA summarizes each attempt in concise language, localizes the decisive moments in the trajectory, aligns feedback with visual state in a shared representation, and converts goal progress and feedback agreement into bounded, step-wise shaping rewardswhose influence is modulated by an adaptive, failure-aware coefficient. This design yields dense signals early when exploration needs direction and gracefully recedes as competence grows. On the Meta-World MT10 and Robotic Fetch embodied manipulation benchmarks, LAGEA improves average success over the state-of-the-art (SOTA) methods by 9.0% on random goals, 5.3% on fixed goals, and 17% on fetch tasks, while converging faster. These results support our hypothesis: language, when structured and grounded in time, is an effective mechanism for teaching robots to self-reflect on mistakes and make better choices. Code will be released soon.

title: LAGEA: Language Guided Embodied Agents for Robotic Manipulation

abstract: Machine Learning surrogates for Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD), particularly Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) and Transformers, have become a new important approach for accelerating physics simulations. However, we identify a critical bottleneck in the field: while architectures have advanced significantly, the common underlying training paradigms remain bound to naive assumptions, such as node-wise supervision and explicit Euler time-stepping. These legacy choices ignore the stiff dynamics and local flux continuity inherent to numerous partial differential equations resolution methods, such as Finite Element, Difference, or Volume (FEM). In this work, we propose a unified framework to bridge the gap between geometric deep learning and rigorous numerical analysis. We introduce three key innovations: (1) Multi Node Prediction, a stencil-level objective that predicts field values for a node’s full local topology, enforcing spatial derivative consistency; (2) Temporal Correction, replacing unstable explicit schemes with a predictor–corrector via temporal Cross-Attention; and (3) Geometric Inductive Biases, leveraging 3D Rotary Positional Embeddings (RoPE) to robustly capture rotational symmetries in unstructured meshes. We evaluate this framework across three architectures (MeshGraphNet, Transolver, and a Transformer) on diverse physics datasets. Our approach yields consistent improvements in accuracy and stability, particularly in long-horizon rollouts, while producing latent representations that generalize to unseen subtasks such as Wall Shear Stress or Pressure prediction. Code is available at https://github.com/DonsetPG/graph-physics.

paragraphs: Learned fluid simulators can accelerate physics computation, but this paper argues that their training procedures often neglect important numerical structure. Supervising individual mesh nodes and using simple explicit time updates can overlook local spatial relationships and stiff dynamics. The authors address these training choices across several model architectures.

The framework consistently improves accuracy and stability, particularly when predictions are repeatedly fed forward over long rollouts. Its latent representations also generalize to unseen subtasks, including wall shear stress and pressure prediction. These results support incorporating numerical and geometric structure into training objectives and time updates, alongside continued development of simulation architectures.
summary.tldr: Spatially coordinated predictions, temporal correction, and geometric embeddings improve the accuracy and long-rollout stability of learned mesh simulators.

title: Mesh Based Simulations with Spatial and Temporal awareness

abstract: Neural collapse (NC) describes the structured geometry that emerges in the features and weights of trained classifiers. Recent theory suggests NC can be suboptimal in deep architectures, attributing this to an explicit low-rank bias from L2 regularization. We study the deep unconstrained feature model (UFM)—equivalent to a deep linear network with orthogonal inputs—trained without regularization, to isolate how gradient descent and depth alone shape NC. We show that depth induces an implicit low-rank bias: low-rank matrices propagate norm more efficiently through successive multiplications, promoting low-rank alternatives to NC. These alternatives, we argue, correspond to softmax codes: max-margin solutions previously found in width-bottlenecked networks. Analyzing training dynamics under spectral initialization, we identify an early-time repulsion among singular values that drives low-rank emergence, and characterize how depth shrinks NC’s basin of attraction. Finally, we show that some effects act in the opposite direction: for randomly initialized networks, increasing width biases training toward higher-rank solutions. Our results provide the first asymptotic and dynamic characterization of implicit bias in deep UFMs trained with unregularized multiclass cross-entropy.

The authors show that depth itself creates an implicit preference for low-rank solutions because low-rank matrices propagate norm more efficiently through repeated multiplication. These results explain competing architectural influences on learned geometry within the studied model, providing both long-run and training-dynamics characterizations without attributing the effect to explicit regularization.
summary.tldr: In deep unconstrained feature models, depth implicitly favors low-rank alternatives to neural collapse, while increased width can favor higher rank.

title: The Implicit Bias of Depth: From Neural Collapse to Softmax Codes

abstract: The rise of model hubs has made it easier to access reusable model components, making model merging a practical tool for combining capabilities. Yet, this modularity also creates a governance gap: downstream users can recompose released weights into unauthorized mixtures that bypass safety alignment or licensing terms. Because existing defenses are largely post-hoc and architecture-specific, they provide inconsistent protection across diverse architectures and release formats in practice. To close this gap, we propose Trap$^{2}$, an architecture-agnostic protection framework that encodes protection into updates during fine-tuning, regardless of whether they are released as adapters or full models. Instead of relying on architecture-dependent approaches, Trap$^{2}$ uses weight re-scaling as a simple proxy for the merging process. It keeps released weights effective in standalone use, but degrades them under re-scaling that often arises in merging, undermining unauthorized recomposition.

paragraphs: Model merging allows released weights to be combined into models with mixed capabilities. This paper addresses the associated governance problem: downstream combinations can bypass safety alignment or licensing terms. The authors propose Trap², a framework that builds protection into fine-tuning updates before those updates are released.

Trap² uses weight rescaling as a proxy for the changes that often occur during merging. It aims to keep the released model useful on its own while making its performance deteriorate when the weights are rescaled. The protection is therefore expressed through how the trained weights respond to modification, rather than through a defense tied to a particular architecture.

The framework is designed to apply whether the release consists of adapters or a full model. Its central idea is to make standalone usefulness compatible with sensitivity to a common merging operation. Because the mechanism targets rescaling that often accompanies merging, the abstract supports protection through that sensitivity, rather than a guarantee that every possible recombination is impossible.
summary.tldr: Trap² trains weights to remain useful alone but degrade under rescaling that often accompanies unauthorized model merging.

title: Making Models Unmergeable via Scaling-Sensitive Loss Landscape

abstract: Rotary Position Embedding (RoPE) is widely adopted in Transformer models, yet its extension to high-dimensional domains lacks a unified theoretical formulation. Most existing approaches either apply rotations independently along each axis or empirically mix frequencies, which limits cross-dimensional interactions and yields direction-dependent representations. To address these limitations, we propose nD-RoPE, a decomposition-free generalization of RoPE to arbitrary dimensions. From a translation-invariant formulation in continuous Hilbert space, we derive a spectral condition for isotropy that requires treating positions and frequencies as coupled $n$-dimensional vectors. We instantiate this formulation with a multi-scale regular-simplex wave-vector design, which provides non-degenerate spatial coverage and a symmetric, directionally balanced second-order response. Experiments across images, videos, and point clouds demonstrate consistent performance gains and improved generalization in high-dimensional settings.

To address these limitations, we propose nD-RoPE, a decomposition-free generalization of RoPE to arbitrary dimensions. From a translation-invariant formulation in continuous Hilbert space, we derive a spectral condition for isotropy that requires treating positions and frequencies as coupled $n$-dimensional vectors. paragraphs: Rotary position embeddings help Transformers represent where inputs are located, but extending them to multidimensional data raises geometric questions. Existing extensions often rotate each axis independently or mix frequencies empirically. According to this paper, those choices limit interactions across dimensions and can make representations behave differently depending on direction.

nD-RoPE develops a unified formulation for arbitrary dimensions without decomposing positions into independent axes. Starting from a translation-invariant formulation in a continuous Hilbert space, the authors derive a spectral condition for isotropy, meaning balanced behavior across directions. This condition requires treating positions and frequencies as coupled multidimensional vectors.

The practical construction uses regular-simplex wave vectors at multiple scales. It provides non-degenerate spatial coverage and a symmetric, directionally balanced second-order response. That specific property should not be broadened into a claim of perfect directional invariance in every respect. Experiments on images, videos, and point clouds show consistent performance gains and improved generalization, supporting the value of a geometrically grounded approach to multidimensional positional representation.
summary.tldr: nD-RoPE generalizes rotary position embeddings through coupled multidimensional geometry and improves performance across images, videos, and point clouds.

title: nD-RoPE: A Generalized RoPE for n-Dimensional Position Embedding

abstract: World models derived from large-scale video generative pre-training have emerged as a promising paradigm for generalist robot policy learning. However, standard approaches often focus on high-fidelity RGB video prediction, this can result in overfitting to irrelevant factors, such as dynamic backgrounds and illumination changes. These distractions reduce the model’s ability to generalize, ultimately leading to unreliable and fragile control policies. To address this, we introduce the Mask World Model (MWM), which leverages video diffusion architectures to predict the evolution of semantic masks instead of pixels. This shift imposes a geometric information bottleneck, forcing the model to capture essential physical dynamics and contact relations while filtering out visual noise. We seamlessly integrate this mask dynamics backbone with a diffusion-based policy head to enable robust end-to-end control. Extensive evaluations demonstrate the superiority of MWM on the LIBERO and RLBench simulation benchmarks, significantly outperforming the state-of-the-art RGB-based world models. Furthermore, real-world experiments and robustness evaluation (via random token pruning) reveal that MWM exhibits superior generalization capabilities and robust resilience to texture information loss.

paragraphs: Robot world models that predict detailed video can devote capacity to changing backgrounds, lighting, and other appearance details unrelated to control. The paper argues that this can weaken generalization and produce fragile policies. Its Mask World Model changes the prediction target from full-color pixels to evolving semantic masks.

The model uses a video diffusion architecture to predict how these masks change over time. Restricting predictions to masks creates a geometric information bottleneck, directing the model toward physical dynamics and contact relationships while filtering visual distractions. A diffusion-based policy head connects this representation of future change to robot actions, forming an end-to-end control system.

On LIBERO and RLBench, the authors report significant improvements over state-of-the-art RGB-based world models. Real-world experiments also show stronger generalization, and evaluations using random token pruning indicate resilience to lost texture information. These findings support the paper’s central design choice: predicting a representation focused on task-relevant geometry can provide a stronger foundation for control than reproducing detailed visual appearance in the evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: Mask World Model predicts future semantic masks to improve robot control and robustness to irrelevant visual detail.

title: Predicting What Matters: Robust Generalist Robot Policy Learning via Future Semantic Mask

abstract: Unlearning in large language models (LLMs) is critical for regulatory compliance and for building ethical generative AI systems that avoid producing private, toxic, illegal, or copyrighted content. Despite rapid progress, in this work, we show that almost all existing unlearning methods fail to achieve true forgetting in practice. Specifically, while evaluations of these ‘unlearned’ models under deterministic (greedy) decoding often suggest successful knowledge removal using standard benchmarks, we show that sensitive information reliably resurfaces when models are sampled with standard probabilistic decoding. To rigorously capture this vulnerability, we introduce leak@$k$, a new meta-evaluation metric that quantifies the likelihood of forgotten knowledge reappearing when generating $k$ samples from the model under realistic decoding strategies. Using three widely adopted benchmarks, TOFU, MUSE, and WMDP, we conduct the first large-scale, systematic study of unlearning reliability using leak@$k$ metric. Our findings demonstrate that knowledge leakage persists across methods and tasks, underscoring that current state-of-the-art (SOTA) unlearning techniques provide only limited forgetting. We propose an algorithm, termed Robust Unlearning under LEak@$k$ metric (RULE) to address this concern. We demonstrate that RULE provides an unlearned model for TOFU benchmark with no information leakage for a large number of generation samples. On the MUSE benchmark, RULE outperforms SOTA unlearning methods under the leak@$k$ metric across most sampling budgets $k$. Codes are available at https://github.com/OptimAI-Lab/Leak-k.

paragraphs: A language model can appear to have forgotten information when evaluated using greedy decoding, which selects the most likely continuation. This paper shows that information suppressed under that evaluation can reappear when outputs are sampled probabilistically. The distinction matters because successful suppression in one deterministic answer does not establish reliable forgetting across repeated sampled generations.

The authors introduce leak@k to measure the likelihood that supposedly forgotten knowledge resurfaces across k samples. Their systematic study uses TOFU, MUSE, and WMDP and finds persistent leakage across methods and tasks. The results indicate that current unlearning techniques often provide limited forgetting when evaluated under realistic sampling strategies, even when standard deterministic evaluations suggest success.

The paper also proposes RULE, an unlearning algorithm aimed at this evaluation criterion. It produces no observed information leakage over a large number of samples on TOFU and beats existing methods on MUSE for most tested sampling budgets. These findings support evaluating and training for repeated-sampling robustness; the TOFU result remains an empirical observation over the evaluated generations.
summary.tldr: Leak@k exposes information that resurfaces after unlearning under repeated probabilistic sampling, while RULE improves robustness on evaluated benchmarks.

title: Leak@$k$: Unlearning Does Not Make LLMs Forget Under Probabilistic Decoding

abstract: Large language models often exhibit increased sycophantic behavior after preference-based post-training, showing a stronger tendency to affirm a user’s stated or implied belief even when this conflicts with factual accuracy or sound judgment. We present a formal analysis of how alignment from human feedback can increase this failure mode by identifying an explicit amplification mechanism that causally links optimization against a learned reward to bias in the human preference data used for alignment. We show that the direction of behavioral drift is determined by a covariance under the base policy between endorsing the belief signal in the prompt and the learned reward, and that the first-order effect reduces to a simple mean-gap condition. We then analyze reward learning from pairwise comparisons under random utility models like Bradley–Terry and characterize when bias in human annotators’ preferences induces this reward gap. Next, we propose a training-time intervention designed to neutralize the amplification mechanism itself. Among all post-trained policies that prevent sycophantic behavior from increasing, we characterize the unique policy closest in KL divergence to the unconstrained post-trained policy, and derive the corresponding minimal reward correction as a closed-form agreement penalty. Computational experiments find that reward gaps are common and cause behavioral drift in all the configurations considered.

title: How RLHF Amplifies Sycophancy

abstract: Cross-layer reuse of early attention projections can improve optimization and data efficiency, but it creates a structural conflict: the first layer must simultaneously act as a stable, reusable anchor for all deeper layers and as an effective computational block. We demonstrate that this tension constrains the performance of internal-anchor designs. We propose ExoFormer, which resolves the conflict by learning exogenous anchor projections outside the sequential layer stack. We introduce a unified normalized mixing framework that mixes queries, keys, values, and gate logits using learnable coefficients (exploring coefficient granularities: elementwise, headwise, and scalar), and we show that normalizing anchor sources is key to stable reuse. ExoFormer variants consistently outperform their internal-anchor counterparts, and the dynamic variant yields 1.5x downstream accuracy points while matching validation loss using 1.5x fewer tokens than Gated Attention. We explain this efficacy via an Offloading Hypothesis: external anchors preserve essential token identity, allowing layers to specialize exclusively in feature transformation. We release code and models to facilitate future research.

paragraphs: Reusing early attention projections across layers can help optimization and data efficiency, but it gives the first layer competing responsibilities. That layer must perform useful computation while providing a stable reference for deeper layers. The paper shows that this conflict constrains designs that use an internal layer as their shared anchor.

ExoFormer moves the anchor projections outside the sequential layer stack and learns them separately. Its normalized mixing framework combines anchor information with queries, keys, values, and gate logits through learned coefficients. The authors investigate coefficients at element, attention-head, and scalar granularity, and identify normalization of anchor sources as important for stable reuse throughout the model.

The tested ExoFormer variants consistently outperform corresponding internal-anchor designs. The dynamic variant reports 1.5 times the downstream accuracy points and matches Gated Attention's validation loss using 1.5 times fewer tokens. The authors interpret these results through an Offloading Hypothesis: external anchors preserve token identity, freeing the sequential layers to specialize in transforming features. This is the proposed explanation for the gains.
summary.tldr: ExoFormer learns shared attention anchors outside the layer stack, improving tested performance and data efficiency over internal-anchor designs.

title: Attention Projection Mixing with Exogenous Anchors

abstract: The detection of synthetic images has traditionally been framed as a binary classification problem. However, we argue that this formulation overlooks a fundamental structural property of generative datasets: synthetic images are not independent samples, but are implicitly paired with real images sharing the same semantic source. Existing methods treat real and fake images as independent instances, failing to capture generation-induced relational discrepancies in real–fake pairs. Moreover, models tend to rapidly overfit to seen fake patterns, leading to poor generalization to unseen ones. To overcome these challenges, we propose a novel detection framework that explicitly mines real–fake pairs by constructing source-guided mappings or leveraging nearest-neighbor relationships in the CLIP embedding space. We then introduce pair-wise discrepancy learning that explicitly enlarges generation-induced deviations and discrepancy inversion to mitigate overfitting. Moreover, to preserve pretrained semantic representations while improving generalization, we adopt a bias-only fine-tuning scheme that restricts model capacity during adaptation. Extensive experiments show that our approach achieves superior generalization across unseen fake patterns.

paragraphs: Synthetic-image detectors can learn the particular fake patterns present during training and then struggle with unfamiliar ones. BPL approaches this problem by focusing on relationships between real and synthetic images that share semantic content. Such relationships can reveal changes introduced by generation that treating each image independently may overlook.

The framework constructs real–fake pairs using source information or nearby representations in CLIP’s embedding space. It learns to enlarge the discrepancies associated with generation and introduces discrepancy inversion to reduce overfitting. This puts the comparison between related images at the center of detector training, rather than relying only on separate real-or-fake labels.

BPL also updates only model biases during fine-tuning. Restricting adaptation in this way is intended to preserve pretrained semantic representations while limiting the capacity to memorize familiar fake patterns. Experiments report stronger generalization to unseen fake patterns. Together, the results support combining pair-based training with restrained adaptation to improve detection beyond the synthetic examples encountered during training.
summary.tldr: BPL combines comparisons of related real–fake image pairs with bias-only fine-tuning to improve detection of unfamiliar synthetic patterns.

title: BPL: Generalizable Deepfake Detection via Bias-only Pair-aware Learning

abstract: Real-world multimodal learning is often hindered by missing modalities. While Incomplete Multimodal Learning (IML) has gained traction, existing methods typically rely on the unrealistic assumption of full-modal availability during training to provide reconstruction supervision or cross-modal priors. This paper tackles the more challenging setting of IML under training-time incomplete observations, which precludes reliance on a "God’s eye view" of complete data. We propose LIMSSR (LLM-Driven Incomplete Multimodal Sequence-to-Score Reasoning), a framework that reformulates this challenge as a conditional sequence reasoning task. LIMSSR leverages the semantic reasoning capabilities of Large Language Models via Prompt-Guided Context-Aware Modality Imputation and Multidimensional Representation Fusion to infer latent semantics from available contexts without direct reconstruction. To mitigate hallucinations, we introduce a Mask-Aware Dual-Path Aggregation to dynamically calibrate inference uncertainty. Extensive experiments on three Action Quality Assessment datasets demonstrate that LIMSSR significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baselines without relying on complete training data, establishing a new paradigm for data-efficient multimodal learning. Code is available at https://github.com/XuHuangbiao/LIMSSR.

paragraphs: Multimodal systems often encounter missing inputs, but methods for handling them commonly assume complete examples are available during training. Those examples provide reconstruction targets or relationships between modalities. LIMSSR addresses a harder setting in which training observations themselves are incomplete, so the model cannot rely on a complete view of every example.

The framework treats prediction as conditional sequence reasoning. It uses a language model's semantic capabilities to infer missing latent meaning from available context through prompt-guided modality imputation and multidimensional representation fusion. Its aim is to recover useful semantic information for scoring without directly reconstructing the missing observations.

Because inferred information can be unreliable, a mask-aware dual-path aggregation mechanism dynamically calibrates inference uncertainty and is designed to mitigate hallucinations. Experiments on three Action Quality Assessment datasets report significant improvements over state-of-the-art baselines without complete training data. The findings support combining contextual semantic inference with explicit awareness of which modalities are missing in this challenging training setting.
summary.tldr: LIMSSR uses language-model reasoning and uncertainty-aware fusion to assess actions when multimodal data is incomplete even during training.

title: LIMSSR: LLM-Driven Sequence-to-Score Reasoning under Training-Time Incomplete Multimodal Observations

abstract: The Neural Tangent Kernel is a theoretical framework for understanding the training dynamics of neural networks. However, standard NTK and its variants fail to properly depict the finetuning of foundation models, as they neglect the preconditioning effects of adaptive gradients. To bridge this gap, we propose the Optimizer Aware Kernel (OAK), which incorporates the optimizer’s influence into standard NTK framework by a preconditioner estimation technique. Furthermore, we conduct an analysis to answer: when and why kernel regime fails in finetuning. We derive explicit error bounds showing that the collapse of kernel regime is primarily due to the cumulative training effects and the task discrepancy between pretraining and finetuning. Theoretically, we justify OAK’s preconditioner estimation by bounding its error term. Empirically, experiments on various model architectures show both the effectiveness of the OAK method and validity of our arguments on kernel regime collapse.

paragraphs: The neural tangent kernel provides a theoretical lens on how neural networks train. This paper argues that standard versions miss an important feature of foundation-model fine-tuning: adaptive optimizers change the scaling of gradient updates. Ignoring that preconditioning can make a kernel description fail to reflect the actual training process.

The proposed Optimizer Aware Kernel, or OAK, incorporates an estimate of the optimizer's preconditioning into the kernel framework. The authors bound the error of that estimate, providing theoretical support for the added component. This makes optimizer behavior an explicit part of the approximation rather than treating it as irrelevant to the model's dynamics.

The paper also investigates when the kernel regime breaks down during fine-tuning. Its error bounds identify accumulated training effects and the discrepancy between pretraining and fine-tuning tasks as primary contributors. Experiments across several architectures support both OAK's effectiveness and the explanation of kernel-regime collapse. The contribution therefore combines a more optimizer-sensitive approximation with an account of why such approximations can cease to describe training well.
summary.tldr: OAK incorporates adaptive-optimizer preconditioning into neural tangent kernels and analyzes how accumulated training and task differences undermine kernel approximations.

title: Preconditioning Neural Tangent Kernel for Adaptive Optimization

abstract: Single-pass uncertainty quantification (UQ) methods for classification represent uncertainty by predicting a tractable distribution over the class probability vector. While existing approaches primarily focus on enhancing the expressiveness of this distribution, they often provide limited insight into how predictive uncertainty is structured and aggregated, resulting in weak interpretability. We introduce the courtroom analogy, which conceptualizes uncertainty-aware classification as a structured debate among class-specific advocates. Each advocate forms a probabilistic opinion, and a final verdict is reached by aggregating these opinions using input-dependent plausibility weights. In this framework, each advocate’s opinion is modeled as a Dirichlet distribution whose concentration parameter is decomposed into shared evidence and class-specific advocacy. This yields a structured mixture of Dirichlet distributions with semantically interpretable parameters. To instantiate this formulation, we propose Mixture of Dirichlet EXperts (MoDEX), a single-pass neural architecture that predicts the courtroom parameters, enabling efficient and expressive UQ while explicitly modeling uncertainty aggregation. We demonstrate that MoDEX enjoys strong theoretical properties and achieves state-of-the-art UQ performance across diverse benchmarks, yielding interpretable uncertainty estimates with meaningful semantics.

paragraphs: A classifier can express uncertainty by predicting a distribution over possible class-probability vectors. However, making that distribution more flexible does not necessarily clarify where uncertainty comes from or how different sources are combined. This paper introduces a courtroom analogy to make the internal structure of an uncertainty estimate easier to interpret.

Each class has an advocate that supplies a probabilistic opinion. The final prediction combines those opinions using plausibility weights that depend on the input. Each opinion is a Dirichlet distribution, with its concentration parameters divided into shared evidence and class-specific advocacy. Together, these components form a structured mixture whose parameters have explicit roles in representing and aggregating uncertainty.

The authors implement this formulation as Mixture of Dirichlet EXperts, or MoDEX. A single neural-network pass predicts the courtroom parameters, combining efficient inference with a flexible uncertainty representation. The paper reports strong theoretical properties and state-of-the-art uncertainty quantification across diverse benchmarks. Its central contribution is to make the combination of competing class opinions part of the model's interpretable structure.
summary.tldr: MoDEX produces interpretable uncertainty estimates by combining class-specific probabilistic opinions in a single neural-network pass.

title: Courtroom Analogy: New Perspective on Uncertainty-Aware Classification

abstract: Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) exhibit sophisticated reasoning but remain susceptible to object hallucination. Deviating from the prevailing attention intensity assumption, we reveal a deeper dynamic structural misalignment: hallucination is triggered at decision-critical steps where specific attention heads, acting as risky mediators, decouple from visual evidence to lock onto language priors. This establishes a pathological shortcut that bypasses visual grounding. To dismantle this, we propose Fox (Faithfulness and Observational-flow via eXpression-rectification), a training-free inference-time framework. Fox diagnoses structural misalignment using a visual attention entropy probe to localize risky mediators unsupervisedly. We then execute a targeted causal intervention via numerical logit saturation to physically sever the shortcut path. Finally, a conflict-gated cooperative decoding strategy reconciles interventional faithfulness with observational fluency. Extensive experiments demonstrate that Fox achieves state-of-the-art performance, outperforming SID by 29.1% while preserving linguistic richness. Code is available at https://github.com/Cc2021start/Fox.

paragraphs: Large vision-language models can describe objects unsupported by an image. This paper attributes such hallucination to a structural failure at critical generation steps: particular attention heads detach from visual evidence and follow language priors. These heads act as intermediaries in a shortcut that allows generation to bypass visual grounding.

Fox is a training-free inference framework that targets this behavior. It first uses a probe based on visual attention entropy to identify risky heads without supervision. It then applies a targeted causal intervention through numerical logit saturation to sever the identified shortcut. A conflict-gated cooperative decoding strategy combines the intervention's contribution to faithfulness with the fluency of ordinary decoding.

The authors report state-of-the-art experimental performance, including a 29.1% improvement over SID while maintaining linguistic richness. The approach matters because it treats hallucination as a problem of which internal pathways control a decision, extending beyond attention intensity alone. Its reported results show that targeted intervention and cooperative decoding can improve visual faithfulness while preserving expressive language in the evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: Fox identifies and interrupts attention pathways that bypass visual evidence, improving grounded decoding without retraining.

title: Dismantling Pathological Shortcuts: A Causal Framework for Faithful LVLM Decoding

abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly integrated into financial workflows, but evaluation practice has not kept up. Finance-specific biases can inflate performance, contaminate backtests, and make reported results useless for any deployment claim. We identify five recurring biases in financial LLM applications. They include look-ahead bias, survivorship bias, narrative bias, objective bias, and cost bias. These biases break financial tasks in distinct ways and they often compound to create an illusion of validity. We reviewed 164 papers from 2023 to 2025 and found that no single bias is discussed in more than 28 percent of studies. This position paper argues that bias in financial LLM systems requires explicit attention and that structural validity should be enforced before any result is used to support a deployment claim. We propose a Structural Validity Framework and an evaluation checklist with minimal requirements for bias diagnosis and future system design. The material is available at https://github.com/Eleanorkong/Awesome-Financial-LLM-Bias-Mitigation.

paragraphs: This paper argues that financial language-model evaluations can look convincing while failing to support deployment claims. Biases specific to financial applications can inflate measured performance and contaminate backtests. The concern is the validity of the evaluation setup itself, because impressive results can arise from a structure that does not provide credible evidence.

The authors identify five recurring categories: look-ahead, survivorship, narrative, objective, and cost bias. These affect tasks in different ways and can compound. In a review of 164 papers published from 2023 through 2025, no individual bias receives discussion in more than 28% of studies. The authors argue that this scrutiny should precede using a result to justify deployment. Their broader contribution is to make validity checks an explicit part of financial LLM evaluation instead of allowing reported performance to carry that burden alone.
summary.tldr: Financial LLM results should undergo explicit checks for five recurring biases before supporting deployment claims.

abstract: Nonnegative matrix factorization (NMF) was popularized as a tool for data mining by Lee and Seung in 1999. NMF attempts to approximate a matrix with nonnegative entries by a product of two low-rank matrices, also with nonnegative entries. We propose an algorithm called rank-one downdate (R1D) for computing a NMF that is partly motivated by singular value decomposition. This algorithm computes the dominant singular values and vectors of adaptively determined submatrices of a matrix. On each iteration, R1D extracts a rank-one submatrix from the dataset according to an objective function. We establish a theoretical result that maximizing this objective function corresponds to correctly classifying articles in a nearly separable corpus. We also provide computational experiments showing the success of this method in identifying features in realistic datasets. The method is much faster than either LSI or other NMF routines.

paragraphs: Nonnegative matrix factorization approximates a nonnegative data matrix using two smaller nonnegative factors. This paper proposes rank-one downdate, or R1D, as a way to compute such a factorization. The method is partly inspired by singular value decomposition and builds its representation through components extracted from adaptively chosen portions of the data.

At each iteration, R1D extracts a rank-one submatrix according to an objective function. It computes dominant singular values and vectors of the selected submatrices, connecting the iterative extraction procedure to established matrix decomposition ideas. The adaptive choice of submatrices determines which portion of the dataset contributes to the component being identified.

The authors establish that maximizing their objective corresponds to correctly classifying articles when the corpus is nearly separable. That condition is part of the theoretical result. Computational experiments also show successful feature identification in realistic datasets, and the paper reports that the method is much faster than LSI and other NMF routines. Together, these contributions connect the extraction objective to a conditional guarantee and practical computational results.
summary.tldr: R1D computes nonnegative factorizations through adaptive rank-one extraction, with a nearly separable-corpus guarantee and strong reported computational performance.

title: Nonnegative matrix factorization via rank-one downdate

abstract: The infinite hidden Markov model is a nonparametric extension of the widely used hidden Markov model. Our paper introduces a new inference algorithm for the infinite hidden Markov model called beam sampling. Beam sampling combines slice sampling, which limits the number of states considered at each time step to a finite number, with dynamic programming, which samples whole state trajectories efficiently. Our algorithm typically outperforms the Gibbs sampler and is more robust. We present applications of iHMM inference using the beam sampler on changepoint detection and text prediction problems.

Our algorithm typically outperforms the Gibbs sampler and is more robust. We present applications of iHMM inference using the beam sampler on changepoint detection and text prediction problems.

paragraphs: The infinite hidden Markov model extends sequence modeling to a setting with a flexible hidden-state space. Working with that model requires an inference procedure that can handle its potentially unbounded collection of states. This paper introduces beam sampling as a way to carry out that inference efficiently.

The method combines slice sampling with dynamic programming. Slice sampling restricts the states considered at each time step to a finite set. Dynamic programming then makes it possible to sample complete hidden-state trajectories efficiently. The two components address complementary parts of the problem: controlling the states under consideration and coordinating inference across the sequence.

The authors report that beam sampling typically outperforms the Gibbs sampler and offers greater robustness. They demonstrate its use in changepoint detection and text prediction. These applications show how the inference method supports both identifying changes in a sequence and predicting its content. The performance claim is typical rather than universal, while the methodological contribution is the combination of finite per-step computation with whole-trajectory sampling.
summary.tldr: Beam sampling combines slice sampling and dynamic programming for efficient, typically more robust inference in infinite hidden Markov models.

title: Beam sampling for the infinite hidden Markov model

abstract: We propose an unbounded-depth, hierarchical, Bayesian nonparametric model for discrete sequence data. This model can be estimated from a single training sequence, yet shares statistical strength between subsequent symbol predictive distributions in such a way that predictive performance generalizes well. The model builds on a specific parameterization of an unbounded-depth hierarchical Pitman-Yor process. We introduce analytic marginalization steps (using coagulation operators) to reduce this model to one that can be represented in time and space linear in the length of the training sequence. We show how to perform inference in such a model without truncation approximation and introduce fragmentation operators necessary to do predictive inference. We demonstrate the sequence memoizer by using it as a language model, achieving state-of-the-art results.

This model can be estimated from a single training sequence, yet shares statistical strength between subsequent symbol predictive distributions in such a way that predictive performance generalizes well. The model builds on a specific parameterization of an unbounded-depth hierarchical Pitman-Yor process. We introduce analytic marginalization steps (using coagulation operators) to reduce this model to one that can be represented in time and space linear in the length of the training sequence. We show how to perform inference in such a model without truncation approximation and introduce fragmentation operators necessary to do predictive inference. We demonstrate the sequence memoizer by using it as a language model, achieving state-of-the-art results.

paragraphs: The sequence memoizer models sequences of discrete symbols without imposing a fixed maximum depth on their history. It uses a hierarchical Bayesian nonparametric construction, allowing predictive distributions for successive symbols to share statistical information. The abstract states that the model can be estimated from a single training sequence while still generalizing well.

The computational challenge is making this unlimited hierarchy manageable. The authors use a particular hierarchical Pitman–Yor process and analytically remove parts of the model through operations called coagulation operators. The resulting representation takes time and space proportional to the training sequence length. This makes the unbounded construction usable without replacing it with a hierarchy cut off at an arbitrary depth.

The paper also develops inference without a truncation approximation and introduces fragmentation operators needed for prediction. In a language-modeling demonstration, the sequence memoizer achieves results described as state of the art. The contribution combines flexible use of sequence history with a representation whose computational requirements grow linearly with the observed sequence.
summary.tldr: The sequence memoizer models unlimited sequence history while retaining a linear-size representation and achieving strong language-modeling results.

title: A stochastic memoizer for sequence data

abstract: Deep generative models with multiple hidden layers have been shown to be able to learn meaningful and compact representations of data. In this work we propose deep energy models, a class of models that use a deep feedforward neural network to model the energy landscape that defines a probabilistic model. We are able to efficiently train all layers of our model at the same time, allowing the lower layers of the model to adapt to the training of the higher layers, producing better generative models. We evaluate the generative performance of our models on natural images and demonstrate that joint training of multiple layers yields qualitative and quantitative improvements over greedy layerwise training. We further generalize our models beyond the commonly used sigmoidal neural networks and show how a deep extension of the product of Student-t distributions model achieves good generative performance. Finally, we introduce a discriminative extension of our model and demonstrate that it outperforms other fully-connected models on object recognition on the NORB dataset.

paragraphs: This paper introduces deep energy models, which use a deep feedforward neural network to define the energy landscape of a probabilistic model. The network therefore helps determine how the model represents the distribution of data. The work builds on the ability of deep generative models to learn compact and meaningful representations.

A central feature is efficient joint training of all layers. This allows lower layers to adapt as higher layers learn, instead of fixing their behavior through greedy layer-by-layer training. On natural images, the authors report both qualitative and quantitative improvements in generative performance from training multiple layers together.

The paper also extends the model family beyond sigmoidal neural networks. A deep version of a product of Student-t distributions achieves good generative performance, showing that the approach accommodates another modeling form. Finally, a discriminative extension outperforms other fully connected models on NORB object recognition. These results support the approach for both modeling data distributions and learning predictors in the evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: Deep energy models enable joint training across layers, improving natural-image generation and supporting a strong object-recognition extension.

title: Learning Deep Energy Models

abstract: Bayesian models offer great flexibility for clustering applications—Bayesian nonparametrics can be used for modeling infinite mixtures, and hierarchical Bayesian models can be utilized for shared clusters across multiple data sets. For the most part, such flexibility is lacking in classical clustering methods such as k-means. In this paper, we revisit the k-means clustering algorithm from a Bayesian nonparametric viewpoint. Inspired by the asymptotic connection between k-means and mixtures of Gaussians, we show that a Gibbs sampling algorithm for the Dirichlet process mixture approaches a hard clustering algorithm in the limit, and further that the resulting algorithm monotonically minimizes an elegant underlying k-means-like clustering objective that includes a penalty for the number of clusters. We generalize this analysis to the case of clustering multiple data sets through a similar asymptotic argument with the hierarchical Dirichlet process. We also discuss further extensions that highlight the benefits of our analysis: i) a spectral relaxation involving thresholded eigenvectors, and ii) a normalized cut graph clustering algorithm that does not fix the number of clusters in the graph.

paragraphs: Bayesian clustering models can accommodate an unbounded collection of clusters and share clusters across datasets. Classical methods such as k-means usually offer less flexibility. This paper investigates whether useful features of Bayesian nonparametric models can be transferred into simpler hard-clustering procedures through an asymptotic connection.

The authors show that a Gibbs sampler for a Dirichlet process mixture approaches a hard-clustering algorithm in a limit. The resulting algorithm monotonically reduces a k-means-like objective containing a penalty for the number of clusters. That penalty makes cluster count part of the optimization criterion, linking the flexibility of the mixture model to an explicit clustering objective.

The analysis extends to multiple datasets through a related argument involving the hierarchical Dirichlet process. The paper also discusses a spectral relaxation using thresholded eigenvectors and a normalized-cut graph clustering algorithm without a fixed cluster count. These extensions show how the same analytical perspective can generate several clustering formulations. The monotonic improvement result concerns the stated objective and does not itself assert a globally optimal clustering.
summary.tldr: Asymptotic analysis of Bayesian nonparametric models yields k-means-like algorithms with a cluster-count penalty and extensions to shared and graph clustering.

title: Revisiting k-means: New Algorithms via Bayesian Nonparametrics
